sections.html:
Propositional Logic for the Hazardous Warehouse

Goal: Encode the Hazardous Warehouse environment in propositional logic and use logical inference to determine safe squares.

Setup: Consider a simplified \(3 \times 3\) warehouse grid. The robot starts at \((1,1)\). The environment contains:

  • At least one damaged floor section (locations unknown)
  • At least one malfunctioning forklift (locations unknown)
  • One package (location unknown)

Use the following propositional symbols:

  • \(D_{i,j}\): Damaged floor at \((i,j)\)
  • \(F_{i,j}\): Forklift at \((i,j)\)
  • \(P_{i,j}\): Package at \((i,j)\)
  • \(C_{i,j}\): Creaking perceived at \((i,j)\)
  • \(R_{i,j}\): Rumbling perceived at \((i,j)\)
  • \(S_{i,j}\): Square \((i,j)\) is safe

Tasks:

  1. Encode the physics: Write propositional sentences that express:
    • Creaking at a location iff damaged floor in an adjacent square
    • Rumbling at a location iff forklift in an adjacent square
    • A square is safe iff it has no damaged floor and no forklift
  2. Initial knowledge: Write sentences expressing:
    • The starting square \((1,1)\) is safe
    • At least one square has damaged floor
    • At least one square has the forklift
  3. Scenario reasoning: The robot is at \((1,1)\) and perceives no creaking and no rumbling.
    • Write the percept as propositional sentences
    • Use logical inference to determine which squares are provably safe
    • Show your reasoning step by step
  4. Exploration: The robot moves to \((2,1)\) and perceives creaking but no rumbling.
    • Add the new percepts to the knowledge base
    • Determine what new conclusions can be drawn about damaged floor locations
    • Which squares are now known to be dangerous? Which remain uncertain?

Deliverables:

  • Written propositional sentences for parts 1-2
  • Step-by-step logical derivations for parts 3-4
  • A diagram showing the \(3 \times 3\) grid with safe/dangerous/unknown labels after each observation

First-Order Logic Translation

Goal: Practice translating natural language statements about the Hazardous Warehouse into first-order logic.

Predicates available: - \(\text{Damaged}(l)\): Location \(l\) has damaged floor - \(\text{Forklift}(l)\): The forklift is at location \(l\) - \(\text{Package}(l)\): The package is at location \(l\) - \(\text{Safe}(l)\): Location \(l\) is safe to enter - \(\text{Adjacent}(l_1, l_2)\): Locations \(l_1\) and \(l_2\) are adjacent - \(\text{Creaking}(l)\): Creaking is perceived at \(l\) - \(\text{Rumbling}(l)\): Rumbling is perceived at \(l\) - \(\text{Visited}(l)\): The robot has visited \(l\) - \(\text{At}(r, l)\): Robot \(r\) is at location \(l\) - \(\text{Carrying}(r, p)\): Robot \(r\) is carrying package \(p\)

Translate each statement to FOL:

  1. "Every location adjacent to a damaged floor has creaking."

  2. "The robot should never enter an unsafe location."

  3. "If a location has no creaking and no rumbling, all adjacent locations are safe."

  4. "There is exactly one forklift in the warehouse."

  5. "If the robot is carrying the package and the robot is at the exit, the mission is complete."

  6. "A location is dangerous if it has damaged floor or if the forklift is there."

  7. "Every visited location is safe." (This reflects the fact that the robot survived visiting it.)

  8. "If rumbling is heard at every location adjacent to \(L\), then the forklift is at \(L\)."

Bonus: For each translation, identify whether the statement uses universal quantification, existential quantification, or both.

Forward and Backward Chaining Trace

Goal: Trace through forward chaining and backward chaining algorithms on a small knowledge base.

Knowledge Base:

Facts: - \(\text{Adjacent}(L_1, L_2)\) - \(\text{Adjacent}(L_1, L_4)\) - \(\text{Adjacent}(L_2, L_1)\) - \(\text{Adjacent}(L_2, L_3)\) - \(\text{Adjacent}(L_2, L_5)\) - \(\text{Adjacent}(L_4, L_1)\) - \(\text{Adjacent}(L_4, L_5)\) - \(\neg\text{Creaking}(L_1)\) - \(\text{Creaking}(L_2)\) - \(\neg\text{Rumbling}(L_1)\) - \(\neg\text{Rumbling}(L_2)\) - \(\text{Safe}(L_1)\) (starting square)

Rules: - R1: \(\forall l.\, \neg\text{Creaking}(l) \Rightarrow \forall l'.\, \text{Adjacent}(l, l') \Rightarrow \neg\text{Damaged}(l')\) - R2: \(\forall l.\, \neg\text{Rumbling}(l) \Rightarrow \forall l'.\, \text{Adjacent}(l, l') \Rightarrow \neg\text{Forklift}(l')\) - R3: \(\forall l.\, \neg\text{Damaged}(l) \land \neg\text{Forklift}(l) \Rightarrow \text{Safe}(l)\)

Grid layout (for reference):

L4 -- L5
|     |
L1 -- L2 -- L3

Tasks:

  1. Forward chaining: Starting from the initial facts, trace the forward chaining process.

    • What new facts are derived in each iteration?
    • Continue until no new facts can be derived.
    • List all derived facts in order.

  2. Backward chaining: Query: Is \(L_5\) safe?

    • Trace the backward chaining process step by step.
    • Show which rules are used and what subgoals are generated.
    • Does the query succeed or fail? Why?

  3. Unification: For each rule application in your traces, explicitly show the substitution (unifier) used.

  4. Comparison: Which approach (forward or backward) examined fewer rules/facts for this query? When would the other approach be preferable?

Building a Knowledge-Based Agent (Guided)

Goal: Follow the walkthrough in [@k7] to build your own knowledge-based agent for the Hazardous Warehouse using Z3.

Setup: You will need z3-solver (install via pip install z3-solver) and hazardous_warehouse_env.py in your working directory.

Tasks:

  1. Setup and exploration: Create a new Python file. Import Bool, Bools, Or, And, Not, Solver, unsat from z3, and HazardousWarehouseEnv from hazardous_warehouse_env.py. Verify you can:

    • Create boolean variables: P, Q = Bools('P Q')
    • Add a biconditional: s.add(P == Q) and a fact: s.add(P)
    • Check satisfiability: s.check() should return sat
    • Inspect the model: s.model() should show P = True, Q = True
    • Implement the z3_entails function from [@k7] using push/pop. Verify that after adding P == Q and P, the solver entails Q.

  2. Symbols and physics: Write the Bool variable helper functions (damaged, forklift_at, creaking_at, rumbling_at, safe) and build_warehouse_kb() as described in [@k7]. After building the solver, verify it is satisfiable (solver.check() returns sat).

  3. Manual reasoning: Before building the full agent, use your solver to replicate the reasoning from [@x9]:

    • Create the solver with build_warehouse_kb()
    • TELL the solver the percepts at \((1,1)\): no creaking, no rumbling
    • ASK whether \((2,1)\) is safe. ASK whether \((1,2)\) is safe. Both should return True.
    • TELL the solver the percepts at \((2,1)\): creaking, no rumbling
    • ASK whether \((3,1)\) is safe. What about \(\neg\mathit{OK}_{3,1}\)? What does the solver conclude about \((2,2)\)?
    • TELL the solver the percepts at \((1,2)\): rumbling, no creaking
    • ASK again about \((3,1)\), \((2,2)\), and \((1,3)\). The solver should now identify the damaged floor and forklift locations.

  4. Agent loop: Implement the full WarehouseKBAgent class with the perceive \(\to\) tell \(\to\) ask \(\to\) act cycle described in [@k7]. Include path planning (BFS through safe squares) and the action conversion logic.

  5. Testing: Run your agent on the example layout (using configure_rn_example_layout from hazardous_warehouse_viz.py). Does it retrieve the package and exit successfully? Record the number of steps and total reward.

  6. Reflection: In 2–3 sentences, describe a situation where the agent either gets stuck (cannot find the package) or behaves conservatively (avoids squares that a human would risk). What additional reasoning capability would help?

Deliverables: Your Python file with the agent implementation, plus a brief summary (replace the template's README.md file) of your results and observations from tasks 3, 5, and 6.

Bonus: Extend the agent to use the emergency shutdown device. The agent should reason about the forklift's location and, when it can identify the forklift along a line from its current position, fire the shutdown device before proceeding.

Building a FOL Agent with Z3 (Guided)

Goal: Follow the walkthrough in [@z3] to extend the propositional agent from [@k7] to use quantified first-order logic, and compare the two encodings.

Setup: You will need z3-solver (install via pip install z3-solver), hazardous_warehouse_env.py, and hazardous_warehouse_viz.py in your working directory. You should have a working propositional agent from [@exe:build-kb-agent].

Tasks:

  1. FOL domain setup: Create a new Python file. Import DeclareSort, Function, BoolSort, Const, ForAll, Exists, Distinct from z3 (in addition to the Or, And, Not, Solver, unsat you already know from [@k7]). Verify you can:

    • Create a sort: Location = DeclareSort('Location')
    • Create a predicate: P = Function('P', Location, BoolSort())
    • Create constants: L1 = Const('L1', Location)
    • Write a quantified sentence: ForAll(L, P(L)) where L = Const('L', Location)
    • Add the sentence to a solver and check satisfiability.

  2. Quantified physics rules: Implement build_warehouse_kb_fol() as described in [@z3]. This includes:

    • Location constants for each grid square
    • Domain closure (ForAll(L, Or([L == loc[...] for ...])) and Distinct)
    • Closed-world adjacency facts
    • Three quantified physics rules: creaking, rumbling, and safety
    • Verify the solver is satisfiable after building the KB.

  3. Manual reasoning: Replicate the reasoning walkthrough from [@k7:walkthrough] using the FOL KB:

    • Build the KB with build_warehouse_kb_fol()
    • TELL the solver: no creaking, no rumbling at \((1,1)\)—using self.preds['Creaking'](loc[(1,1)]) instead of creaking_at(1, 1)
    • ASK: is \((2,1)\) safe? Is \((1,2)\) safe? (Both should return True.)
    • TELL: creaking, no rumbling at \((2,1)\)
    • ASK: is \((3,1)\) safe? Is \((2,2)\) safe? (Both should be unknown.)
    • TELL: no creaking, rumbling at \((1,2)\)
    • ASK: is \((2,2)\) safe? Is \((3,1)\) dangerous? Is \((1,3)\) dangerous? (All True.)
    • Verify your results match the propositional agent's conclusions.

  4. Full agent: Implement the WarehouseZ3Agent class with the same decision loop as [@k7]. The key difference is using FOL predicates applied to location constants instead of grounded Bool variables. Run it on the example layout using configure_rn_example_layout. Record the number of steps and total reward. Confirm the results are identical to the propositional agent.

  5. Domain closure investigation (challenge): Remove the domain closure axiom from build_warehouse_kb_fol() and re-run the manual reasoning from task 3. Which entailment queries now fail? Explain why Z3 can construct a satisfying model where no real grid square is damaged, even when creaking is perceived. Restore the axiom when done.

  6. Reflection: In 3–4 sentences, compare the propositional and FOL encodings. Address: (a) How does rule count scale with grid size for each approach? (b) Which encoding is more readable? (c) What is the role of domain closure, and why doesn't the propositional encoding need it?

Deliverables: Your Python file with the FOL agent, the output trace from task 4, and the written comparison from task 6.

Propositional vs. First-Order Expressiveness

Goal: Understand the expressiveness gap between propositional and first-order logic.

Part A: Propositional Encoding Cost

Consider an \(n \times n\) warehouse grid. Count the number of propositional sentences needed to encode:

  1. The adjacency relation (which squares are adjacent to which)
  2. The creaking rule: "Creaking at \(L\) iff damaged floor adjacent to \(L\)"
  3. The safety rule: "Safe at \(L\) iff no damaged floor and no forklift at \(L\)"

Express your answers as functions of \(n\). What happens as \(n\) grows to 100?

Part B: FOL Comparison

Write the same rules in first-order logic. How many sentences are needed regardless of \(n\)?

Part C: Translation Challenge

Can the following statement be expressed in propositional logic? If so, how? If not, why not?

"There is exactly one damaged floor section in the entire warehouse."

Write the statement in FOL. Then attempt a propositional encoding for a \(3 \times 3\) grid. How does the complexity scale?

Part D: Practical Implications

A real warehouse might be \(100 \times 100\) with 10,000 locations. Discuss:

  1. Is propositional encoding practical at this scale?
  2. What restrictions on FOL would make inference tractable?
  3. How might a hybrid approach work (FOL for general rules, propositionalization for local reasoning)?

Model Checking and Entailment

Goal: Practice model checking by enumerating interpretations.

Setup: Consider a tiny \(2 \times 2\) warehouse with squares \(A\), \(B\), \(C\), \(D\) arranged as:

C -- D
|    |
A -- B

Use propositional symbols: - \(D_X\): Damaged floor at square \(X\) (for \(X \in \{A, B, C, D\}\)) - \(C_X\): Creaking at square \(X\)

Knowledge Base: - \(C_A \Leftrightarrow D_B \lor D_C\) (creaking at A iff damage at adjacent B or C) - \(C_B \Leftrightarrow D_A \lor D_D\) (creaking at B iff damage at adjacent A or D) - \(\neg D_A\) (starting square A is safe) - \(\neg C_A\) (no creaking at A) - \(C_B\) (creaking at B)

Tasks:

  1. List all propositional symbols in this KB.

  2. Enumerate all interpretations (there are \(2^n\) for \(n\) symbols—use only the 4 damage symbols since creaking is determined by the rules).

  3. Filter models: Which interpretations satisfy all sentences in the KB?

  4. Check entailment: Does the KB entail \(D_D\)? Does it entail \(\neg D_B\)? Does it entail \(D_B \lor D_C\)?

  5. Practical reflection: With 4 damage symbols, we have 16 interpretations. How many interpretations would a \(10 \times 10\) warehouse have? Is model enumeration practical at that scale?

Logic Encoding and Inference

A fire-response robot inspects a small building with three rooms: A, B, and C. The adjacency is:

   A --- B --- C

(A and B are adjacent; B and C are adjacent; A and C are not adjacent.)

Each room may or may not contain a fire. Each room has a smoke detector. Variables: \(F_A, F_B, F_C\) (fire present) and \(S_A, S_B, S_C\) (detector positive).

Rules encoded (given to you):

  • Rule 1 (fire causes alarm): \(F_A \Rightarrow S_A\), \(F_B \Rightarrow S_B\), \(F_C \Rightarrow S_C\)
  • Rule 2 (alarm means fire nearby): \(S_A \Rightarrow F_A \lor F_B\), \(S_B \Rightarrow F_A \lor F_B \lor F_C\), \(S_C \Rightarrow F_B \lor F_C\)

Observations: \(S_A\) = true, \(\neg S_B\) = true (B's detector is negative), \(S_C\) = true.

First derivation (given): The contrapositive of \(F_B \Rightarrow S_B\) is \(\neg S_B \Rightarrow \neg F_B\). Since \(\neg S_B\) is observed, we conclude \(\neg F_B\) by modus tollens.

(a) Using \(\neg F_B\) and Rule 2 for room A (\(S_A \Rightarrow F_A \lor F_B\)), derive whether Room A has fire. Name the inference rule(s) you use.

(b) Using \(\neg F_B\) and Rule 2 for room C, derive whether Room C has fire.

(c) Translate Rule 1 into first-order logic using a predicate \(\text{Fire}(x)\) and \(\text{Alarm}(x)\) with a universal quantifier. Recall: FOL uses variables, predicates, and quantifiers like \(\forall\) and \(\exists\) ([@y2]). What advantage does the FOL version have over writing three separate propositional sentences?

(d) Recall: \(\text{KB} \models \alpha\) (entailment) means \(\alpha\) is true in every model where KB is true, whereas \(\alpha\) is merely consistent with KB if there exists some model where both are true ([@def:entailment]). Is your conclusion \(\neg F_B\) in (b) entailed by the KB, or only consistent with it? Explain in one sentence.

:::

exe:propositional-warehouse.content:
Grid layout (for reference):

(1,3) -- (2,3) -- (3,3)
  |        |        |
(1,2) -- (2,2) -- (3,2)
  |        |        |
(1,1) -- (2,1) -- (3,1)

1. Physics encoding

Creaking rules — 9 biconditionals, one per square. Creaking at \((i,j)\) iff damaged floor in at least one adjacent square:

\[C_{1,1} \Leftrightarrow D_{2,1} \lor D_{1,2}\] \[C_{2,1} \Leftrightarrow D_{1,1} \lor D_{3,1} \lor D_{2,2}\] \[C_{3,1} \Leftrightarrow D_{2,1} \lor D_{3,2}\] \[C_{1,2} \Leftrightarrow D_{1,1} \lor D_{2,2} \lor D_{1,3}\] \[C_{2,2} \Leftrightarrow D_{2,1} \lor D_{1,2} \lor D_{3,2} \lor D_{2,3}\] \[C_{3,2} \Leftrightarrow D_{3,1} \lor D_{2,2} \lor D_{3,3}\] \[C_{1,3} \Leftrightarrow D_{1,2} \lor D_{2,3}\] \[C_{2,3} \Leftrightarrow D_{2,2} \lor D_{1,3} \lor D_{3,3}\] \[C_{3,3} \Leftrightarrow D_{2,3} \lor D_{3,2}\]

Rumbling rules — 9 biconditionals with the same structure, replacing \(C\) with \(N\) and \(D\) with \(F\):

\[R_{1,1} \Leftrightarrow F_{2,1} \lor F_{1,2}\] \[R_{2,1} \Leftrightarrow F_{1,1} \lor F_{3,1} \lor F_{2,2}\] \[R_{3,1} \Leftrightarrow F_{2,1} \lor F_{3,2}\] \[R_{1,2} \Leftrightarrow F_{1,1} \lor F_{2,2} \lor F_{1,3}\] \[R_{2,2} \Leftrightarrow F_{2,1} \lor F_{1,2} \lor F_{3,2} \lor F_{2,3}\] \[R_{3,2} \Leftrightarrow F_{3,1} \lor F_{2,2} \lor F_{3,3}\] \[R_{1,3} \Leftrightarrow F_{1,2} \lor F_{2,3}\] \[R_{2,3} \Leftrightarrow F_{2,2} \lor F_{1,3} \lor F_{3,3}\] \[R_{3,3} \Leftrightarrow F_{2,3} \lor F_{3,2}\]

Safety rules — 9 biconditionals:

\[S_{i,j} \Leftrightarrow \neg D_{i,j} \land \neg F_{i,j} \quad \text{for each } (i,j) \in \{1,2,3\}^2\]

Total: 27 propositional sentences encode the physics.

2. Initial knowledge

Starting square is safe:

\[S_{1,1}\]

which, combined with the safety biconditional, entails \(\neg D_{1,1} \land \neg F_{1,1}\).

At least one square has damaged floor:

\[D_{1,1} \lor D_{2,1} \lor D_{3,1} \lor D_{1,2} \lor D_{2,2} \lor D_{3,2} \lor D_{1,3} \lor D_{2,3} \lor D_{3,3}\]

At least one forklift — same structure with \(F\):

\[F_{1,1} \lor F_{2,1} \lor F_{3,1} \lor F_{1,2} \lor F_{2,2} \lor F_{3,2} \lor F_{1,3} \lor F_{2,3} \lor F_{3,3}\]

Total initial knowledge: \(1 + 1 + 1 = 3\) sentences.

3. Scenario reasoning

Percepts at \((1,1)\):

\[\neg C_{1,1}, \quad \neg R_{1,1}\]

Step 1: From \(\neg C_{1,1}\) and the creaking biconditional \(C_{1,1} \Leftrightarrow D_{2,1} \lor D_{1,2}\):

\[\neg C_{1,1} \Rightarrow \neg(D_{2,1} \lor D_{1,2}) \Rightarrow \neg D_{2,1} \land \neg D_{1,2}\]

Step 2: From \(\neg R_{1,1}\) and the rumbling biconditional \(R_{1,1} \Leftrightarrow F_{2,1} \lor F_{1,2}\):

\[\neg R_{1,1} \Rightarrow \neg(F_{2,1} \lor F_{1,2}) \Rightarrow \neg F_{2,1} \land \neg F_{1,2}\]

Step 3: Apply the safety biconditionals to the newly cleared squares:

  • \((2,1)\): \(\neg D_{2,1} \land \neg F_{2,1} \Rightarrow S_{2,1}\) ✓
  • \((1,2)\): \(\neg D_{1,2} \land \neg F_{1,2} \Rightarrow S_{1,2}\) ✓

Step 4: For all other squares — \((3,1), (2,2), (3,2), (1,3), (2,3), (3,3)\) — we have no information about either damage or forklift presence. Their safety cannot be determined.

Provably safe squares: \(\{(1,1),\; (2,1),\; (1,2)\}\).

Grid after observation at \((1,1)\):

  ?    ?    ?        (1,3)  (2,3)  (3,3)
  S    ?    ?        (1,2)  (2,2)  (3,2)
  S    S    ?        (1,1)  (2,1)  (3,1)

4. Exploration

New percepts at \((2,1)\):

\[C_{2,1}, \quad \neg R_{2,1}\]

Step 1: From \(C_{2,1}\) and \(C_{2,1} \Leftrightarrow D_{1,1} \lor D_{3,1} \lor D_{2,2}\):

\[D_{1,1} \lor D_{3,1} \lor D_{2,2}\]

We already know \(\neg D_{1,1}\) (starting square is safe), so:

\[D_{3,1} \lor D_{2,2}\]

Step 2: From \(\neg R_{2,1}\) and \(R_{2,1} \Leftrightarrow F_{1,1} \lor F_{3,1} \lor F_{2,2}\):

\[\neg F_{1,1} \land \neg F_{3,1} \land \neg F_{2,2}\]

Step 3: Forklift exclusions so far: \(\neg F_{1,1}, \neg F_{2,1}, \neg F_{1,2}, \neg F_{3,1}, \neg F_{2,2}\). The at-least-one-forklift constraint then tells us the forklift is at one or more of \((3,2), (1,3), (2,3), (3,3)\).

Step 4: Check safety of each unknown square:

Square Damage? Forklift? Safe?
\((3,1)\) Possible (\(D_{3,1} \lor D_{2,2}\)) \(\neg F_{3,1}\) Unknown
\((2,2)\) Possible (\(D_{3,1} \lor D_{2,2}\)) \(\neg F_{2,2}\) Unknown
\((3,2)\) Unknown Possible Unknown
\((1,3)\) Unknown Possible Unknown
\((2,3)\) Unknown Possible Unknown
\((3,3)\) Unknown Possible Unknown

No individual square is provably dangerous. However, we know \(D_{3,1} \lor D_{2,2}\), so at least one of \((3,1)\) and \((2,2)\) has damaged floor. Note that without an "exactly one" constraint, we cannot rule out damage at other unvisited squares either.

Grid after observation at \((2,1)\):

  ?    ?    ?        (1,3)  (2,3)  (3,3)
  S    ?    ?        (1,2)  (2,2)  (3,2)
  S    S    ?        (1,1)  (2,1)  (3,1)

Key new knowledge: at least one of \((3,1)\) and \((2,2)\) has damaged floor; the forklift is somewhere among the uncleared squares. The next useful move would be to explore \((1,2)\) — its percepts would help narrow down the remaining locations.
exe:propositional-warehouse.title: Propositional Logic for the Hazardous Warehouse

exe:z3-agent.content:
Tasks 1–4 are walked through step-by-step in [@z3]. Follow the code listings and explanations in that section to complete the FOL domain setup (task 1), quantified physics rules (task 2), manual reasoning walkthrough (task 3), and full agent implementation (task 4). The manual reasoning results should match those of the propositional agent from [@k7]; the agent should retrieve the package and exit with the same step count and reward.

5. Domain closure investigation

Removing the domain closure axiom (ForAll(L, Or([L == loc[...] ...])) and Distinct(...)) from build_warehouse_kb_fol() causes the elimination-based entailment queries in the manual reasoning trace to fail, while queries derived directly from negative percepts still succeed.

Queries that still work: After TELLing no creaking and no rumbling at \((1,1)\), the entailments \(\text{Safe}(L_{2,1})\) and \(\text{Safe}(L_{1,2})\) still hold. This is because the reasoning relies on ground adjacency facts: \(\text{Adjacent}(L_{1,1}, L_{2,1})\) is asserted, and \(\neg\text{Creaking}(L_{1,1})\) forces \(\neg\text{Damaged}(L_{2,1})\) via the quantified rule instantiated at \(L' = L_{2,1}\). No phantom location is involved—the conclusion follows directly from a ground fact and a universal instantiation. Similarly, after three percepts, \(\text{Safe}(L_{2,2})\) is still entailed because \(\neg\text{Damaged}(L_{2,2})\) follows from no creaking at \((1,2)\) (via the ground fact \(\text{Adjacent}(L_{1,2}, L_{2,2})\)) and \(\neg\text{Forklift}(L_{2,2})\) follows from no rumbling at \((2,1)\) (via \(\text{Adjacent}(L_{2,1}, L_{2,2})\)).

Queries that fail: After TELLing creaking at \((2,1)\), the quantified rule requires:

\[\exists L'\, \text{Adjacent}(L_{2,1}, L') \land \text{Damaged}(L')\]

With domain closure, this existential can only be witnessed by real grid squares. Since \(\neg\text{Damaged}(L_{1,1})\) is known, the solver concludes \(\text{Damaged}(L_{3,1}) \lor \text{Damaged}(L_{2,2})\). Without domain closure, DeclareSort('Location') creates an uninterpreted sort, and Z3 is free to invent a phantom location \(L_\text{phantom}\). The closed-world adjacency facts only cover pairs of known grid constants; \(\text{Adjacent}(L_{2,1}, L_\text{phantom})\) is unconstrained, so the solver can set it to true and let \(\text{Damaged}(L_\text{phantom})\) witness the existential. In this model, no real grid square needs to be damaged.

As a result, the elimination chain breaks: after all three percepts, the solver cannot conclude \(\text{Damaged}(L_{3,1})\) (damage at \((3,1)\)), \(\text{Forklift}(L_{1,3})\) (forklift at \((1,3)\)), or that \((3,1)\) and \((1,3)\) are dangerous. Any query that requires process-of-elimination—ruling out all alternatives to pin down a specific location—fails because phantom locations always offer an escape.

6. Reflection

The propositional encoding requires \(O(n^2)\) grounded biconditionals (one per square per predicate type), totaling \(3n^2\) physics sentences for an \(n \times n\) grid. The FOL encoding uses exactly 3 quantified sentences for the physics rules regardless of grid size, though it still needs \(O(n^4)\) closed-world adjacency assertions and the domain closure axiom to specify the grid structure. The FOL encoding is more readable because each quantified sentence maps directly to the English statement of the rule (e.g., "creaking at \(L\) iff damage adjacent to \(L\)"), whereas the propositional version repeats the same pattern for every square. Domain closure is needed in FOL because DeclareSort creates an open-ended, uninterpreted sort—the solver can invent phantom elements unless told the domain is finite. The propositional encoding needs no such axiom because the set of Bool variables is inherently fixed and closed: there are no phantom propositions to worry about.
exe:z3-agent.title: Building a FOL Agent with Z3 (Guided)

exe:expressiveness.content:
Part A: Propositional Encoding Cost

In the propositional encoding (as in [@x9] and [@k7]), adjacency is not encoded as a separate relation—it is embedded in the structure of each biconditional. We count the sentences that explicitly reference which squares neighbor which.

  1. Adjacency: In propositional logic there is no binary predicate, so adjacency is implicit. If we wanted to state it explicitly (e.g., using propositions \(A_{(i,j),(i',j')}\)), we would need one assertion for every ordered pair of locations: \((n^2)^2 = n^4\) sentences (true for adjacent pairs, false otherwise). For \(n=100\): \(10^8\) sentences.

  2. Creaking rule: One biconditional per square, each listing the adjacent \(D\) variables in the disjunction. There are \(n^2\) squares, so \(n^2\) sentences. For \(n = 100\): \(10{,}000\) sentences.

  3. Safety rule: One biconditional per square: \(S_{i,j} \Leftrightarrow \neg D_{i,j} \land \neg F_{i,j}\). Again \(n^2\) sentences. For \(n = 100\): \(10{,}000\) sentences.

Including the rumbling rule (another \(n^2\)), the physics encoding requires \(3n^2\) biconditionals. For \(n = 100\): \(30{,}000\) propositional sentences for physics alone.

Part B: FOL Comparison

In first-order logic, the three physics rules each require a single quantified sentence:

  1. Creaking: \(\forall L\; \text{Creaking}(L) \Leftrightarrow \exists L'\; \text{Adjacent}(L, L') \land \text{Damaged}(L')\)
  2. Rumbling: \(\forall L\; \text{Rumbling}(L) \Leftrightarrow \exists L'\; \text{Adjacent}(L, L') \land \text{Forklift}(L')\)
  3. Safety: \(\forall L\; \text{Safe}(L) \Leftrightarrow \neg\text{Damaged}(L) \land \neg\text{Forklift}(L)\)

3 sentences encode the physics for any grid size. Structural facts still scale: closed-world adjacency requires \(O(n^4)\) ground assertions (one per ordered pair of locations, stating adjacent or not), and domain closure adds \(O(n^2)\) terms. But the physics rules themselves—the part that grows as \(3n^2\) in the propositional encoding—are constant in FOL.

Part C: Translation Challenge

FOL: The statement "there is exactly one damaged floor section" is concise:

\[\exists L\; \text{Damaged}(L) \land \forall L'\; (\text{Damaged}(L') \Rightarrow L' = L)\]

Propositional logic for \(3 \times 3\): With 9 damage variables \(D_{1,1}, D_{2,1}, \ldots, D_{3,3}\), we need:

  • At-least-one: \(D_{1,1} \lor D_{2,1} \lor D_{3,1} \lor D_{1,2} \lor D_{2,2} \lor D_{3,2} \lor D_{1,3} \lor D_{2,3} \lor D_{3,3}\) (1 clause)
  • At-most-one: For every pair of distinct variables, assert that they are not both true: \(\neg D_{i,j} \lor \neg D_{i',j'}\). There are \(\binom{9}{2} = 36\) such clauses.

Total: \(1 + 36 = 37\) clauses for \(3 \times 3\).

Scaling: For an \(n \times n\) grid with \(n^2\) damage variables, the at-most-one constraint requires \(\binom{n^2}{2} = \frac{n^2(n^2 - 1)}{2}\) pairwise exclusion clauses, which is \(O(n^4)\). For \(n = 100\): \(\binom{10000}{2} = 49{,}995{,}000\) clauses. The FOL version remains 1 sentence regardless of \(n\).

So yes, the statement can be expressed in propositional logic, but the encoding cost grows as \(O(n^4)\)—a dramatic illustration of the expressiveness gap.

Part D: Practical Implications

  1. Propositional at scale: The basic physics encoding (\(3n^2 = 30{,}000\) biconditionals for \(n=100\)) is well within the capacity of modern SAT solvers, which routinely handle millions of clauses. However, richer constraints like "exactly one damaged floor" add \(O(n^4) \approx 50\) million clauses, which is feasible but pushing practical limits. Adding multiple such cardinality constraints rapidly becomes unwieldy.

  2. FOL restrictions for tractability: Unrestricted FOL is semi-decidable (and undecidable for satisfiability in general). Tractable restrictions include: (a) Horn clauses, which enable polynomial-time forward and backward chaining; (b) function-free FOL over finite domains, which is decidable; (c) description logics, which restrict quantifier patterns to guarantee decidability while retaining useful expressiveness; (d) bounded-variable fragments, which limit the number of variables.

  3. Hybrid approach: Use FOL for the general physics rules (3 quantified sentences, grid-size independent), and propositionalize only in the local neighborhood around the agent's current position for fast inference. For example, the agent could maintain a FOL KB for global constraints but ground the creaking/rumbling rules only for the squares within \(k\) steps of its current location. This combines FOL's compact representation with propositional logic's efficient (and decidable) inference. Z3 effectively does this internally via MBQI (Model-Based Quantifier Instantiation), grounding quantifiers on demand.
exe:expressiveness.title: Propositional vs. First-Order Expressiveness

exe:final-logic.content:
(a) From \(S_A\) (observed) and Rule 2: \(S_A \Rightarrow F_A \lor F_B\), by modus ponens we get \(F_A \lor F_B\). Combined with \(\neg F_B\) (already derived), by disjunctive syllogism we conclude \(F_A\). Room A has fire.

(b) From \(S_C\) (observed) and Rule 2: \(S_C \Rightarrow F_B \lor F_C\), by modus ponens we get \(F_B \lor F_C\). Combined with \(\neg F_B\), by disjunctive syllogism: \(F_C\). Room C has fire.

(c) \(\forall x, \text{Fire}(x) \Rightarrow \text{Alarm}(x)\). Advantage: one sentence covers any number of rooms. Adding a room D requires no new sentences in FOL; in propositional logic you'd need a new \(F_D \Rightarrow S_D\).

(d) Entailed. The derivation uses sound inference rules (modus tollens) on the KB; there is no model satisfying the KB in which \(F_B\) is true (it would require \(S_B\), contradicting \(\neg S_B\)).
exe:final-logic.title: Logic Encoding and Inference

exe:propositional-warehouse.content:
Goal: Encode the Hazardous Warehouse environment in propositional logic and use logical inference to determine safe squares.

Setup: Consider a simplified \(3 \times 3\) warehouse grid. The robot starts at \((1,1)\). The environment contains:

  • At least one damaged floor section (locations unknown)
  • At least one malfunctioning forklift (locations unknown)
  • One package (location unknown)

Use the following propositional symbols:

  • \(D_{i,j}\): Damaged floor at \((i,j)\)
  • \(F_{i,j}\): Forklift at \((i,j)\)
  • \(P_{i,j}\): Package at \((i,j)\)
  • \(C_{i,j}\): Creaking perceived at \((i,j)\)
  • \(R_{i,j}\): Rumbling perceived at \((i,j)\)
  • \(S_{i,j}\): Square \((i,j)\) is safe

Tasks:

  1. Encode the physics: Write propositional sentences that express:
    • Creaking at a location iff damaged floor in an adjacent square
    • Rumbling at a location iff forklift in an adjacent square
    • A square is safe iff it has no damaged floor and no forklift
  2. Initial knowledge: Write sentences expressing:
    • The starting square \((1,1)\) is safe
    • At least one square has damaged floor
    • At least one square has the forklift
  3. Scenario reasoning: The robot is at \((1,1)\) and perceives no creaking and no rumbling.
    • Write the percept as propositional sentences
    • Use logical inference to determine which squares are provably safe
    • Show your reasoning step by step
  4. Exploration: The robot moves to \((2,1)\) and perceives creaking but no rumbling.
    • Add the new percepts to the knowledge base
    • Determine what new conclusions can be drawn about damaged floor locations
    • Which squares are now known to be dangerous? Which remain uncertain?

Deliverables:

  • Written propositional sentences for parts 1-2
  • Step-by-step logical derivations for parts 3-4
  • A diagram showing the \(3 \times 3\) grid with safe/dangerous/unknown labels after each observation
exe:propositional-warehouse.title: Propositional Logic for the Hazardous Warehouse

exe:fol-translation.content:
Goal: Practice translating natural language statements about the Hazardous Warehouse into first-order logic.

Predicates available: - \(\text{Damaged}(l)\): Location \(l\) has damaged floor - \(\text{Forklift}(l)\): The forklift is at location \(l\) - \(\text{Package}(l)\): The package is at location \(l\) - \(\text{Safe}(l)\): Location \(l\) is safe to enter - \(\text{Adjacent}(l_1, l_2)\): Locations \(l_1\) and \(l_2\) are adjacent - \(\text{Creaking}(l)\): Creaking is perceived at \(l\) - \(\text{Rumbling}(l)\): Rumbling is perceived at \(l\) - \(\text{Visited}(l)\): The robot has visited \(l\) - \(\text{At}(r, l)\): Robot \(r\) is at location \(l\) - \(\text{Carrying}(r, p)\): Robot \(r\) is carrying package \(p\)

Translate each statement to FOL:

  1. "Every location adjacent to a damaged floor has creaking."

  2. "The robot should never enter an unsafe location."

  3. "If a location has no creaking and no rumbling, all adjacent locations are safe."

  4. "There is exactly one forklift in the warehouse."

  5. "If the robot is carrying the package and the robot is at the exit, the mission is complete."

  6. "A location is dangerous if it has damaged floor or if the forklift is there."

  7. "Every visited location is safe." (This reflects the fact that the robot survived visiting it.)

  8. "If rumbling is heard at every location adjacent to \(L\), then the forklift is at \(L\)."

Bonus: For each translation, identify whether the statement uses universal quantification, existential quantification, or both.
exe:fol-translation.title: First-Order Logic Translation

exe:inference-trace.content:
Goal: Trace through forward chaining and backward chaining algorithms on a small knowledge base.

Knowledge Base:

Facts: - \(\text{Adjacent}(L_1, L_2)\) - \(\text{Adjacent}(L_1, L_4)\) - \(\text{Adjacent}(L_2, L_1)\) - \(\text{Adjacent}(L_2, L_3)\) - \(\text{Adjacent}(L_2, L_5)\) - \(\text{Adjacent}(L_4, L_1)\) - \(\text{Adjacent}(L_4, L_5)\) - \(\neg\text{Creaking}(L_1)\) - \(\text{Creaking}(L_2)\) - \(\neg\text{Rumbling}(L_1)\) - \(\neg\text{Rumbling}(L_2)\) - \(\text{Safe}(L_1)\) (starting square)

Rules: - R1: \(\forall l.\, \neg\text{Creaking}(l) \Rightarrow \forall l'.\, \text{Adjacent}(l, l') \Rightarrow \neg\text{Damaged}(l')\) - R2: \(\forall l.\, \neg\text{Rumbling}(l) \Rightarrow \forall l'.\, \text{Adjacent}(l, l') \Rightarrow \neg\text{Forklift}(l')\) - R3: \(\forall l.\, \neg\text{Damaged}(l) \land \neg\text{Forklift}(l) \Rightarrow \text{Safe}(l)\)

Grid layout (for reference):

L4 -- L5
|     |
L1 -- L2 -- L3

Tasks:

  1. Forward chaining: Starting from the initial facts, trace the forward chaining process.

    • What new facts are derived in each iteration?
    • Continue until no new facts can be derived.
    • List all derived facts in order.

  2. Backward chaining: Query: Is \(L_5\) safe?

    • Trace the backward chaining process step by step.
    • Show which rules are used and what subgoals are generated.
    • Does the query succeed or fail? Why?

  3. Unification: For each rule application in your traces, explicitly show the substitution (unifier) used.

  4. Comparison: Which approach (forward or backward) examined fewer rules/facts for this query? When would the other approach be preferable?
exe:inference-trace.title: Forward and Backward Chaining Trace

exe:build-kb-agent.content:
Goal: Follow the walkthrough in [@k7] to build your own knowledge-based agent for the Hazardous Warehouse using Z3.

Setup: You will need z3-solver (install via pip install z3-solver) and hazardous_warehouse_env.py in your working directory.

Tasks:

  1. Setup and exploration: Create a new Python file. Import Bool, Bools, Or, And, Not, Solver, unsat from z3, and HazardousWarehouseEnv from hazardous_warehouse_env.py. Verify you can:

    • Create boolean variables: P, Q = Bools('P Q')
    • Add a biconditional: s.add(P == Q) and a fact: s.add(P)
    • Check satisfiability: s.check() should return sat
    • Inspect the model: s.model() should show P = True, Q = True
    • Implement the z3_entails function from [@k7] using push/pop. Verify that after adding P == Q and P, the solver entails Q.

  2. Symbols and physics: Write the Bool variable helper functions (damaged, forklift_at, creaking_at, rumbling_at, safe) and build_warehouse_kb() as described in [@k7]. After building the solver, verify it is satisfiable (solver.check() returns sat).

  3. Manual reasoning: Before building the full agent, use your solver to replicate the reasoning from [@x9]:

    • Create the solver with build_warehouse_kb()
    • TELL the solver the percepts at \((1,1)\): no creaking, no rumbling
    • ASK whether \((2,1)\) is safe. ASK whether \((1,2)\) is safe. Both should return True.
    • TELL the solver the percepts at \((2,1)\): creaking, no rumbling
    • ASK whether \((3,1)\) is safe. What about \(\neg\mathit{OK}_{3,1}\)? What does the solver conclude about \((2,2)\)?
    • TELL the solver the percepts at \((1,2)\): rumbling, no creaking
    • ASK again about \((3,1)\), \((2,2)\), and \((1,3)\). The solver should now identify the damaged floor and forklift locations.

  4. Agent loop: Implement the full WarehouseKBAgent class with the perceive \(\to\) tell \(\to\) ask \(\to\) act cycle described in [@k7]. Include path planning (BFS through safe squares) and the action conversion logic.

  5. Testing: Run your agent on the example layout (using configure_rn_example_layout from hazardous_warehouse_viz.py). Does it retrieve the package and exit successfully? Record the number of steps and total reward.

  6. Reflection: In 2–3 sentences, describe a situation where the agent either gets stuck (cannot find the package) or behaves conservatively (avoids squares that a human would risk). What additional reasoning capability would help?

Deliverables: Your Python file with the agent implementation, plus a brief summary (replace the template's README.md file) of your results and observations from tasks 3, 5, and 6.

Bonus: Extend the agent to use the emergency shutdown device. The agent should reason about the forklift's location and, when it can identify the forklift along a line from its current position, fire the shutdown device before proceeding.
exe:build-kb-agent.title: Building a Knowledge-Based Agent (Guided)

exe:z3-agent.content:
Goal: Follow the walkthrough in [@z3] to extend the propositional agent from [@k7] to use quantified first-order logic, and compare the two encodings.

Setup: You will need z3-solver (install via pip install z3-solver), hazardous_warehouse_env.py, and hazardous_warehouse_viz.py in your working directory. You should have a working propositional agent from [@exe:build-kb-agent].

Tasks:

  1. FOL domain setup: Create a new Python file. Import DeclareSort, Function, BoolSort, Const, ForAll, Exists, Distinct from z3 (in addition to the Or, And, Not, Solver, unsat you already know from [@k7]). Verify you can:

    • Create a sort: Location = DeclareSort('Location')
    • Create a predicate: P = Function('P', Location, BoolSort())
    • Create constants: L1 = Const('L1', Location)
    • Write a quantified sentence: ForAll(L, P(L)) where L = Const('L', Location)
    • Add the sentence to a solver and check satisfiability.

  2. Quantified physics rules: Implement build_warehouse_kb_fol() as described in [@z3]. This includes:

    • Location constants for each grid square
    • Domain closure (ForAll(L, Or([L == loc[...] for ...])) and Distinct)
    • Closed-world adjacency facts
    • Three quantified physics rules: creaking, rumbling, and safety
    • Verify the solver is satisfiable after building the KB.

  3. Manual reasoning: Replicate the reasoning walkthrough from [@k7:walkthrough] using the FOL KB:

    • Build the KB with build_warehouse_kb_fol()
    • TELL the solver: no creaking, no rumbling at \((1,1)\)—using self.preds['Creaking'](loc[(1,1)]) instead of creaking_at(1, 1)
    • ASK: is \((2,1)\) safe? Is \((1,2)\) safe? (Both should return True.)
    • TELL: creaking, no rumbling at \((2,1)\)
    • ASK: is \((3,1)\) safe? Is \((2,2)\) safe? (Both should be unknown.)
    • TELL: no creaking, rumbling at \((1,2)\)
    • ASK: is \((2,2)\) safe? Is \((3,1)\) dangerous? Is \((1,3)\) dangerous? (All True.)
    • Verify your results match the propositional agent's conclusions.

  4. Full agent: Implement the WarehouseZ3Agent class with the same decision loop as [@k7]. The key difference is using FOL predicates applied to location constants instead of grounded Bool variables. Run it on the example layout using configure_rn_example_layout. Record the number of steps and total reward. Confirm the results are identical to the propositional agent.

  5. Domain closure investigation (challenge): Remove the domain closure axiom from build_warehouse_kb_fol() and re-run the manual reasoning from task 3. Which entailment queries now fail? Explain why Z3 can construct a satisfying model where no real grid square is damaged, even when creaking is perceived. Restore the axiom when done.

  6. Reflection: In 3–4 sentences, compare the propositional and FOL encodings. Address: (a) How does rule count scale with grid size for each approach? (b) Which encoding is more readable? (c) What is the role of domain closure, and why doesn't the propositional encoding need it?

Deliverables: Your Python file with the FOL agent, the output trace from task 4, and the written comparison from task 6.
exe:z3-agent.title: Building a FOL Agent with Z3 (Guided)

exe:expressiveness.content:
Goal: Understand the expressiveness gap between propositional and first-order logic.

Part A: Propositional Encoding Cost

Consider an \(n \times n\) warehouse grid. Count the number of propositional sentences needed to encode:

  1. The adjacency relation (which squares are adjacent to which)
  2. The creaking rule: "Creaking at \(L\) iff damaged floor adjacent to \(L\)"
  3. The safety rule: "Safe at \(L\) iff no damaged floor and no forklift at \(L\)"

Express your answers as functions of \(n\). What happens as \(n\) grows to 100?

Part B: FOL Comparison

Write the same rules in first-order logic. How many sentences are needed regardless of \(n\)?

Part C: Translation Challenge

Can the following statement be expressed in propositional logic? If so, how? If not, why not?

"There is exactly one damaged floor section in the entire warehouse."

Write the statement in FOL. Then attempt a propositional encoding for a \(3 \times 3\) grid. How does the complexity scale?

Part D: Practical Implications

A real warehouse might be \(100 \times 100\) with 10,000 locations. Discuss:

  1. Is propositional encoding practical at this scale?
  2. What restrictions on FOL would make inference tractable?
  3. How might a hybrid approach work (FOL for general rules, propositionalization for local reasoning)?
exe:expressiveness.title: Propositional vs. First-Order Expressiveness

exe:model-checking.content:
Goal: Practice model checking by enumerating interpretations.

Setup: Consider a tiny \(2 \times 2\) warehouse with squares \(A\), \(B\), \(C\), \(D\) arranged as:

C -- D
|    |
A -- B

Use propositional symbols: - \(D_X\): Damaged floor at square \(X\) (for \(X \in \{A, B, C, D\}\)) - \(C_X\): Creaking at square \(X\)

Knowledge Base: - \(C_A \Leftrightarrow D_B \lor D_C\) (creaking at A iff damage at adjacent B or C) - \(C_B \Leftrightarrow D_A \lor D_D\) (creaking at B iff damage at adjacent A or D) - \(\neg D_A\) (starting square A is safe) - \(\neg C_A\) (no creaking at A) - \(C_B\) (creaking at B)

Tasks:

  1. List all propositional symbols in this KB.

  2. Enumerate all interpretations (there are \(2^n\) for \(n\) symbols—use only the 4 damage symbols since creaking is determined by the rules).

  3. Filter models: Which interpretations satisfy all sentences in the KB?

  4. Check entailment: Does the KB entail \(D_D\)? Does it entail \(\neg D_B\)? Does it entail \(D_B \lor D_C\)?

  5. Practical reflection: With 4 damage symbols, we have 16 interpretations. How many interpretations would a \(10 \times 10\) warehouse have? Is model enumeration practical at that scale?
exe:model-checking.title: Model Checking and Entailment

exe:final-logic.content:
A fire-response robot inspects a small building with three rooms: A, B, and C. The adjacency is:

   A --- B --- C

(A and B are adjacent; B and C are adjacent; A and C are not adjacent.)

Each room may or may not contain a fire. Each room has a smoke detector. Variables: \(F_A, F_B, F_C\) (fire present) and \(S_A, S_B, S_C\) (detector positive).

Rules encoded (given to you):

  • Rule 1 (fire causes alarm): \(F_A \Rightarrow S_A\), \(F_B \Rightarrow S_B\), \(F_C \Rightarrow S_C\)
  • Rule 2 (alarm means fire nearby): \(S_A \Rightarrow F_A \lor F_B\), \(S_B \Rightarrow F_A \lor F_B \lor F_C\), \(S_C \Rightarrow F_B \lor F_C\)

Observations: \(S_A\) = true, \(\neg S_B\) = true (B's detector is negative), \(S_C\) = true.

First derivation (given): The contrapositive of \(F_B \Rightarrow S_B\) is \(\neg S_B \Rightarrow \neg F_B\). Since \(\neg S_B\) is observed, we conclude \(\neg F_B\) by modus tollens.

(a) Using \(\neg F_B\) and Rule 2 for room A (\(S_A \Rightarrow F_A \lor F_B\)), derive whether Room A has fire. Name the inference rule(s) you use.

(b) Using \(\neg F_B\) and Rule 2 for room C, derive whether Room C has fire.

(c) Translate Rule 1 into first-order logic using a predicate \(\text{Fire}(x)\) and \(\text{Alarm}(x)\) with a universal quantifier. Recall: FOL uses variables, predicates, and quantifiers like \(\forall\) and \(\exists\) ([@y2]). What advantage does the FOL version have over writing three separate propositional sentences?

(d) Recall: \(\text{KB} \models \alpha\) (entailment) means \(\alpha\) is true in every model where KB is true, whereas \(\alpha\) is merely consistent with KB if there exists some model where both are true ([@def:entailment]). Is your conclusion \(\neg F_B\) in (b) entailed by the KB, or only consistent with it? Explain in one sentence.
exe:final-logic.title: Logic Encoding and Inference

sections.title: Quantifying Uncertainty
sections.html:
In Chapter 3, we built agents that reason with logical certainty: a square is safe or it isn't, a sentence is entailed or it isn't. This works beautifully when percepts are reliable and world dynamics are deterministic. But real-world agents rarely enjoy such guarantees {% cite 'russell2020' note='ch. 12' %}.

Consider our warehouse robot again. In the Hazardous Warehouse of Chapter 3, sensors were perfect: creaking always meant adjacent damaged floor, and its absence always meant safety. Now suppose the sensors are imperfect:

  • The creaking detector has a 10% false-negative rate: it fails to report creaking 10% of the time when damaged floor is actually adjacent.
  • It also has a 5% false-positive rate: it sometimes reports creaking when no damaged floor is nearby.

Suddenly, the logical agent from Chapter 3 is in trouble. Hearing no creaking at \((1,1)\) no longer entails that \((2,1)\) and \((1,2)\) are safe—it merely makes it likely. Moving to \((2,1)\) now carries real risk, and the agent must decide whether that risk is acceptable.

This chapter develops the mathematical framework for reasoning under uncertainty: probability theory. We then extend it to sequential decision-making with Markov decision processes, which form the foundation for the reinforcement learning techniques we will study in Chapter 7.

Why Logic Isn't Enough

The logical approach to uncertainty has three fundamental problems {% cite 'russell2020' note='sec. 12.1' %}:

  1. Laziness: Listing every possible cause of creaking (damaged floor, temperature changes, settling, vibration from nearby equipment, ...) and every exception is impractical. A complete logical theory of sensor behavior would be enormous.

  2. Theoretical ignorance: We may not have a complete theory. Does humidity affect the creaking detector? We don't know, and we can't write a rule for something we don't understand.

  3. Practical ignorance: Even with a complete theory, we may lack the specific information needed. The exact condition of every floor tile, the calibration curve of every sensor—this information is unavailable.

The result is that the agent's knowledge base is inevitably incomplete. With incomplete knowledge, logical inference produces one of three outcomes for any proposition: entailed, entailed to be false, or unknown. The "unknown" category can be very large, leaving the agent unable to make decisions.

The Qualification Problem

Attempting to handle uncertainty with logic leads to the qualification problem: for any rule like "if no creaking, then no adjacent damage," there are always additional qualifications (sensor malfunction, unusual acoustics, battery low, ...). No finite set of qualifications is truly complete.

Degrees of Belief

Probability provides a way to handle the "unknown" category: instead of three truth values (true, false, unknown), we assign a degree of belief between 0 and 1 to each proposition.

Degree of Belief

The degree of belief in a proposition \(A\), written \(P(A)\), is a number in \([0, 1]\) representing how strongly the agent believes \(A\) to be true, given the evidence available. \(P(A) = 0\) means \(A\) is certainly false; \(P(A) = 1\) means \(A\) is certainly true.

For the warehouse robot:

  • \(P(\text{Damaged}_{2,1}) = 0.04\) means the robot believes there is a 4% chance of damaged floor at \((2,1)\), given no creaking at \((1,1)\) but accounting for the false-negative rate.
  • \(P(\text{Safe}_{2,1}) = 0.96\) means 96% confidence that \((2,1)\) is safe.

These are not arbitrary numbers—they are constrained by the laws of probability and updated rigorously as new evidence arrives.

Acting Rationally Under Uncertainty

Given uncertain beliefs, how should an agent act? The answer is the principle of maximum expected utility (MEU).

Utility

A utility function \(U(s)\) assigns a real number to each outcome state \(s\), representing how desirable that state is to the agent.

Expected Utility

The expected utility of an action \(a\) is the average utility over all possible outcomes, weighted by their probabilities: \[ \text{EU}(a) = \sum_{s} P(s \mid a) \, U(s) \] where the sum ranges over all possible outcome states \(s\) and \(P(s \mid a)\) is the probability of reaching state \(s\) given action \(a\).

Maximum Expected Utility (MEU)

A rational agent should choose the action that maximizes expected utility: \[ a^* = \arg\max_a \text{EU}(a) \]

Example: The warehouse robot at \((1,1)\) considers moving to \((2,1)\). Two outcomes are possible:

  • \((2,1)\) is safe (probability 0.96): the robot advances toward its goal. Utility: +10.
  • \((2,1)\) has damaged floor (probability 0.04): the robot is destroyed. Utility: \(-1000\).

Where do these numbers come from? The probabilities are the robot's beliefs, computed from its sensor model and prior knowledge—for instance, the 0.04 might result from a Bayesian update after hearing no creaking at \((1,1)\) with a sensor that has a 10% false-negative rate (we will compute exactly this in [@b1]). The utility values are design choices made by the system engineer: \(+10\) reflects the value of progress toward the goal, while \(-1000\) reflects the catastrophic cost of losing the robot. Different utility assignments would lead to different behavior.

The expected utility calculation weights each outcome by its probability and sums:

\[ \text{EU}(\text{move to } (2,1)) = \underbrace{0.96 \times 10}_{\text{likely safe: }+9.6} + \underbrace{0.04 \times (-1000)}_{\text{unlikely but catastrophic: }-40} = 9.6 - 40 = -30.4 \]

Even though the robot will almost certainly be fine (96% chance), the small probability of a devastating outcome (\(-1000\)) dominates the calculation. The expected utility is negative, meaning this action is worse than doing nothing in expectation. A rational agent might instead choose to gather more evidence before moving, or take a different path.

This simple calculation illustrates why probability and utility work together: probability quantifies what might happen, and utility quantifies how much we care. Neither alone is sufficient for rational decision-making.

Probability: Axioms and Notation

We now develop the formal machinery of probability. The treatment follows {% cite 'russell2020' note='sec. 12.2' %}.

Random Processes, Sample Spaces, and Events

Random Process (Random Experiment)

A random process (or random experiment) is any procedure or observation whose outcome is not known in advance, even if the mechanism is fully understood. Examples include rolling a die, measuring a sensor reading, or inspecting a warehouse square.

Sample Space

A sample space \(\Omega\) is the set of all possible outcomes of a random process. Each element \(\omega \in \Omega\) is called a sample point or elementary event.

Event

An event \(A\) is a subset of the sample space: \(A \subseteq \Omega\). An event occurs when the actual outcome is a member of \(A\).

Example: Rolling a six-sided die. The random process is the act of rolling. The sample space is \(\Omega = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\). The event "roll is even" is \(A = \{2, 4, 6\}\).

Example: The true state of square \((2,1)\) in the warehouse. The random process is the "draw" from the warehouse's configuration that determined what occupies that square. The sample space for this square is \(\Omega = \{\text{safe}, \text{damaged}, \text{forklift}\}\).

Sample Spaces Are Modeling Choices

The sample space depends on how we choose to model the situation. For the warehouse square, we chose three categories. A more detailed model might distinguish between types of damage (structural vs. chemical), giving a larger \(\Omega\). A coarser model might only distinguish \(\{\text{safe}, \text{not safe}\}\). The "right" sample space depends on what distinctions matter for the agent's decisions. This is an engineering judgment, not a mathematical fact.

Axioms of Probability

Kolmogorov Axioms

A probability function \(P\) assigns a real number to each event, satisfying:

  1. Non-negativity: \(P(A) \geq 0\) for every event \(A\)
  2. Normalization: \(P(\Omega) = 1\)
  3. Additivity: For mutually exclusive events \(A\) and \(B\) (i.e., \(A \cap B = \emptyset\)): \[P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)\]

From these three axioms, all of probability theory follows. Some immediate consequences:

  • \(P(\emptyset) = 0\) (the impossible event has probability zero)
  • \(P(\neg A) = 1 - P(A)\) (the complement rule)
  • \(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\) (inclusion-exclusion)
  • \(0 \leq P(A) \leq 1\) for all events \(A\)

Random Variables

Random Variable

A random variable is a function from the sample space to some range of values. We denote random variables with uppercase letters (e.g., \(X\), \(Y\)) and their values with lowercase letters (e.g., \(x\), \(y\)).

Random variables come in two types:

Discrete random variables take values from a finite or countably infinite set. Examples:

  • \(\text{Floor}_{2,1} \in \{\text{safe}, \text{damaged}\}\)
  • \(\text{DieRoll} \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\)

Continuous random variables take values from an interval of real numbers. Examples:

  • \(\text{SensorReading} \in [0, 1]\) (normalized signal strength)
  • \(\text{Temperature} \in \mathbb{R}\)

Probability Distributions

Probability Mass Function (PMF)

For a discrete random variable \(X\), the probability mass function (PMF) gives the probability of each value: \[ P_X(x) = P(X = x) \] The PMF satisfies \(P_X(x) \geq 0\) for all \(x\) and \(\sum_x P_X(x) = 1\).

The notation \(P_X(x)\) is not a new function—it is shorthand for the probability function \(P\) applied to the event \(\{X = x\}\). The subscript \(X\) identifies which random variable we are talking about, and the argument \(x\) specifies the value. So \(P\) always means "the probability of," whether applied to an event (\(P(A)\)), a random variable taking a value (\(P(X = x)\)), or as the PMF shorthand (\(P_X(x)\)). These are three notations for the same underlying concept.

PMF Notation

Some texts write the PMF as \(p(x)\) or \(p_X(x)\) with a lowercase \(p\) to visually distinguish the PMF from the probability function. We avoid this because lowercase \(p\) frequently appears as a parameter (e.g., the success probability \(p\) in a Bernoulli distribution), creating a different kind of ambiguity. Using \(P_X(x)\) keeps one consistent letter \(P\) for all probabilities while the subscript \(X\) clarifies which random variable is involved. When the random variable is clear from context, we may drop the subscript and write simply \(P(x)\).

Probability Density Function (PDF)

For a continuous random variable \(X\), the probability density function \(f(x)\) is defined such that: \[ P(a \leq X \leq b) = \int_a^b f(x) \, dx \] The PDF satisfies \(f(x) \geq 0\) for all \(x\) and \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) \, dx = 1\).

Densities Are Not Probabilities

For a continuous random variable, \(f(x)\) is not a probability—it can exceed 1. Only integrals of the density over intervals give probabilities. The probability that a continuous random variable takes any single exact value is zero: \(P(X = x) = 0\).

Common Distributions

Several distributions will appear repeatedly in later chapters. The first two are discrete (defined by PMFs); the third is continuous (defined by a PDF).

Discrete Distributions (PMFs)

Bernoulli distribution: The simplest nontrivial distribution. A Bernoulli random variable models a single trial with two outcomes: "success" (encoded as \(X = 1\)) and "failure" (encoded as \(X = 0\)). The distribution has one parameter \(p \in [0, 1]\), the probability of success. Written \(X \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)\), its PMF is:

\[ P_X(x) = p^x (1-p)^{1-x}, \quad x \in \{0, 1\} \]

This compact formula covers both cases via exponent tricks: when \(x = 1\), we get \(P_X(1) = p^1(1-p)^0 = p\); when \(x = 0\), we get \(P_X(0) = p^0(1-p)^1 = 1 - p\). One could equivalently write the PMF as a table:

Bernoulli PMF
\(x\) \(P_X(x)\)
0 (failure) \(1 - p\)
1 (success) \(p\)

The two probabilities sum to 1, as required. The compact exponential form above is preferred because it generalizes cleanly and is convenient for mathematical manipulation (e.g., taking logarithms when we encounter maximum likelihood estimation in later chapters).

The Bernoulli models any binary outcome: a coin flip (\(p = 0.5\) for a fair coin), a sensor triggered or not, floor damaged or not. Note that the parameter \(p\) here is the success probability, distinct from the PMF function \(P_X\).

Categorical distribution: The generalization of the Bernoulli to \(k\) mutually exclusive outcomes. The distribution is parameterized by a vector of probabilities \((p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k)\) with \(p_i \geq 0\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^k p_i = 1\). A random variable \(X \sim \text{Categorical}(p_1, \ldots, p_k)\) takes one of the values \(\{1, 2, \ldots, k\}\), and its PMF simply reads off the corresponding probability:

\[ P_X(i) = p_i, \quad i \in \{1, \ldots, k\} \]

That is, the probability of outcome \(i\) is the \(i\)-th entry of the parameter vector. The constraint \(\sum_i p_i = 1\) ensures the PMF is a valid distribution.

Example: The state of a warehouse square can be modeled as a categorical random variable with \(k = 3\) outcomes:

Categorical distribution for warehouse square state
Outcome \(i\) Label Probability \(p_i\)
1 Safe 0.80
2 Damaged floor 0.15
3 Forklift 0.05

The PMF gives \(P_X(1) = 0.80\), \(P_X(2) = 0.15\), \(P_X(3) = 0.05\), and the probabilities sum to 1. A fair six-sided die is a categorical with \(k = 6\) and \(p_i = 1/6\) for all \(i\).

Note that the Bernoulli is the special case \(k = 2\): the two outcomes are "success" (\(i = 1\), probability \(p\)) and "failure" (\(i = 2\), probability \(1 - p\)).

Continuous Distributions (PDFs)

Gaussian (normal) distribution: A continuous random variable \(X\) with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\). Written \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\). Its PDF is:

\[ f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right), \quad x \in \mathbb{R} \]

The Gaussian is the most widely used continuous distribution. It arises naturally as the limiting distribution of sums of many small, independent effects (the central limit theorem). In engineering, sensor noise is often modeled as Gaussian: if the warehouse robot's distance sensor returns a reading \(X\) when the true distance is \(\mu\), we might model \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) where \(\sigma\) captures sensor precision. We will encounter the Gaussian frequently in the machine learning and deep learning chapters.

Joint, Marginal, and Conditional Probability

Most interesting problems involve multiple random variables. The relationships between them are captured by joint distributions.

Joint Probability

Joint Probability

The joint probability \(P(X = x, Y = y)\), often written \(P(x, y)\), is the probability that \(X\) takes value \(x\) and \(Y\) takes value \(y\) simultaneously.

Example: Consider two adjacent warehouse squares. Let \(D_1\) and \(D_2\) be Bernoulli random variables indicating damaged floor at each. A joint distribution might be:

Joint distribution of floor damage at two squares
\(D_1\) \(D_2\) \(P(D_1, D_2)\)
0 0 0.80
0 1 0.10
1 0 0.08
1 1 0.02

The four probabilities sum to 1. This table encodes everything about how damage at the two squares relates.

Marginal Probability

Marginal Probability (Marginalization)

The marginal probability (or marginal distribution) of \(X\) is obtained from the joint distribution by eliminating the other variables. For discrete random variables, we sum out the unwanted variable: \[ P(X = x) = \sum_y P(X = x, Y = y) \] For continuous random variables with a joint density \(f_{X,Y}\), we integrate out the unwanted variable: \[ f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x, y) \, dy \] In mixed cases (one discrete, one continuous), the appropriate operation—sum or integral—is applied to each variable according to its type.

Discrete example (from [@tbl:joint-dist]): \[P(D_1 = 0) = P(D_1 = 0, D_2 = 0) + P(D_1 = 0, D_2 = 1) = 0.80 + 0.10 = 0.90\] \[P(D_1 = 1) = 0.08 + 0.02 = 0.10\]

Continuous example: If two sensor readings \(X\) and \(Y\) have a joint density \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)\), and we only care about \(X\), we integrate over all possible values of \(Y\) to obtain the marginal density \(f_X(x)\). The integral collapses the two-dimensional density down to a one-dimensional density, just as summation collapses a joint PMF table down to a single column.

In both cases, marginalization eliminates variables we don't care about, reducing a joint distribution to a distribution over fewer variables.

Conditional Probability

Conditional Probability

The conditional probability of \(X = x\) given \(Y = y\) is: \[ P(X = x \mid Y = y) = \frac{P(X = x, Y = y)}{P(Y = y)} \] provided \(P(Y = y) > 0\). This is the probability of \(X = x\) when we know \(Y = y\).

Example: What is the probability that square 1 has damaged floor, given that square 2 has damaged floor?

\[P(D_1 = 1 \mid D_2 = 1) = \frac{P(D_1 = 1, D_2 = 1)}{P(D_2 = 1)} = \frac{0.02}{0.10 + 0.02} = \frac{0.02}{0.12} \approx 0.167\]

Knowing that square 2 is damaged increases our belief that square 1 is damaged (from 0.10 to 0.167). This makes sense: damage might cluster due to shared structural causes.

The Product Rule

Rearranging [@eq:conditional-prob] gives the product rule:

\[ P(X, Y) = P(X \mid Y) \, P(Y) = P(Y \mid X) \, P(X) \]

This is a fundamental identity. The joint probability can be decomposed into a conditional probability and a marginal probability, and the decomposition can go in either direction.

The Chain Rule

The product rule generalizes to any number of variables:

\[ P(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n) = P(X_1) \prod_{i=2}^{n} P(X_i \mid X_1, \ldots, X_{i-1}) \]

This chain rule is useful for decomposing complex joint distributions into manageable pieces. It holds for any ordering of the variables.

Independence

Independence

Two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, written \(X \perp Y\), if knowing the value of one provides no information about the other: \[ P(X, Y) = P(X) \, P(Y) \] Equivalently, \(P(X \mid Y) = P(X)\).

Independence is a strong assumption. In [@tbl:joint-dist], \(D_1\) and \(D_2\) are not independent: \(P(D_1 = 1 \mid D_2 = 1) = 0.167 \neq 0.10 = P(D_1 = 1)\).

Conditional Independence

\(X\) and \(Y\) are conditionally independent given \(Z\), written \(X \perp Y \mid Z\), if: \[ P(X, Y \mid Z) = P(X \mid Z) \, P(Y \mid Z) \]

Conditional independence is weaker than independence and far more common in practice.

Example: Suppose the warehouse robot has two sensors at square \((1,1)\): an acoustic sensor \(C\) (detects creaking) and a thermal sensor \(T\) (detects heat from structural stress). Let \(D\) be the event that adjacent square \((2,1)\) has damaged floor.

Without knowing \(D\), the two sensor readings are correlated. If \(C = 1\) (creaking detected), that makes \(D = 1\) more likely, which in turn makes \(T = 1\) more likely. So \(P(T = 1 \mid C = 1) > P(T = 1)\)—the sensors are not independent.

But once we know the true state of the floor, the correlation disappears. If we are told \(D = 1\) (the floor is damaged), then the acoustic sensor responds to the damage with some probability and the thermal sensor responds independently with its own probability. Knowing that the acoustic sensor beeped doesn't change our expectation of the thermal sensor, because the damage itself already explains both. Formally:

\[P(C, T \mid D) = P(C \mid D) \, P(T \mid D)\]

The sensors are conditionally independent given the hazard state: \(C \perp T \mid D\). The common cause \(D\) "explains away" the correlation between \(C\) and \(T\). This pattern—observed variables correlated marginally but conditionally independent given a hidden cause—is pervasive in probabilistic modeling and is the key assumption behind the Naive Bayes model in [@b1].

Expectation and Variance

Two summary statistics of a distribution are so fundamental that they appear throughout the rest of this book.

Expectation (Expected Value)

The expected value of a discrete random variable \(X\) is: \[ \mathbb{E}[X] = \sum_x x \, P(X = x) \] For a continuous random variable with density \(f\): \[ \mathbb{E}[X] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \, f(x) \, dx \]

The expected value is the probability-weighted average of all possible values. It is not necessarily a value that \(X\) can take—for example, the expected value of a fair die roll is 3.5.

Key properties:

  • Linearity: \(\mathbb{E}[aX + bY] = a\,\mathbb{E}[X] + b\,\mathbb{E}[Y]\) for any constants \(a, b\), whether or not \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent.
  • Expectation of a function (LOTUS): If \(g\) is any function, then \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)] = \sum_x g(x) \, P(X = x)\). This is the Law of the Unconscious Statistician: it lets us compute \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)]\) directly from the distribution of \(X\), without first deriving the distribution of \(Y = g(X)\). Despite being called "unconscious," this is an exact identity, not an approximation. (What is generally false is that \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)] = g(\mathbb{E}[X])\)—that only holds when \(g\) is linear.)

Variance

The variance of a random variable \(X\) measures the spread of its distribution around the mean: \[ \text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}\left[(X - \mathbb{E}[X])^2\right] = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2 \] The standard deviation is \(\sigma = \sqrt{\text{Var}(X)}\), which has the same units as \(X\).

Example: For the warehouse robot's utility when moving to \((2,1)\):

\[\mathbb{E}[U] = 0.96 \times 10 + 0.04 \times (-1000) = -30.4\] \[\mathbb{E}[U^2] = 0.96 \times 100 + 0.04 \times 1{,}000{,}000 = 96 + 40{,}000 = 40{,}096\] \[\text{Var}(U) = 40{,}096 - (-30.4)^2 = 40{,}096 - 924.16 = 39{,}171.84\] \[\sigma_U \approx 197.9\]

The large standard deviation reflects the high stakes: most of the time the outcome is +10, but occasionally it is \(-1000\). A risk-sensitive agent might prefer actions with lower variance even at the cost of somewhat lower expected utility.

Chapter Overview

The remainder of this chapter builds on these foundations:

  • [@b1]: Bayes' rule for updating beliefs as new evidence arrives, applied to the warehouse robot with noisy sensors
  • [@m1]: Markov decision processes for sequential decision-making under uncertainty, forming the bridge to reinforcement learning

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to design agents that reason probabilistically about uncertain environments and make rational decisions over sequences of actions.
