sections.title: Bayesian Reasoning
sections.html:
The previous section established the language of probability: random variables, distributions, conditional probability, and expectation. Now we turn to the central question of uncertain reasoning: how should an agent update its beliefs when new evidence arrives?

The answer is Bayes' rule—a direct consequence of the product rule—which provides a principled, mathematically rigorous procedure for revising probabilities in light of observations {% cite 'russell2020' note='sec. 12.5' %}.

Bayes' Rule

Derivation

From the product rule ([@eq:product-rule]), we have two expressions for the joint probability \(P(H, E)\) of a hypothesis \(H\) and evidence \(E\):

\[ P(H, E) = P(E \mid H) \, P(H) = P(H \mid E) \, P(E) \]

Setting the right-hand sides equal and solving for \(P(H \mid E)\):

Bayes' Rule

\[ P(H \mid E) = \frac{P(E \mid H) \, P(H)}{P(E)} \]

Each term has a name and interpretation:

Term Name Meaning
\(P(H \mid E)\) Posterior Belief in \(H\) after observing evidence \(E\)
\(P(H)\) Prior Belief in \(H\) before observing \(E\)
\(P(E \mid H)\) Likelihood Probability of observing \(E\) if \(H\) is true
\(P(E)\) Evidence (or marginal likelihood) Total probability of observing \(E\)

The denominator \(P(E)\) can be computed by marginalization: \[ P(E) = \sum_h P(E \mid H = h) \, P(H = h) \]

This is the law of total probability: the probability of the evidence is the weighted average of the likelihood over all hypotheses.

Interpretation

Bayes' rule tells us how to learn from evidence:

\[ \underbrace{P(H \mid E)}_{\text{what we believe now}} = \frac{\overbrace{P(E \mid H)}^{\text{how well } H \text{ predicts } E} \times \overbrace{P(H)}^{\text{what we believed before}}}{\underbrace{P(E)}_{\text{how surprising } E \text{ is overall}}} \]

Hypotheses that predict the observed evidence well (high likelihood) get a boost in probability. The denominator normalizes so that all posterior probabilities sum to 1.

The Denominator as Normalizer

In practice, we often compute the numerator \(P(E \mid H) \, P(H)\) for each hypothesis and normalize afterward, since \(P(E)\) is the same for all hypotheses. We write: \[ P(H \mid E) \propto P(E \mid H) \, P(H) \] where \(\propto\) means "proportional to."

Diagnostic vs. Causal Reasoning

A key insight is the direction of reasoning. In the warehouse:

  • Causal direction (cause → effect): "If the floor is damaged, what is the probability of hearing creaking?" This is \(P(\text{Creaking} \mid \text{Damaged})\)—the likelihood. This direction is often easier to specify because it follows physical causation.

  • Diagnostic direction (effect → cause): "Given that we hear creaking, what is the probability that the floor is damaged?" This is \(P(\text{Damaged} \mid \text{Creaking})\)—the posterior. This is what the agent actually needs for decision-making.

Bayes' rule converts causal knowledge into diagnostic conclusions. We encode the physics of the world (causal direction) and use Bayes' rule to reason backward from observations (diagnostic direction).

Warehouse Example: Noisy Sensors

Let us apply Bayes' rule to the warehouse robot with imperfect sensors. We focus on a single square, say \((2,1)\), and the creaking sensor at the adjacent square \((1,1)\).

Setup

Define the random variables:

  • \(D\): the floor at \((2,1)\) is damaged (\(D = 1\)) or not (\(D = 0\))
  • \(C\): creaking is detected at \((1,1)\) (\(C = 1\)) or not (\(C = 0\))

We are given:

  • Prior: \(P(D = 1) = 0.1\) (10% of squares have damaged floor, based on warehouse records)
  • Sensor model (likelihood):
    • \(P(C = 1 \mid D = 1) = 0.9\) (90% true positive rate—sensor detects creaking when damage is adjacent)
    • \(P(C = 1 \mid D = 0) = 0.05\) (5% false positive rate)

Simplification

For clarity, we focus on a single adjacent square. In reality, creaking at \((1,1)\) could be caused by damage at \((2,1)\) or \((1,2)\). A complete model would account for all adjacent squares. The principle is the same; the computation is just larger.

Case 1: No Creaking Observed

The robot is at \((1,1)\) and hears no creaking (\(C = 0\)). What is \(P(D = 1 \mid C = 0)\)?

Step 1: Compute the likelihoods for \(C = 0\): \[P(C = 0 \mid D = 1) = 1 - 0.9 = 0.1 \quad \text{(false negative)}\] \[P(C = 0 \mid D = 0) = 1 - 0.05 = 0.95\]

Step 2: Compute \(P(C = 0)\) via the law of total probability: \[P(C = 0) = P(C = 0 \mid D = 1) \, P(D = 1) + P(C = 0 \mid D = 0) \, P(D = 0)\] \[= 0.1 \times 0.1 + 0.95 \times 0.9 = 0.01 + 0.855 = 0.865\]

Step 3: Apply Bayes' rule: \[P(D = 1 \mid C = 0) = \frac{P(C = 0 \mid D = 1) \, P(D = 1)}{P(C = 0)} = \frac{0.1 \times 0.1}{0.865} = \frac{0.01}{0.865} \approx 0.012\]

No creaking reduces the probability of damage from 10% (prior) to about 1.2% (posterior). The absence of evidence is evidence of absence—but not certainty. Compare this to the logical agent from Chapter 3, which would have concluded \(P = 0\) with absolute confidence.

Case 2: Creaking Observed

Now suppose the robot hears creaking (\(C = 1\)). What is \(P(D = 1 \mid C = 1)\)?

\[P(C = 1) = P(C = 1 \mid D = 1) \, P(D = 1) + P(C = 1 \mid D = 0) \, P(D = 0)\] \[= 0.9 \times 0.1 + 0.05 \times 0.9 = 0.09 + 0.045 = 0.135\]

\[P(D = 1 \mid C = 1) = \frac{0.9 \times 0.1}{0.135} = \frac{0.09}{0.135} \approx 0.667\]

Hearing creaking raises the probability of damage from 10% to about 67%. This is substantial but not certain—the false-positive rate means creaking might be spurious.

Summary of Updates

Bayesian updates for the warehouse creaking sensor
Observation \(P(D = 1)\) before \(P(D = 1)\) after
No creaking (\(C = 0\)) 0.10 0.012
Creaking (\(C = 1\)) 0.10 0.667

The updates are asymmetric: positive evidence (creaking) has a stronger effect than negative evidence (no creaking). This is because the sensor has a high true-positive rate and a low false-positive rate, so hearing creaking is quite informative.

What Changes with Multiple Adjacent Squares?

The analysis above focused on a single adjacent square \((2,1)\) for clarity. In reality, the robot at \((1,1)\) has two adjacent squares—\((2,1)\) and \((1,2)\)—and creaking could be caused by damage at either (or both). Let us spell out what changes.

Define three random variables:

  • \(D_1\): damage at \((2,1)\) (prior \(P(D_1 = 1) = 0.1\))
  • \(D_2\): damage at \((1,2)\) (prior \(P(D_2 = 1) = 0.1\))
  • \(C\): creaking detected at \((1,1)\)

Assume \(D_1\) and \(D_2\) are independent (damage at one square tells us nothing about another). The sensor model now depends on whether at least one adjacent square is damaged:

\[P(C = 1 \mid \text{at least one damaged}) = 0.9, \qquad P(C = 1 \mid \text{none damaged}) = 0.05\]

Step 1: Compute \(P(\text{at least one damaged})\) using independence:

\[P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - P(D_1 = 0) \, P(D_2 = 0) = 1 - 0.9 \times 0.9 = 0.19\]

Step 2: Compute \(P(C = 1)\) via total probability:

\[P(C = 1) = 0.9 \times 0.19 + 0.05 \times 0.81 = 0.171 + 0.0405 = 0.2115\]

Step 3: To find \(P(D_1 = 1 \mid C = 1)\), we need to be more careful. We must condition on all four \((D_1, D_2)\) combinations. Let \(A\) denote the event "at least one damaged":

\[P(D_1 = 1, C = 1) = \sum_{d_2} P(C = 1 \mid D_1 = 1, D_2 = d_2) \, P(D_1 = 1) \, P(D_2 = d_2)\]

When \(D_1 = 1\), at least one square is damaged regardless of \(D_2\), so \(P(C = 1 \mid D_1 = 1, D_2 = d_2) = 0.9\) for both values of \(d_2\):

\[P(D_1 = 1, C = 1) = 0.9 \times 0.1 \times 0.9 + 0.9 \times 0.1 \times 0.1 = 0.9 \times 0.1 = 0.09\]

Therefore:

\[P(D_1 = 1 \mid C = 1) = \frac{0.09}{0.2115} \approx 0.426\]

Compare this to the single-square result of \(0.667\). The posterior is lower because creaking now has a competing explanation: damage at \((1,2)\) instead. This is a form of explaining away—the more alternative causes exist, the less any single cause is implicated by the evidence.

The no-creaking case changes too: \(P(D_1 = 1 \mid C = 0) \approx 0.014\), slightly higher than the single-square value of \(0.012\), because the absence of creaking is slightly less exonerating when it must simultaneously speak to two squares.

See [@c4-p:exe:bayes-sensor] for a practice problem exploring this multi-square scenario further.

Inference with the Full Joint Distribution

For problems with multiple random variables, we can in principle compute any query by working with the full joint distribution—the probability assigned to every combination of values for all variables.

Full Joint Distribution

The full joint distribution over random variables \(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n\) is the function: \[ P(X_1 = x_1, X_2 = x_2, \ldots, X_n = x_n) \] for all possible combinations of values. It contains complete probabilistic information about the variables and their relationships.

Inference by Enumeration

Any conditional probability can be computed from the full joint distribution:

\[ P(X \mid E = e) = \frac{P(X, E = e)}{P(E = e)} = \frac{\sum_{y} P(X, E = e, Y = y)}{\sum_{x, y} P(X = x, E = e, Y = y)} \]

where \(Y\) represents all variables other than \(X\) and \(E\). The numerator marginalizes out the hidden variables \(Y\); the denominator normalizes.

Example: Suppose we have three warehouse squares with random variables \(D_1\), \(D_2\), \(D_3\) (damaged or not) and a creaking observation \(C\) at an adjacent location. If we have the full joint \(P(D_1, D_2, D_3, C)\), we can compute, say, \(P(D_1 \mid C = 1)\) by summing over all values of \(D_2\) and \(D_3\):

\[ P(D_1 = 1 \mid C = 1) = \frac{\sum_{d_2, d_3} P(D_1 = 1, D_2 = d_2, D_3 = d_3, C = 1)}{\sum_{d_1, d_2, d_3} P(D_1 = d_1, D_2 = d_2, D_3 = d_3, C = 1)} \]

The Curse of Dimensionality

For \(n\) binary random variables, the full joint distribution has \(2^n\) entries. Even for a modest \(4 \times 4\) warehouse with one binary variable per square, the joint distribution has \(2^{16} = 65{,}536\) entries. This exponential blowup makes direct enumeration impractical for large problems. Techniques like Bayesian networks (which we will not cover in this course) exploit conditional independence to compactly represent and efficiently query joint distributions.

Naive Bayes

One powerful simplification of the full joint distribution arises when we assume that all evidence variables are conditionally independent given the hypothesis.

Naive Bayes Model

In a Naive Bayes model, the evidence variables \(E_1, E_2, \ldots, E_k\) are conditionally independent given the hypothesis \(H\): \[ P(E_1, E_2, \ldots, E_k \mid H) = \prod_{i=1}^{k} P(E_i \mid H) \]

Combined with Bayes' rule, the posterior becomes: \[ P(H \mid E_1, \ldots, E_k) \propto P(H) \prod_{i=1}^{k} P(E_i \mid H) \]

The name "naive" comes from the conditional independence assumption, which is often unrealistic. Despite this, Naive Bayes classifiers perform surprisingly well in practice.

Warehouse Application

Suppose the robot has two sensor readings at \((1,1)\): creaking (\(C\)) and rumbling (\(R\)). It wants to assess the probability of damaged floor at \((2,1)\), with hypothesis \(D = D_{2,1}\).

Assuming creaking and rumbling are conditionally independent given the floor state:

\[ P(D = 1 \mid C, R) \propto P(D = 1) \, P(C \mid D = 1) \, P(R \mid D = 1) \]

With the creaking sensor model from before and a rumbling sensor that is independent of floor damage (\(P(R \mid D) = P(R)\)), the rumbling observation factors out and doesn't affect our belief about floor damage—exactly as we would expect.

If instead both sensors were informative about damage (perhaps a thermal sensor and an acoustic sensor), we could combine their evidence multiplicatively:

\[ P(D = 1 \mid C = 1, T = 1) \propto P(D = 1) \, P(C = 1 \mid D = 1) \, P(T = 1 \mid D = 1) \]

Each piece of evidence independently contributes to our belief update.

Belief State Updates

A probabilistic agent maintains a belief state: a probability distribution over the possible states of the world. As it acts and perceives, it updates this distribution using Bayes' rule.

The Probabilistic Agent Cycle

The cycle mirrors the knowledge-based agent from Chapter 3, but with probabilities instead of logical sentences:

  1. Maintain a belief state \(\mathbf{b}(s) = P(S = s \mid \text{all evidence so far})\)
  2. Perceive new evidence \(e\)
  3. Update the belief state using Bayes' rule: \[ \mathbf{b}'(s) = P(S = s \mid e, \text{prior evidence}) \propto P(e \mid S = s) \, \mathbf{b}(s) \]
  4. Act by choosing the action that maximizes expected utility under the current belief state
  5. Repeat

Warehouse Belief State Example

Consider the robot maintaining beliefs about all 16 squares of the \(4 \times 4\) warehouse. Initially, each square (other than the start) has some prior probability of being damaged.

As the robot moves and observes:

Belief updates as the robot explores
Step Location Observation Key belief updates
0 \((1,1)\) No creaking, no rumbling \(P(D_{2,1}) \downarrow\), \(P(D_{1,2}) \downarrow\)
1 \((2,1)\) Creaking, no rumbling \(P(D_{3,1}) \uparrow\), \(P(D_{2,2}) \uparrow\)
2 \((1,2)\) Rumbling, no creaking \(P(F_{1,3}) \uparrow\); \(P(D_{2,2}) \downarrow\) (which pushes \(P(D_{3,1}) \uparrow\) further)

Each observation narrows the belief state. After enough observations, the robot can identify hazard locations with high confidence—though never with absolute certainty, unlike the logical agent.

Comparison with the Logic-Based Agent

Comparison of logic-based and probabilistic reasoning
Feature Logic-based (Ch. 3) Probabilistic (Ch. 4)
Sensor model Perfect Noisy (false positives/negatives)
Conclusion type Certain (entailed / not entailed) Degree of belief (\([0, 1]\))
Unknown states "Unknown" (no information) Probability (quantified uncertainty)
Decision criterion Only enter provably safe squares Maximize expected utility
Failure mode Gets stuck when proof is impossible May accept calculated risk

The probabilistic agent is strictly more general: if sensors are perfect, the posterior probabilities collapse to 0 and 1, recovering logical certainty. Probability theory subsumes logic as a special case.

Summary

Bayes' rule provides a principled mechanism for updating beliefs:

  • The prior encodes what we believed before observing evidence
  • The likelihood models how evidence relates to hypotheses (typically in the causal direction)
  • The posterior is our revised belief, combining prior knowledge with new evidence
  • Naive Bayes simplifies multi-evidence problems via conditional independence
  • A probabilistic agent maintains a belief state and updates it with each observation

The next section extends this framework from single decisions to sequences of decisions: Markov decision processes, where the agent must plan ahead under uncertainty over multiple time steps.

sections.title: Markov Decision Processes
sections.html:
So far in this chapter, we have developed tools for reasoning about uncertainty at a single moment: computing posteriors, updating beliefs, and choosing the action with highest expected utility. But the warehouse robot doesn't make just one decision—it makes a sequence of decisions, and each decision affects what situations it will face in the future.

Moving to \((2,1)\) isn't just about whether \((2,1)\) is safe. It also determines what the robot will perceive next, which squares it can reach, and ultimately whether it can complete its mission. A rational agent must reason about the long-term consequences of its actions, not just immediate outcomes.

Markov decision processes (MDPs) formalize this kind of sequential decision-making under uncertainty {% cite 'russell2020' note='ch. 17' %}. They provide the mathematical framework that underlies the reinforcement learning algorithms we will study in Chapter 7.

From Single Decisions to Sequential Decisions

Consider a simplified warehouse navigation problem. The robot is at \((1,1)\) and wants to reach \((4,4)\) where the package is located. The environment is stochastic: when the robot tries to move north, it succeeds 80% of the time but drifts east or west with 10% probability each (and stays put if it would hit a wall).

This is fundamentally different from the deterministic search problems of Chapter 2. The robot cannot plan a fixed path and execute it blindly—the path may go wrong at any step. It needs a policy: a plan that specifies what to do in every state, because the robot may end up in states it didn't intend to visit.

The MDP Framework

Markov Decision Process (MDP)

A Markov decision process is defined by:

  • \(\mathcal{S}\): a finite set of states
  • \(\mathcal{A}\): a finite set of actions
  • \(T(s' \mid s, a)\): the transition model, giving the probability of reaching state \(s'\) when taking action \(a\) in state \(s\)
  • \(R(s)\): the reward function, giving the immediate reward for being in state \(s\)
  • \(\gamma \in [0, 1)\): the discount factor, which controls how much the agent values future rewards relative to immediate ones (detailed in [@m1:discounted-return])

The name "Markov" reflects the Markov property: the transition probabilities depend only on the current state and action, not on the history of how the agent arrived at that state:

\[ P(S_{t+1} = s' \mid S_t = s, A_t = a, S_{t-1}, A_{t-1}, \ldots) = P(S_{t+1} = s' \mid S_t = s, A_t = a) = T(s' \mid s, a) \]

This is a significant simplification: the current state captures all relevant information about the past. It is the probabilistic analog of the state-space formulations we used in Chapter 2, but now transitions are stochastic rather than deterministic.

Reward Function Variants

Some formulations use \(R(s, a)\) (reward depends on state and action) or \(R(s, a, s')\) (reward depends on the full transition). Any of these can simulate the others: for instance, an \(R(s, a)\) model can be rewritten as \(R(s)\) by folding the action-dependent component into the transition model. We use \(R(s)\) for simplicity, following {% cite 'russell2020' %}.

Warehouse MDP

Let us formulate the warehouse navigation as an MDP.

States: The robot's position \((x, y)\) on the \(4 \times 4\) grid defines the state. (This is a simplification: the full warehouse state would include battery level, cargo status, etc., but position captures the essential structure of the navigation problem.) Additionally, there is a terminal state reached when the robot is destroyed or exits successfully. Total: 17 states.

Actions: \(\mathcal{A} = \{\text{North}, \text{South}, \text{East}, \text{West}\}\).

Transition model: The robot's movement is stochastic:

  • With probability 0.8, the robot moves in the intended direction
  • With probability 0.1, the robot drifts 90\(^\circ\) to the left of the intended direction
  • With probability 0.1, the robot drifts 90\(^\circ\) to the right of the intended direction
  • If any of these movements would take the robot into a wall, the robot stays in its current cell

For example, from state \((2,2)\) taking action North:

\[ \begin{aligned} T((2,3) \mid (2,2), \text{North}) &= 0.8 & &\text{(success)} \\ T((1,2) \mid (2,2), \text{North}) &= 0.1 & &\text{(drift left/west)} \\ T((3,2) \mid (2,2), \text{North}) &= 0.1 & &\text{(drift right/east)} \end{aligned} \]

Rewards:

  • \(R(s) = -0.04\) for each non-terminal state (small cost of living, encouraging efficiency)
  • \(R(s) = +1\) for the goal state (package location)
  • \(R(s) = -1\) for states with damaged floor (the robot is destroyed)

Discount factor: \(\gamma = 0.99\). This means the robot values future rewards almost as much as immediate ones, but it still prefers to achieve the goal sooner rather than later.

Policies

Policy

A policy \(\pi\) is a function from states to actions: \(\pi(s) \in \mathcal{A}\) specifies which action to take in each state. A policy is stationary if it depends only on the current state, not on the time step.

A policy is a complete strategy: it tells the agent what to do in every possible situation. The agent follows the policy without deliberation at execution time—all the reasoning happens when computing the policy.

Example: A simple policy for the warehouse might be "always move North." This is a valid policy but a poor one: it ignores the locations of hazards and the goal.

The goal of solving an MDP is to find an optimal policy \(\pi^*\) that maximizes the expected cumulative reward.

Utility Over Time

Since the agent makes a sequence of decisions, we need to define what "total reward" means over time.

Cumulative Reward

The agent receives a reward \(R(s_t)\) at each time step \(t\). A natural measure of total performance is the sum of rewards:

\[ G_t = R(s_t) + R(s_{t+1}) + R(s_{t+2}) + \cdots \]

But this sum may be infinite for non-terminating tasks. The discount factor \(\gamma\) solves this problem.

Discounted Return

Discounted Return

The discounted return from time step \(t\) is: \[ G_t = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k R(s_{t+k}) \] where \(\gamma \in [0, 1)\) is the discount factor.

Discounting has two effects:

  1. Mathematical: It guarantees the sum converges (since \(\gamma^k \to 0\)). If rewards are bounded by \(R_{\max}\), then \(G_t \leq R_{\max} / (1 - \gamma)\).

  2. Behavioral: It makes the agent prefer rewards sooner rather than later. A reward received now is worth more than the same reward in the future. This is rational when there is any uncertainty about whether the agent will survive to collect future rewards.

Interpreting the Discount Factor

\(\gamma = 0\) makes the agent completely myopic: it considers only the immediate reward. \(\gamma\) close to 1 makes the agent far-sighted: it weighs future rewards almost as much as present ones. For the warehouse robot, \(\gamma = 0.99\) means a reward 100 steps in the future is worth \(0.99^{100} \approx 0.37\) of an immediate reward.

Value Functions

To find an optimal policy, we need to evaluate how good each state is under a given policy.

State Value Function

The state value function \(V^\pi(s)\) is the expected discounted return starting from state \(s\) and following policy \(\pi\): \[ V^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_\pi \left[ \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k R(s_{t+k}) \;\middle|\; s_t = s \right] \]

\(V^\pi(s)\) answers the question: "How much total reward can I expect to accumulate if I start in state \(s\) and always follow policy \(\pi\)?"

Optimal Value Function

The optimal value function \(V^*(s)\) is the maximum value achievable from state \(s\) under any policy: \[ V^*(s) = \max_\pi V^\pi(s) \]

An optimal policy \(\pi^*\) is any policy that achieves \(V^*\) in every state.

The Bellman Equation

The value function satisfies a recursive relationship that is central to all MDP solution methods.

Bellman Equation for $V^\pi$

For a policy \(\pi\), the value of state \(s\) satisfies: \[ V^\pi(s) = R(s) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, \pi(s)) \, V^\pi(s') \]

This says: the value of a state equals the immediate reward plus the discounted expected value of the next state. The expectation is over the stochastic transitions—the agent takes the action prescribed by \(\pi\), and nature determines the outcome.

For the optimal value function:

Bellman Optimality Equation

\[ V^*(s) = R(s) + \gamma \max_a \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, a) \, V^*(s') \]

The only difference: instead of following a fixed policy, the agent chooses the action that maximizes the expected value. The optimal policy is then:

\[ \pi^*(s) = \arg\max_a \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, a) \, V^*(s') \]

Bellman Equation Intuition

The Bellman equation expresses the principle of optimality: an optimal policy from state \(s\) consists of taking the best immediate action and then behaving optimally from whatever state results. This recursive structure is what makes dynamic programming possible.

Warehouse Bellman Example

Consider the robot at \((2,2)\) in our warehouse MDP. The Bellman equation for the optimal value at this state is:

\[V^*((2,2)) = R((2,2)) + \gamma \max_a \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid (2,2), a) \, V^*(s')\]

For action North:

\[\sum_{s'} T(s' \mid (2,2), \text{North}) \, V^*(s') = 0.8 \, V^*((2,3)) + 0.1 \, V^*((1,2)) + 0.1 \, V^*((3,2))\]

The \(\max\) in the Bellman equation selects whichever action yields the highest expected next-state value. But notice the circularity: each \(V^*(s')\) is itself defined by the same equation, depending on the optimal values of its successors, and so on recursively down to terminal states. We cannot evaluate the equation by simple substitution—this is precisely why we need iterative algorithms like value iteration ([@m1:value-iteration]) to solve it.

Value Iteration

The Bellman optimality equation is a system of \(|\mathcal{S}|\) simultaneous equations—one per state. We cannot solve them by simple substitution because the equations are mutually dependent (the value of each state depends on the values of other states). Value iteration solves this system iteratively.

Algorithm

Value Iteration

Initialize \(V_0(s) = 0\) for all states \(s\). Repeat until convergence: \[ V_{k+1}(s) = R(s) + \gamma \max_a \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, a) \, V_k(s') \quad \text{for all } s \in \mathcal{S} \]

The iteration terminates when \(\max_s |V_{k+1}(s) - V_k(s)| < \epsilon\) for a small tolerance \(\epsilon\).

The algorithm repeatedly applies the Bellman update, propagating value information through the state space. States near high-reward terminal states get high values first; these values gradually propagate to more distant states.

Convergence

Value iteration is guaranteed to converge to \(V^*\) because the Bellman update is a contraction mapping: each iteration brings the value function closer to \(V^*\) by a factor of at least \(\gamma\). After \(k\) iterations, the error is at most \(\gamma^k \cdot \text{span}(V_0 - V^*)\).

In practice, convergence is fast: the number of iterations needed for \(\epsilon\)-convergence is \(O\left(\frac{\log(1/\epsilon)}{1 - \gamma}\right)\), independent of the number of states.

Extracting the Policy

Once \(V^*\) is computed, the optimal policy is extracted using [@eq:optimal-policy]:

\[\pi^*(s) = \arg\max_a \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, a) \, V^*(s')\]

This requires one more pass through the states, computing the argmax for each.

Warehouse Value Iteration

Consider a simplified \(3 \times 3\) version of the warehouse MDP:

(1,3)  (2,3)  (3,3)
(1,2)  (2,2)  (3,2)
(1,1)  (2,1)  (3,1)
  • Goal at \((3,3)\): \(R((3,3)) = +1\) (terminal)
  • Damaged floor at \((3,2)\): \(R((3,2)) = -1\) (terminal)
  • All other states: \(R(s) = -0.04\)
  • \(\gamma = 0.99\), stochastic transitions (80/10/10 as above)

Iteration 0: \(V_0(s) = 0\) for all \(s\).

Iteration 1: Only terminal states get nonzero values from the Bellman update. For \((2,3)\) with action East:

\[V_1((2,3)) = -0.04 + 0.99 \max_a \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid (2,3), a) \, V_0(s') = -0.04 + 0 = -0.04\]

Since \(V_0 = 0\) everywhere, the first non-trivial iteration assigns \(V_1(s) = R(s)\) for terminal states and \(V_1(s) = R(s) = -0.04\) for non-terminal states.

Subsequent iterations: Values propagate outward from the goal and hazard. States closer to \((3,3)\) with safe paths accumulate positive value; states near \((3,2)\) accumulate negative value. After convergence, the value function encodes the "desirability" of every state, accounting for both the goal and the hazard.

The optimal policy typically navigates toward \((3,3)\) while keeping distance from \((3,2)\). Near the hazard, the policy may prefer a longer but safer route.

Policy Iteration

An alternative to value iteration is policy iteration, which alternates between evaluating a policy and improving it.

Policy Iteration

  1. Initialize: Start with an arbitrary policy \(\pi_0\).
  2. Policy evaluation: Compute \(V^{\pi_i}\) by solving the linear system: \[V^{\pi_i}(s) = R(s) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, \pi_i(s)) \, V^{\pi_i}(s')\]
  3. Policy improvement: Update the policy: \[\pi_{i+1}(s) = \arg\max_a \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, a) \, V^{\pi_i}(s')\]
  4. If \(\pi_{i+1} = \pi_i\), stop. Otherwise, go to step 2.

Policy iteration converges in a finite number of steps (at most \(|\mathcal{A}|^{|\mathcal{S}|}\) iterations, though in practice far fewer). Each policy improvement step is guaranteed to produce a policy that is at least as good as the previous one.

Policy Evaluation

The policy evaluation step solves the Bellman equation ([@eq:bellman-policy]) for a fixed policy. Since the policy is fixed, this is a system of \(|\mathcal{S}|\) linear equations in \(|\mathcal{S}|\) unknowns—unlike the nonlinear Bellman optimality equation. It can be solved directly by matrix inversion or iteratively.

Direct solution: Writing the equations in matrix form:

\[\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{R} + \gamma \mathbf{T}_\pi \mathbf{V}\]

where \(\mathbf{T}_\pi\) is the transition matrix under policy \(\pi\) (with entries \(T_\pi(s, s') = T(s' \mid s, \pi(s))\)). Solving:

\[\mathbf{V} = (\mathbf{I} - \gamma \mathbf{T}_\pi)^{-1} \mathbf{R}\]

This is \(O(|\mathcal{S}|^3)\) due to the matrix inversion, which is feasible for small to moderate state spaces.

Value Iteration vs. Policy Iteration

Comparison of value iteration and policy iteration
Aspect Value iteration Policy iteration
Per iteration One Bellman update per state Full policy evaluation + improvement
Iterations to converge Many (gradual convergence) Few (each step improves the policy)
Per-iteration cost \(O(|\mathcal{S}|^2 |\mathcal{A}|)\) \(O(|\mathcal{S}|^3 + |\mathcal{S}|^2 |\mathcal{A}|)\)
Best for Large state spaces Small to moderate state spaces

In practice, both methods produce the same optimal policy. Value iteration is simpler to implement; policy iteration often converges in fewer iterations but each iteration is more expensive.

The Warehouse MDP: Putting It Together

Let us trace through the complete solution of our warehouse MDP to build intuition for how the optimal policy emerges.

Grid Setup

         +------+------+------+------+
  y = 4  | -0.04| -0.04| -0.04|  +1  |
         +------+------+------+------+
  y = 3  | -0.04| -0.04| -0.04|  -1  |
         +------+------+------+------+
  y = 2  | -0.04| -0.04| -0.04| -0.04|
         +------+------+------+------+
  y = 1  |Start | -0.04| -0.04| -0.04|
         +------+------+------+------+
           x=1    x=2    x=3    x=4

Goal at \((4,4)\) with reward \(+1\). Damaged floor at \((4,3)\) with reward \(-1\). Both are terminal (the episode ends when the robot reaches either). All other states have reward \(-0.04\).

Optimal Policy

After running value iteration to convergence, the optimal policy looks like this (arrows indicate the action chosen in each state):

         +------+------+------+------+
  y = 4  |  →   |  →   |  →   | GOAL |
         +------+------+------+------+
  y = 3  |  ↑   |  ↑   |  ↑   | HAZD |
         +------+------+------+------+
  y = 2  |  ↑   |  ↑   |  ↑   |  ←   |
         +------+------+------+------+
  y = 1  |  ↑   |  ←   |  ↑   |  ←   |
         +------+------+------+------+
           x=1    x=2    x=3    x=4

Notice the policy at \((3,3)\): the robot moves up rather than right, even though moving right would take it directly toward the goal. Why? Because the stochastic transitions mean that moving right from \((3,3)\) has a 10% chance of drifting into the hazard at \((4,3)\). The policy trades a longer path for lower risk.

At \((4,2)\), the robot moves left rather than up, because moving up would have a 10% chance of drifting into \((4,3)\). The robot retreats to a safer column before navigating upward.

This is the power of MDPs: the optimal policy automatically balances efficiency (reaching the goal quickly) against safety (avoiding hazards), accounting for the stochastic nature of transitions.

Effect of the Living Penalty

The reward of \(-0.04\) for non-terminal states is the living penalty. It discourages the robot from wandering indefinitely. If we change this value, the optimal policy changes:

  • \(R(s) = -2\) (large penalty): The robot takes extreme risks to terminate quickly, preferring even the hazard to a long life of large penalties.
  • \(R(s) = -0.04\) (moderate penalty): The robot avoids hazards but doesn't dawdle.
  • \(R(s) = -0.001\) (tiny penalty): The robot is very cautious, taking long detours around hazards.
  • \(R(s) = +0.04\) (positive reward): The robot avoids all terminal states, including the goal, because living forever accumulates infinite positive reward.

This sensitivity to the reward function is important for engineering applications: the reward must be designed carefully to produce the desired behavior.

Connection to Reinforcement Learning

MDPs assume the agent knows the transition model \(T\) and reward function \(R\). In many real-world problems, the agent must learn these from experience—interacting with the environment and observing the results.

This is the setting of reinforcement learning (Chapter 7):

  • Model-based RL: Learn \(T\) and \(R\) from experience, then solve the MDP
  • Model-free RL: Learn the value function or policy directly from experience, without explicitly modeling \(T\) and \(R\)

The concepts from this section—policies, value functions, the Bellman equation, and discounting—carry directly into reinforcement learning. Understanding MDPs is essential preparation for that material.

Summary

Markov decision processes extend probabilistic reasoning to sequential decision-making:

  • An MDP is defined by states, actions, transition probabilities, rewards, and a discount factor
  • The Markov property means the current state captures all relevant history
  • A policy specifies an action for every state; the optimal policy maximizes expected discounted return
  • The Bellman equation relates the value of a state to the values of its successors
  • Value iteration and policy iteration are algorithms for computing optimal policies
  • The reward function critically shapes behavior—reward design is an engineering problem

These ideas form the foundation for reinforcement learning, where the agent must discover the optimal policy through interaction with an unknown environment.

sections.title: Implementation: Value Iteration for the Warehouse
sections.html:
The previous section developed the theory of Markov decision processes: states, actions, transitions, rewards, the Bellman equation, and the value iteration algorithm. In this section, we implement value iteration in Python for the \(4 \times 4\) warehouse MDP defined in [@m1:warehouse-mdp-full]. The implementation translates each component of the MDP framework directly into code, so that every function corresponds to a mathematical object we have already defined.

Defining the MDP

We begin by encoding the grid, the terminal states, and the reward function.

# Grid dimensions
WIDTH, HEIGHT = 4, 4

# Terminal states and their rewards
GOAL = (4, 4)
HAZARD = (4, 3)
TERMINALS = {GOAL: +1.0, HAZARD: -1.0}

# Living reward for non-terminal states
LIVING_REWARD = -0.04

# All states: every grid cell
STATES = [(x, y) for x in range(1, WIDTH + 1) for y in range(1, HEIGHT + 1)]

# Actions and their (dx, dy) displacements
ACTIONS = {
    "North": (0, 1),
    "South": (0, -1),
    "East": (1, 0),
    "West": (-1, 0),
}

States are represented as \((x, y)\) tuples matching the coordinate system from [@m1:warehouse-mdp]. The ACTIONS dictionary maps each action name to a displacement vector, which we will use in the transition model.

The reward function implements \(R(s)\) from [@m1:warehouse-mdp]: terminal states have their assigned reward; all other states pay the living penalty.

def reward(state):
    """R(s): immediate reward for being in state s."""
    if state in TERMINALS:
        return TERMINALS[state]
    return LIVING_REWARD

The Transition Model

The transition model \(T(s' \mid s, a)\) is the most involved piece. Recall from [@m1:warehouse-mdp] that when the robot takes an action, it moves in the intended direction with probability 0.8 and drifts 90\(^\circ\) to either side with probability 0.1 each. If any of these movements would take the robot off the grid, it stays in its current cell.

We build this in three helper functions.

Perpendicular actions. Given an action, return the two actions perpendicular to it. These are the possible drift directions.

def get_perpendicular(action):
    """Return the two actions perpendicular to the given action."""
    if action in ("North", "South"):
        return ["West", "East"]
    else:
        return ["North", "South"]

Attempting a move. Given a state and a direction, return the resulting state—or the original state if the move would leave the grid.

def attempt_move(state, action):
    """Return the state that results from attempting to move in the
    given direction. If the move would leave the grid, return the
    original state (the robot stays put)."""
    dx, dy = ACTIONS[action]
    nx, ny = state[0] + dx, state[1] + dy
    if 1 <= nx <= WIDTH and 1 <= ny <= HEIGHT:
        return (nx, ny)
    return state  # hit a wall, stay in place

The full transition function. Combine the intended move (probability 0.8) with the two perpendicular drifts (probability 0.1 each) to produce a distribution over next states.

def transitions(state, action):
    """T(s' | s, a): return a dict {s': probability} for all reachable
    states s' when taking action a in state s."""
    if state in TERMINALS:
        return {}  # no transitions from terminal states

    # Intended direction (80%) and two perpendicular drifts (10% each)
    outcomes = {}
    intended = attempt_move(state, action)
    outcomes[intended] = outcomes.get(intended, 0) + 0.8

    for perp in get_perpendicular(action):
        drifted = attempt_move(state, perp)
        outcomes[drifted] = outcomes.get(drifted, 0) + 0.1

    return outcomes

Notice the use of outcomes.get(intended, 0) + 0.8 rather than simple assignment. This handles the case where the intended direction and a drift direction both result in the same state—for example, when the robot is in a corner and multiple movements are blocked by walls. The probabilities accumulate correctly: if the robot is at \((1,1)\) and takes action West, the intended move (West, blocked) and one drift (South, blocked) both leave the robot at \((1,1)\), so \(T((1,1) \mid (1,1), \text{West}) = 0.8 + 0.1 = 0.9\).

Value Iteration

The core algorithm applies the Bellman update ([@eq:value-iteration]) to every non-terminal state until the value function converges.

def value_iteration(gamma=0.99, epsilon=1e-6):
    """Run value iteration and return the converged value function
    and the number of iterations."""
    # Initialize V(s) = 0 for all states
    V = {s: 0.0 for s in STATES}

    iteration = 0
    while True:
        V_new = {}
        delta = 0  # track the largest change

        for s in STATES:
            if s in TERMINALS:
                V_new[s] = reward(s)  # terminal values are fixed
                continue

            # Bellman update: V(s) = R(s) + gamma * max_a sum_s' T(s'|s,a) V(s')
            best_value = float("-inf")
            for a in ACTIONS:
                expected = sum(
                    prob * V[s_next]
                    for s_next, prob in transitions(s, a).items()
                )
                best_value = max(best_value, expected)

            V_new[s] = reward(s) + gamma * best_value
            delta = max(delta, abs(V_new[s] - V[s]))

        V = V_new
        iteration += 1

        if delta < epsilon:
            break

    return V, iteration

Let us trace through how this corresponds to the mathematics:

  • Initialization: \(V_0(s) = 0\) for all \(s\) corresponds to V = {s: 0.0 for s in STATES}.
  • The inner loop over states computes \(V_{k+1}(s)\) for each \(s\). For each state, it evaluates every action by computing \(\sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, a) \, V_k(s')\) (the expected variable), takes the \(\max\) over actions (best_value), and applies the full Bellman update \(V_{k+1}(s) = R(s) + \gamma \cdot \max_a(\cdots)\).
  • Convergence check: delta tracks \(\max_s |V_{k+1}(s) - V_k(s)|\). When this falls below \(\epsilon\), the algorithm terminates.
  • Synchronous updates: The new values go into V_new while the old values in V are still used for all lookups within the same iteration. This ensures the update is synchronous—every state uses the values from iteration \(k\), not a mix of \(k\) and \(k+1\).

Asynchronous Updates

An alternative is to update V in place (asynchronous or Gauss–Seidel updates). This can converge faster in practice because states immediately benefit from their neighbors' updated values, but the convergence analysis is more involved. Our synchronous implementation matches the algorithm as stated in [@m1:value-iteration-algorithm].

Extracting the Policy

Once \(V^*\) is known, the optimal policy follows from [@eq:optimal-policy]: for each state, pick the action that maximizes the expected next-state value.

def extract_policy(V, gamma=0.99):
    """Compute the optimal policy from a converged value function."""
    policy = {}
    for s in STATES:
        if s in TERMINALS:
            policy[s] = None  # no action in terminal states
            continue

        best_action = None
        best_value = float("-inf")
        for a in ACTIONS:
            expected = sum(
                prob * V[s_next]
                for s_next, prob in transitions(s, a).items()
            )
            value = reward(s) + gamma * expected
            if value > best_value:
                best_value = value
                best_action = a

        policy[s] = best_action
    return policy

This is almost identical to the inner loop of value_iteration, but instead of keeping the best value, it keeps the best action. The argmax and max are computed over the same quantity.

Displaying the Results

A helper function prints the value function and policy as grids, matching the visual format from [@m1:grid-setup].

ARROWS = {"North": "\u2191", "South": "\u2193", "East": "\u2192", "West": "\u2190"}


def display_grid(V, policy):
    """Print the value function and policy as grids."""
    print("Value function V*:")
    for y in range(HEIGHT, 0, -1):
        row = []
        for x in range(1, WIDTH + 1):
            s = (x, y)
            row.append(f"{V[s]:7.3f}")
        print("  ".join(row))

    print("\nOptimal policy:")
    for y in range(HEIGHT, 0, -1):
        row = []
        for x in range(1, WIDTH + 1):
            s = (x, y)
            if s == GOAL:
                row.append("  GOAL ")
            elif s == HAZARD:
                row.append("  HAZD ")
            else:
                row.append(f"   {ARROWS[policy[s]]}   ")
        print("".join(row))

Running the Implementation

Putting it all together:

V, num_iterations = value_iteration(gamma=0.99)
policy = extract_policy(V, gamma=0.99)
print(f"Converged in {num_iterations} iterations.\n")
display_grid(V, policy)

Output:

Converged in 55 iterations.

Value function V*:
  0.812   0.868   0.918   1.000
  0.762   0.812   0.660  -1.000
  0.705   0.655   0.611   0.388
  0.655   0.611   0.572   0.344

Optimal policy:
   →      →      →     GOAL
   ↑      ↑      ↑     HAZD
   ↑      ↑      ↑      ←
   ↑      ←      ↑      ←

The output confirms what we predicted in [@m1:optimal-policy-result]. The value function is highest near the goal and decreases with distance. The policy steers the robot upward along the left side of the grid, avoiding the column adjacent to the hazard. At \((4,1)\) and \((4,2)\), the robot moves away from the goal (leftward) to avoid the risk of drifting into the hazard at \((4,3)\).

Verifying the Policy

It is worth checking whether the policy makes physical sense. Consider \((4,2)\), where the policy says \(\leftarrow\) (West)—the robot moves away from the goal. Why not go North? From \((4,2)\), North goes to \((4,3) = \text{HAZARD}\) with probability 0.8. That single transition has expected next-state value \(0.8 \times (-1.0) = -0.8\) before even considering the drifts. West, by contrast, moves to \((3,2)\) with probability 0.8, avoiding the hazard entirely. The policy sacrifices proximity to the goal for safety—exactly the tradeoff that MDPs are designed to reason about.

Effect of the Living Reward

The living reward \(R(s) = -0.04\) shapes the policy by penalizing each step the robot takes. We can rerun value iteration with different living rewards to see how the policy changes.

for r in [-2.0, -0.4, -0.04, -0.01, +0.01]:
    LIVING_REWARD = r
    V, iters = value_iteration(gamma=0.99)
    policy = extract_policy(V, gamma=0.99)
    print(f"\nLiving reward = {r:+.2f} (converged in {iters} iterations)")

    # Show just the policy
    print("Policy:")
    for y in range(HEIGHT, 0, -1):
        row = []
        for x in range(1, WIDTH + 1):
            s = (x, y)
            if s == GOAL:
                row.append(" GOAL")
            elif s == HAZARD:
                row.append(" HAZD")
            else:
                row.append(f"  {ARROWS[policy[s]]} ")
        print("".join(row))

Output (abbreviated):

Living reward = -2.00 (converged in 7 iterations)
Policy:
  →   →   →  GOAL
  →   ↑   →  HAZD
  →   ↑   ↑   ↑
  →   →   ↑   ↑

Living reward = -0.40 (converged in 27 iterations)
Policy:
  →   →   →  GOAL
  ↑   ↑   ↑  HAZD
  ↑   ↑   ↑   ←
  ↑   ←   ↑   ←

Living reward = -0.04 (converged in 55 iterations)
Policy:
  →   →   →  GOAL
  ↑   ↑   ↑  HAZD
  ↑   ↑   ↑   ←
  ↑   ←   ↑   ←

Living reward = -0.01 (converged in 98 iterations)
Policy:
  →   →   →  GOAL
  ↑   ↑   ↑  HAZD
  ↑   ↑   ↑   ←
  ↑   ←   ↑   ←

Living reward = +0.01 (converged in 131 iterations)
Policy:
  ←   ↓   ↓  GOAL
  ←   ←   ↓  HAZD
  ←   ←   ←   ↓
  ←   ←   ←   ←

The results match the qualitative predictions from [@m1:living-penalty]:

  • \(R = -2.00\): The penalty for existing is so severe that the robot rushes toward any terminal state. It takes the shortest path even if that means risking the hazard. Some states even point directly toward the hazard—quick termination is preferable to accumulating large penalties.
  • \(R = -0.40\) and \(R = -0.04\): The robot avoids the hazard but still moves efficiently toward the goal. The policies are similar because both penalties are large enough to discourage dawdling but small enough that the hazard's \(-1\) reward is worth avoiding.
  • \(R = -0.01\): Very cautious. The robot takes the same safe route but convergence is slower because there is less urgency.
  • \(R = +0.01\): The robot avoids all terminal states—including the goal. Every step earns positive reward, so the optimal strategy is to wander forever, staying as far from terminal states as possible. This pathological behavior illustrates why reward design matters: a positive living reward creates an agent that never completes its task.

Summary

This implementation demonstrates the complete pipeline for solving an MDP:

  1. Encode the MDP: represent states, actions, \(T(s' \mid s, a)\), and \(R(s)\) as data structures and functions
  2. Run value iteration: repeatedly apply the Bellman update until convergence
  3. Extract the policy: take the argmax over actions at each state
  4. Analyze: vary parameters (living reward, discount factor) to understand how they shape behavior

The code is compact—under 100 lines for the core algorithm—because the mathematical framework does the heavy lifting. Each function maps directly to a concept from [@m1:mdp-framework]: reward implements \(R(s)\), transitions implements \(T(s' \mid s, a)\), value_iteration implements the update rule from [@def:value-iteration], and extract_policy implements [@eq:optimal-policy].

sections.title: Problems
sections.html:
Bayesian Sensor Reasoning

Goal: Apply Bayes' rule to reason about hazards in the warehouse with noisy sensors.

Setup: A warehouse robot is at position \((1,1)\) in a \(3 \times 3\) grid. Its creaking sensor has a true-positive rate of 85% and a false-positive rate of 8%. The prior probability of damaged floor at any given square is 0.15.

The robot's adjacent squares from \((1,1)\) are \((2,1)\) and \((1,2)\).

Simplification: For parts 1–3, consider the creaking sensor's response to a single adjacent square (i.e., treat the sensor as reporting on one square at a time). Part 4 considers the multi-square case.

Tasks:

  1. No creaking observed: The robot hears no creaking at \((1,1)\). Using Bayes' rule, compute the posterior probability that \((2,1)\) has damaged floor. Show all steps, clearly labeling the prior, likelihood, evidence, and posterior.

  2. Creaking observed: Now suppose the robot does hear creaking at \((1,1)\). Compute the posterior probability that \((2,1)\) has damaged floor.

  3. Sensor comparison: A newer sensor model has a true-positive rate of 95% and a false-positive rate of 2%. Repeat parts 1 and 2 with this sensor. How does sensor quality affect the posterior?

  4. Multiple adjacent squares: In reality, creaking at \((1,1)\) means damage at \((2,1)\) or \((1,2)\) (or both). Assume floor damage at different squares is independent with prior probability 0.15 each. Define:

    • \(C\): creaking detected at \((1,1)\)
    • \(D_1\): damage at \((2,1)\)
    • \(D_2\): damage at \((1,2)\)

    The sensor detects creaking iff at least one adjacent square is damaged, subject to the noise model: \(P(C = 1 \mid \text{at least one damaged}) = 0.85\) and \(P(C = 1 \mid \text{none damaged}) = 0.08\).

    Compute \(P(D_1 = 1 \mid C = 0)\). (Hint: first compute \(P(\text{at least one damaged})\) using independence, then apply the law of total probability.)

Belief State Tracking

Goal: Track a probability distribution over multiple hypotheses as evidence accumulates.

Setup: A warehouse has four rooms: A, B, C, D. A high-value package is hidden in exactly one room. The prior is uniform: \(P(\text{Package in } X) = 0.25\) for each room \(X\).

The robot has a package scanner with the following characteristics:

  • When the robot is in the room with the package: scanner beeps with probability 0.9
  • When the robot is in a room without the package: scanner beeps with probability 0.05

Tasks:

  1. The robot enters Room A and the scanner does not beep. Update the belief state over all four rooms. (Hint: compute the posterior for each room. The posteriors should sum to 1.)

  2. The robot then enters Room B and the scanner beeps. Starting from the belief state computed in part 1, update again. Show the new belief state.

  3. How many rooms must the robot visit (in the worst case) before it can identify the package location with at least 99% confidence?

  4. Suppose the scanner is perfect (\(P(\text{beep} \mid \text{package here}) = 1\), \(P(\text{beep} \mid \text{no package}) = 0\)). How does the belief update simplify? Connect this to the logical agent from Chapter 3.

Formulating an MDP

Goal: Practice defining MDPs for different problems.

Setup: A delivery robot operates on the following \(3 \times 4\) grid:

+------+------+------+------+
|      |      |      | +1   |
+------+------+------+------+
|      | XXXX |      | -1   |
+------+------+------+------+
|Start |      |      |      |
+------+------+------+------+
  • The robot starts at the bottom-left cell.
  • The cell marked XXXX is a wall (the robot cannot enter it).
  • The top-right cell has reward \(+1\) (goal, terminal).
  • The cell at row 2, column 4 has reward \(-1\) (hazard, terminal).
  • All other cells have reward \(-0.04\).
  • Actions: North, South, East, West.
  • Transitions: 80% intended direction, 10% each perpendicular direction. If the resulting cell is a wall or outside the grid, the robot stays in place.

Tasks:

  1. State and action spaces: List all states and actions. How many non-terminal states are there?

  2. Transition probabilities: Compute the full transition distribution \(T(s' \mid s, a)\) for the robot at \((1,2)\) taking action East. List every reachable state and its probability. (Remember the wall at \((2,2)\).)

  3. Bellman equation: Write the Bellman optimality equation for state \((3,2)\). Expand the equation for at least two actions (e.g., North and East), listing all terms.

  4. Value iteration by hand: Initialize \(V_0(s) = 0\) for all non-terminal states and \(V_0 = R(s)\) for terminal states. Compute \(V_1(s)\) for every state. Then compute \(V_2(s)\) for states \((3,2)\) and \((3,1)\). Use \(\gamma = 1\) for simplicity.

  5. Qualitative policy: Without running value iteration to full convergence, sketch the optimal policy. Which states should the robot be most cautious in? Where might the policy differ from the shortest path?

Building an MDP Agent (Guided)

Goal: Design a complete warehouse agent that uses value iteration to plan offline, then executes its optimal policy in a stochastic environment. This bridges the MDP theory from [@m1] and the implementation from [@vi] with the agent framework from Chapter 3.

Setup: Use the MDP code from [@vi] (states, actions, transitions, rewards, value_iteration, extract_policy). You will add an environment simulator and an agent that interacts with it.

Tasks:

  1. Environment simulator: Write a function simulate_step(state, action) that returns a next state sampled from the transition distribution \(T(s' \mid s, a)\). Use Python's random.choices (or equivalent) to sample according to the probabilities returned by transitions(state, action). Verify your function by calling simulate_step((3, 1), "North") many times and checking that the empirical frequencies approximate 80/10/10.

  2. Agent loop: Write a function run_episode(policy, start=(1, 1), max_steps=100) that simulates a full episode:

    • Start at start.
    • At each step, look up \(\pi^*(s)\) in the policy, call simulate_step, accumulate the (undiscounted) reward, and record the trajectory.
    • Stop when a terminal state is reached or max_steps is exceeded.
    • Return the trajectory (list of states visited), the total reward, and whether the agent reached the goal, hit the hazard, or timed out.

    Run 1000 episodes with the optimal policy from [@vi]. Report: (a) the fraction of episodes that reach the goal, (b) the fraction that hit the hazard, (c) the average total reward.

  3. Comparison with a naive policy: Define a greedy policy that always moves in the direction of the goal (East if the goal is east of the robot, North if the goal is north, etc.), without considering the hazard. Run 1000 episodes with this policy and report the same three statistics. How does the MDP-optimal policy compare?

  4. Discount factor experiment: Compute optimal policies for \(\gamma \in \{0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 0.99\}\) (with living reward \(-0.04\)). For each, run 1000 episodes and report the goal-reach rate and average reward. At what value of \(\gamma\) does the agent first consistently avoid the hazard?

  5. A harder warehouse: Add a second hazard at \((2, 3)\) with reward \(-1\). Recompute the optimal policy and run 1000 episodes. Display the new policy. In 2–3 sentences, describe how the agent's behavior changed and whether the goal-reach rate decreased.

Naive Bayes for Warehouse Classification

Goal: Build a Naive Bayes classifier to classify warehouse zones as safe or hazardous based on sensor features.

Setup: A warehouse inspection robot collects the following features at each location:

Feature Values Description
Vibration Low, Medium, High Floor vibration level
Temperature Normal, Elevated Surface temperature
Sound Quiet, Creaking, Loud Ambient sound level

Historical inspection data provides the following statistics:

Class priors: \(P(\text{Safe}) = 0.75\), \(P(\text{Hazardous}) = 0.25\)

Likelihoods (conditional probabilities of each feature given the class):

Feature Value \(P(\cdot \mid \text{Safe})\) \(P(\cdot \mid \text{Hazardous})\)
Vibration Low 0.7 0.1
Vibration Medium 0.2 0.3
Vibration High 0.1 0.6
Temperature Normal 0.85 0.4
Temperature Elevated 0.15 0.6
Sound Quiet 0.6 0.1
Sound Creaking 0.3 0.5
Sound Loud 0.1 0.4

Tasks:

  1. Classify a new observation: The robot observes Vibration=High, Temperature=Elevated, Sound=Creaking. Compute the posterior probability of each class using Naive Bayes. Show the numerator computation for each class and the final normalized posteriors. What is the classification?

  2. Classify an ambiguous case: The robot observes Vibration=Medium, Temperature=Normal, Sound=Quiet. Compute the posteriors. Is this a clear classification or is there significant uncertainty?

  3. Missing features: Suppose the temperature sensor fails and the robot can only observe Vibration and Sound. How does the Naive Bayes computation change? Classify the observation Vibration=High, Sound=Loud with and without the temperature feature.

  4. Conditional independence assumption: Give one concrete example where the conditional independence assumption might be violated for these warehouse features (i.e., where knowing one feature value would change your estimate of another, even after conditioning on the class). How might this affect classification accuracy?

Expected Utility and Decision Making

Goal: Practice computing expected utility and making rational decisions under uncertainty.

Setup: The warehouse robot is at position \((2,2)\) and must choose one of three actions:

  • Action A (Move North to \((2,3)\)): Safe with probability 0.9, leads to damaged floor with probability 0.1
  • Action B (Move East to \((3,2)\)): Safe with probability 0.7, leads to the forklift with probability 0.3
  • Action C (Stay and scan): Always safe, but costs time (one action penalty)

Utility values: - Reaching a safe square and advancing toward goal: \(U = +5\) - Being destroyed by damaged floor: \(U = -100\) - Being destroyed by the forklift: \(U = -100\) - Staying and scanning (gaining information): \(U = -1\)

Tasks:

  1. Compute the expected utility of each action. Which action should a rational (MEU) agent choose?

  2. Suppose after scanning (Action C), the robot updates its beliefs: the probability of damage at \((2,3)\) drops to 0.02 and the probability of the forklift at \((3,2)\) drops to 0.05. Now compute EU(A) and EU(B) with the updated probabilities. Was scanning worth it?

  3. Risk sensitivity: At what probability of damage \(p\) does Action A have zero expected utility? What does this tell us about the threshold where the agent should become cautious?

  4. Value of information: Compute the expected utility of the strategy "scan first, then choose the better of A or B with updated probabilities" and compare it to the best single-action expected utility from part 1. The difference is the value of information from scanning.

Bayesian Reasoning and MDP Policy

Part A — Bayesian Update

A warehouse robot has a battery sensor that triggers an alarm when the battery is low. The sensor is not perfect:

  • \(P(\text{alarm} \mid \text{low}) = 0.90\) (90% true-positive rate)
  • \(P(\text{alarm} \mid \text{ok}) = 0.10\) (10% false-positive rate)
  • \(P(\text{low}) = 0.05\) (prior: 5% of the time the battery is actually low)

(a) The alarm triggers. Compute the posterior \(P(\text{low} \mid \text{alarm})\) using Bayes' rule ([@def:bayes-rule]):

\[P(\text{low} \mid \text{alarm}) = \frac{P(\text{alarm} \mid \text{low}) \cdot P(\text{low})}{P(\text{alarm})}\]

The denominator is: \(P(\text{alarm}) = 0.90 \times 0.05 + 0.10 \times 0.95 = 0.14\). Compute the numerator and the final posterior.

(b) A second independent sensor also triggers. Using your answer from (a) as the new prior, apply Bayes' rule again. Has the belief changed substantially?

Part B — Markov Decision Process

\(3 \times 2\) grid MDP. Deterministic transitions (moving into a wall stays in place). \(\gamma = 0.9\).

Col 1 Col 2 Col 3
Row 2 S (\(-0.04\)) M (\(-0.04\)) G (\(+1\), terminal)
Row 1 \(-0.04\) \(-0.04\) H (\(-1\), terminal)

After iteration 1 (from \(V_0 = 0\)): \(V_1(s) = R(s)\) for all non-terminal states, so \(V_1(S) = V_1(M) = -0.04\). Terminal values: \(V_1(G) = +1\), \(V_1(H) = -1\).

(c) Perform the second iteration for state M. M can go East to G (\(V_1 = +1\)), South (\(V_1 = -0.04\)), West to S (\(V_1 = -0.04\)), or North (hits wall, stays at M, \(V_1 = -0.04\)). Compute \(V_2(M) = R(M) + \gamma \max_a V_1(\text{next state})\) ([@def:bellman-optimal]).

(d) What is the greedy policy at M after iteration 2? What about at S? Draw arrows on the grid.

the goal). After a few more iterations this stabilizes. :::
