exe:bayes-sensor.content:
Setup

  • Prior: \(P(D = 1) = 0.15\), so \(P(D = 0) = 0.85\)
  • Old sensor: true-positive rate \(P(C = 1 \mid D = 1) = 0.85\), false-positive rate \(P(C = 1 \mid D = 0) = 0.08\)

Part 1: No Creaking Observed

We want \(P(D = 1 \mid C = 0)\).

Prior: \(P(D = 1) = 0.15\)

Likelihood (for \(C = 0\)):

\[P(C = 0 \mid D = 1) = 1 - 0.85 = 0.15 \quad \text{(false negative: damage present but no creaking)}\] \[P(C = 0 \mid D = 0) = 1 - 0.08 = 0.92 \quad \text{(true negative: no damage, no creaking)}\]

Evidence (law of total probability):

\[P(C = 0) = P(C = 0 \mid D = 1) \, P(D = 1) + P(C = 0 \mid D = 0) \, P(D = 0)\] \[= 0.15 \times 0.15 + 0.92 \times 0.85 = 0.0225 + 0.782 = 0.8045\]

Posterior (Bayes' rule):

\[P(D = 1 \mid C = 0) = \frac{P(C = 0 \mid D = 1) \, P(D = 1)}{P(C = 0)} = \frac{0.15 \times 0.15}{0.8045} = \frac{0.0225}{0.8045} \approx 0.0280\]

No creaking reduces the probability of damage from 15% to about 2.8%.

Part 2: Creaking Observed

We want \(P(D = 1 \mid C = 1)\).

Likelihood (for \(C = 1\)):

\[P(C = 1 \mid D = 1) = 0.85, \qquad P(C = 1 \mid D = 0) = 0.08\]

Evidence:

\[P(C = 1) = 0.85 \times 0.15 + 0.08 \times 0.85 = 0.1275 + 0.068 = 0.1955\]

Posterior:

\[P(D = 1 \mid C = 1) = \frac{0.85 \times 0.15}{0.1955} = \frac{0.1275}{0.1955} \approx 0.6522\]

Hearing creaking raises the probability from 15% to about 65%.

Check: The two posteriors should be consistent with the evidence probabilities:

\[P(D = 1 \mid C = 0) \times P(C = 0) + P(D = 1 \mid C = 1) \times P(C = 1) = P(D = 1)\] \[0.0280 \times 0.8045 + 0.6522 \times 0.1955 \approx 0.0225 + 0.1275 = 0.15 \checkmark\]

Part 3: Sensor Comparison

New sensor: \(P(C = 1 \mid D = 1) = 0.95\), \(P(C = 1 \mid D = 0) = 0.02\).

No creaking (\(C = 0\)):

\[P(C = 0 \mid D = 1) = 0.05, \qquad P(C = 0 \mid D = 0) = 0.98\] \[P(C = 0) = 0.05 \times 0.15 + 0.98 \times 0.85 = 0.0075 + 0.833 = 0.8405\] \[P(D = 1 \mid C = 0) = \frac{0.05 \times 0.15}{0.8405} = \frac{0.0075}{0.8405} \approx 0.0089\]

Creaking (\(C = 1\)):

\[P(C = 1) = 0.95 \times 0.15 + 0.02 \times 0.85 = 0.1425 + 0.017 = 0.1595\] \[P(D = 1 \mid C = 1) = \frac{0.95 \times 0.15}{0.1595} = \frac{0.1425}{0.1595} \approx 0.8934\]

Comparison summary:

Old sensor New sensor
\(P(D = 1 \mid C = 0)\) 0.028 0.009
\(P(D = 1 \mid C = 1)\) 0.652 0.893

The better sensor is more informative in both directions: silence is stronger evidence of safety (0.9% vs. 2.8%), and creaking is stronger evidence of damage (89% vs. 65%). The lower false-positive rate means creaking is more trustworthy; the higher true-positive rate means silence is more exonerating.

Part 4: Multiple Adjacent Squares

Define:

  • \(D_1\): damage at \((2,1)\), \(D_2\): damage at \((1,2)\), both with prior 0.15
  • \(D_1, D_2\) independent
  • \(A\): at least one adjacent square is damaged

Step 1: Probability of at least one damaged square.

\[P(A) = 1 - P(D_1 = 0) \, P(D_2 = 0) = 1 - 0.85 \times 0.85 = 1 - 0.7225 = 0.2775\]

So \(P(\text{none damaged}) = 0.7225\).

Step 2: Compute \(P(C = 0)\) via total probability.

\[P(C = 0) = P(C = 0 \mid A) \, P(A) + P(C = 0 \mid \overline{A}) \, P(\overline{A})\] \[= (1 - 0.85) \times 0.2775 + (1 - 0.08) \times 0.7225\] \[= 0.15 \times 0.2775 + 0.92 \times 0.7225\] \[= 0.041625 + 0.6647 = 0.7063\]

Step 3: Compute \(P(D_1 = 1 \mid C = 0)\).

We need \(P(D_1 = 1, C = 0)\), which requires summing over \(D_2\):

\[P(D_1 = 1, C = 0) = \sum_{d_2} P(C = 0 \mid D_1 = 1, D_2 = d_2) \, P(D_1 = 1) \, P(D_2 = d_2)\]

When \(D_1 = 1\), at least one square is damaged regardless of \(D_2\), so \(P(C = 0 \mid D_1 = 1, D_2 = d_2) = 1 - 0.85 = 0.15\) for both values of \(d_2\):

\[P(D_1 = 1, C = 0) = 0.15 \times 0.15 \times 0.85 + 0.15 \times 0.15 \times 0.15 = 0.15 \times 0.15 \times (0.85 + 0.15) = 0.15 \times 0.15 = 0.0225\]

Therefore:

\[\boxed{P(D_1 = 1 \mid C = 0) = \frac{0.0225}{0.7063} \approx 0.0319}\]

This is slightly higher than the single-square result from Part 1 (\(\approx 0.028\)). Why? The numerator \(P(D_1 = 1, C = 0) = 0.0225\) is identical in both cases. The difference is entirely in the denominator: \(P(C = 0) = 0.7063\) here versus \(0.8045\) in Part 1. With two potential damage sources, no-creaking is a rarer event overall (there are more ways for at least one square to be damaged and trigger the sensor). Since no-creaking is less common, observing it is less informative about any single square—it doesn't exonerate \((2,1)\) as strongly.
exe:bayes-sensor.title: Bayesian Sensor Reasoning

exe:belief-update.content:
Setup

  • Four rooms: A, B, C, D. Package is in exactly one.
  • Prior: \(b_0(X) = P(\text{Package in } X) = 0.25\) for each \(X\).
  • Scanner: \(P(\text{beep} \mid \text{package here}) = 0.9\), \(P(\text{beep} \mid \text{no package}) = 0.05\).

Part 1: Room A, No Beep

The robot enters Room A and the scanner does not beep. Let \(E_1 = \overline{\text{beep}}\) denote this evidence. We update the belief for each hypothesis about where the package is.

Likelihoods of "no beep in Room A" under each hypothesis:

  • Package in A: \(P(E_1 \mid A) = 1 - 0.9 = 0.10\) (scanner missed it)
  • Package in B: \(P(E_1 \mid B) = 1 - 0.05 = 0.95\) (no package here, no beep is expected)
  • Package in C: \(P(E_1 \mid C) = 0.95\) (same reasoning)
  • Package in D: \(P(E_1 \mid D) = 0.95\) (same reasoning)

Unnormalized posteriors \(P(E_1 \mid X) \, b_0(X)\):

Room \(X\) \(P(E_1 \mid X)\) \(b_0(X)\) Unnormalized
A 0.10 0.25 0.025
B 0.95 0.25 0.2375
C 0.95 0.25 0.2375
D 0.95 0.25 0.2375

Normalizing constant: \(Z = 0.025 + 3 \times 0.2375 = 0.025 + 0.7125 = 0.7375\)

Normalized posteriors \(b_1(X)\):

\[b_1(A) = \frac{0.025}{0.7375} \approx 0.0339\] \[b_1(B) = b_1(C) = b_1(D) = \frac{0.2375}{0.7375} \approx 0.3220\]

Check: \(0.0339 + 3 \times 0.3220 = 0.0339 + 0.9661 = 1.0000 \checkmark\)

The no-beep in Room A dramatically reduced \(b(A)\) from 25% to 3.4%, and the probability mass shifted roughly equally to the other three rooms.

Part 2: Room B, Beep

Starting from \(b_1\), the robot enters Room B and the scanner beeps. Let \(E_2 = \text{beep}\).

Likelihoods of "beep in Room B" under each hypothesis:

  • Package in A: \(P(E_2 \mid A) = 0.05\) (no package in B, false positive)
  • Package in B: \(P(E_2 \mid B) = 0.90\) (package is here, true positive)
  • Package in C: \(P(E_2 \mid C) = 0.05\) (no package in B, false positive)
  • Package in D: \(P(E_2 \mid D) = 0.05\) (no package in B, false positive)

Unnormalized posteriors \(P(E_2 \mid X) \, b_1(X)\):

Room \(X\) \(P(E_2 \mid X)\) \(b_1(X)\) Unnormalized
A 0.05 0.0339 0.001695
B 0.90 0.3220 0.28983
C 0.05 0.3220 0.01610
D 0.05 0.3220 0.01610

Normalizing constant: \(Z = 0.001695 + 0.28983 + 2 \times 0.01610 = 0.32373\)

Normalized posteriors \(b_2(X)\):

\[b_2(A) = \frac{0.001695}{0.32373} \approx 0.0052\] \[b_2(B) = \frac{0.28983}{0.32373} \approx 0.8953\] \[b_2(C) = b_2(D) = \frac{0.01610}{0.32373} \approx 0.0497\]

Check: \(0.0052 + 0.8953 + 2 \times 0.0497 = 0.9999 \approx 1.0 \checkmark\)

After two observations, the robot is about 90% confident the package is in Room B. Room A has been nearly eliminated (0.5%), and Rooms C and D each have about 5%.

Part 3: Rooms to 99% Confidence (Worst Case)

The question is: how many rooms must the robot visit before it can identify the package location with at least 99% confidence, in the worst case?

Key observations: With noisy sensors, no single observation can give certainty. Each no-beep reduces a room's posterior but doesn't eliminate it. Each beep boosts a room's posterior but doesn't confirm it. The worst case for the number of visits occurs when the package is in the last room the robot checks, so the robot accumulates only no-beep evidence for the first several visits.

Scenario: The robot visits A, B, C, D in order. The package is in D. Assume the robot gets the most likely observation at each step (no-beep when the package is absent, beep when present).

After visiting A (no beep): From Part 1, \(b(A) \approx 0.034\), \(b(B) = b(C) = b(D) \approx 0.322\).

After visiting B (no beep): The likelihood of no-beep-in-B is 0.10 if the package is in B (false negative) and 0.95 if the package is elsewhere. So B's posterior drops sharply, while all other rooms' posteriors increase slightly after normalization:

  • Unnormalized: \(A\): \(0.95 \times 0.034 = 0.032\), \(B\): \(0.10 \times 0.322 = 0.032\), \(C\): \(0.95 \times 0.322 = 0.306\), \(D\): \(0.95 \times 0.322 = 0.306\)

  • Normalizing (\(Z = 0.676\)): \(b(A) \approx 0.048\), \(b(B) \approx 0.048\), \(b(C) \approx 0.452\), \(b(D) \approx 0.452\).

Note that \(b(A)\) went up (from 0.034 to 0.048). This is correct: a no-beep in B is expected if the package is in A, so the observation is mildly favorable for A. After normalization, A gains a small share from B's loss.

After visiting C (no beep):

  • Unnormalized: \(A\): \(0.95 \times 0.048 = 0.046\), \(B\): \(0.95 \times 0.048 = 0.046\), \(C\): \(0.10 \times 0.452 = 0.045\), \(D\): \(0.95 \times 0.452 = 0.429\)

  • Normalizing (\(Z = 0.566\)): \(b(A) \approx 0.080\), \(b(B) \approx 0.080\), \(b(C) \approx 0.080\), \(b(D) \approx 0.760\).

After 3 visits (all no-beep), the robot is 76% confident the package is in D—the only unvisited room. Not yet 99%.

After visiting D (beep):

  • Unnormalized: \(A\): \(0.05 \times 0.080 = 0.0040\), \(B\): \(0.05 \times 0.080 = 0.0040\), \(C\): \(0.05 \times 0.080 = 0.0040\), \(D\): \(0.90 \times 0.760 = 0.6840\)

  • Normalizing (\(Z = 0.696\)): \(b(D) \approx 0.983\). Close but not yet 99%.

After visiting D again (second beep):

  • Unnormalized: \(D\): \(0.90 \times 0.983 = 0.885\), others: \(0.05 \times (\sim 0.006) \approx 0.0003\) each.

  • Normalizing: \(b(D) \approx 0.999\). Now past 99%.

Answer: 5 visits (A, B, C, D, D again). Visiting all 4 rooms once yields \(\approx 98\%\) confidence; one additional visit to the room that beeped pushes past 99%. With noisy sensors, repeated evidence is needed to reach high confidence—a single beep is not enough because it could be a false positive.

Part 4: Perfect Scanner

With \(P(\text{beep} \mid \text{package here}) = 1\) and \(P(\text{beep} \mid \text{no package}) = 0\):

No beep in Room A: \(P(\text{no beep} \mid \text{package in A}) = 0\), so the likelihood is zero. After normalization:

\[b_1(A) = 0, \quad b_1(B) = b_1(C) = b_1(D) = \frac{1}{3}\]

The package is definitely not in A. One observation eliminates a room entirely.

Beep in Room B: \(P(\text{beep} \mid \text{package in B}) = 1\) and \(P(\text{beep} \mid \text{package elsewhere}) = 0\). So:

\[b_2(B) = 1, \quad b_2(\text{others}) = 0\]

One beep identifies the room with certainty.

Connection to the logical agent (Chapter 3): With a perfect scanner, the Bayesian update reduces to logical elimination. A no-beep entails that the package is not in the current room (the hypothesis is ruled out with probability 0, not merely reduced). A beep entails that the package is here (probability 1). This is exactly how the knowledge-based agent from Chapter 3 operates: each percept narrows the set of possible worlds until only one remains. The probabilistic framework subsumes the logical one as a special case—when sensors are perfect, posteriors collapse to 0 or 1, and Bayesian reasoning becomes logical deduction.
exe:belief-update.title: Belief State Tracking

exe:mdp-formulation.content:
Grid Reference

Using \((x, y)\) coordinates with \((1,1)\) at bottom-left:

(1,3)  (2,3)  (3,3)  (4,3)  ← row 3 (top)
(1,2)  (2,2)  (3,2)  (4,2)  ← row 2 (middle)
(1,1)  (2,1)  (3,1)  (4,1)  ← row 1 (bottom)
  • \((4,3)\): goal, reward \(+1\), terminal
  • \((4,2)\): hazard, reward \(-1\), terminal
  • \((2,2)\): wall (not a valid state)
  • All other cells: reward \(-0.04\)
  • Start: \((1,1)\)

Part 1: State and Action Spaces

States: All grid cells except the wall at \((2,2)\):

\[\mathcal{S} = \{(1,1), (2,1), (3,1), (4,1), (1,2), (3,2), (4,2), (1,3), (2,3), (3,3), (4,3)\}\]

That is 11 states total.

Terminal states: \((4,3)\) (goal) and \((4,2)\) (hazard).

Non-terminal states: \(11 - 2 = 9\).

Actions: \(\mathcal{A} = \{\text{North}, \text{South}, \text{East}, \text{West}\}\).

Part 2: Transition Probabilities from \((1,2)\) Taking East

From \((1,2)\), the intended action is East (toward \((2,2)\)).

  • Intended (East, \(p = 0.8\)): \((2,2)\) is a wall \(\to\) stay at \((1,2)\).
  • Drift left/North (\(p = 0.1\)): \((1,3)\) is a valid cell \(\to\) move to \((1,3)\).
  • Drift right/South (\(p = 0.1\)): \((1,1)\) is a valid cell \(\to\) move to \((1,1)\).

Since the intended move is blocked, that probability stays at the current cell:

\[ \begin{aligned} T((1,2) \mid (1,2), \text{East}) &= 0.8 & &\text{(intended blocked by wall)} \\ T((1,3) \mid (1,2), \text{East}) &= 0.1 & &\text{(drift north)} \\ T((1,1) \mid (1,2), \text{East}) &= 0.1 & &\text{(drift south)} \end{aligned} \]

Check: \(0.8 + 0.1 + 0.1 = 1.0 \checkmark\)

The wall at \((2,2)\) makes East from \((1,2)\) essentially a "stay" action with small chances of drifting north or south.

Part 3: Bellman Optimality Equation for \((3,2)\)

\[V^*((3,2)) = R((3,2)) + \gamma \max_a \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid (3,2), a) \, V^*(s')\]

With \(R((3,2)) = -0.04\), we expand two actions:

Action North (intended: \((3,3)\), drift left: \((2,2)\) wall, drift right: \((4,2)\)):

  • Intended North \(\to\) \((3,3)\): probability 0.8
  • Drift West \(\to\) \((2,2)\) is a wall \(\to\) stay at \((3,2)\): probability 0.1
  • Drift East \(\to\) \((4,2)\): probability 0.1

\[\sum_{s'} T(s' \mid (3,2), \text{N}) \, V^*(s') = 0.8 \, V^*((3,3)) + 0.1 \, V^*((3,2)) + 0.1 \, V^*((4,2))\]

Note that \((4,2)\) is the hazard with \(V^*((4,2)) = -1\). This means going North from \((3,2)\) has a 10% chance of entering the hazard.

Action East (intended: \((4,2)\), drift left: \((3,3)\), drift right: \((3,1)\)):

  • Intended East \(\to\) \((4,2)\): probability 0.8
  • Drift North \(\to\) \((3,3)\): probability 0.1
  • Drift South \(\to\) \((3,1)\): probability 0.1

\[\sum_{s'} T(s' \mid (3,2), \text{E}) \, V^*(s') = 0.8 \, V^*((4,2)) + 0.1 \, V^*((3,3)) + 0.1 \, V^*((3,1))\]

This sends the robot into the hazard with 80% probability—clearly a poor choice.

The full Bellman equation selects the max over all four actions:

\[V^*((3,2)) = -0.04 + \gamma \max\!\big(\text{N-value}, \text{S-value}, \text{E-value}, \text{W-value}\big)\]

Part 4: Value Iteration by Hand

Use \(\gamma = 1\).

Initialization: \(V_0(s) = 0\) for non-terminal states, \(V_0((4,3)) = +1\), \(V_0((4,2)) = -1\).

Iteration 1

For every non-terminal state \(s\):

\[V_1(s) = R(s) + \gamma \max_a \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, a) \, V_0(s')\]

Since \(V_0 = 0\) for all non-terminal states, only transitions into terminal states contribute to the sum. A state can only get a nonzero expected value if one of its actions can reach \((4,3)\) or \((4,2)\).

States adjacent to \((4,3)\): \((3,3)\) and \((4,3)\) itself (terminal, skip). From \((3,3)\), East reaches \((4,3)\) with \(p = 0.8\).

States adjacent to \((4,2)\): \((3,2)\), \((4,1)\), and \((4,3)\) (terminal, skip). From \((3,2)\), East reaches \((4,2)\) with \(p = 0.8\). From \((4,1)\), North reaches \((4,2)\) with \(p = 0.8\).

Let's compute \(V_1\) for each non-terminal state by finding the best action:

\((3,3)\): Best action is East. - East: \(0.8 \times V_0((4,3)) + 0.1 \times V_0((3,3)) + 0.1 \times V_0((3,2)) = 0.8 \times 1 + 0 + 0 = 0.8\) - North: hits wall with 0.8, drift to \((2,3)\) with 0.1, drift to \((4,3)\) with 0.1 \(= 0 + 0 + 0.1 \times 1 = 0.1\) - \(V_1((3,3)) = -0.04 + 1 \times 0.8 = 0.76\)

\((2,3)\): Best action is East. - East: \(0.8 \times V_0((3,3)) + 0.1 \times V_0((2,3)) + 0.1 \times V_0((2,2))\). But \((2,2)\) is a wall, so drift south stays at \((2,3)\). All \(V_0\) values are 0. - No action reaches a terminal state, so \(\max_a(\cdots) = 0\). - \(V_1((2,3)) = -0.04 + 0 = -0.04\)

\((1,3)\): No action reaches a terminal state. - \(V_1((1,3)) = -0.04\)

\((3,2)\): Best action needs care—East goes directly to the hazard.

  • East: intended \((4,2)\), drift-N \((3,3)\), drift-S \((3,1)\): \(0.8 \times (-1) + 0.1 \times 0 + 0.1 \times 0 = -0.8\)
  • North: intended \((3,3)\), drift-W \((2,2)\) wall \(\to\) stay \((3,2)\), drift-E \((4,2)\): \(0.8 \times 0 + 0.1 \times 0 + 0.1 \times (-1) = -0.1\)
  • South: intended \((3,1)\), drift-W \((2,2)\) wall \(\to\) stay \((3,2)\), drift-E \((4,2)\): \(0.8 \times 0 + 0.1 \times 0 + 0.1 \times (-1) = -0.1\)
  • West: intended \((2,2)\) wall \(\to\) stay \((3,2)\), drift-N \((3,3)\), drift-S \((3,1)\): \(0.8 \times 0 + 0.1 \times 0 + 0.1 \times 0 = 0\)

Best is West with value 0. \(V_1((3,2)) = -0.04 + 0 = -0.04\).

\((4,1)\): Adjacent to the hazard—several actions risk drifting into \((4,2)\).

  • North: intended \((4,2)\) hazard, drift-W \((3,1)\), drift-E off-grid \(\to\) stay: \(0.8 \times (-1) + 0.1 \times 0 + 0.1 \times 0 = -0.8\)
  • East: intended off-grid \(\to\) stay, drift-N \((4,2)\) hazard, drift-S off-grid \(\to\) stay: \(0.8 \times 0 + 0.1 \times (-1) + 0.1 \times 0 = -0.1\)
  • West: intended \((3,1)\), drift-N \((4,2)\) hazard, drift-S off-grid \(\to\) stay: \(0.8 \times 0 + 0.1 \times (-1) + 0.1 \times 0 = -0.1\)
  • South: intended off-grid \(\to\) stay, drift-W \((3,1)\), drift-E off-grid \(\to\) stay: \(0.8 \times 0 + 0.1 \times 0 + 0.1 \times 0 = 0\)

Best is South with value 0. (South is safe because all outcomes avoid the hazard.) \(V_1((4,1)) = -0.04\).

Remaining states \(\{(1,1), (2,1), (3,1), (1,2)\}\): No action from any of these can reach a terminal state in one step (they are too far away). So \(\max_a(\cdots) = 0\) and \(V_1 = -0.04\) for all of them.

Summary of \(V_1\):

State \(V_1\)
\((4,3)\) \(+1.00\) (terminal)
\((4,2)\) \(-1.00\) (terminal)
\((3,3)\) \(+0.76\)
All others \(-0.04\)

Iteration 2 for \((3,2)\)

\[V_2((3,2)) = -0.04 + \max_a \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid (3,2), a) \, V_1(s')\]

North: intended \((3,3)\), drift-W stays (wall at \((2,2)\)), drift-E \(\to (4,2)\): \[0.8 \times 0.76 + 0.1 \times (-0.04) + 0.1 \times (-1) = 0.608 - 0.004 - 0.1 = 0.504\]

South: intended \((3,1)\), drift-W stays (wall), drift-E \(\to (4,2)\): \[0.8 \times (-0.04) + 0.1 \times (-0.04) + 0.1 \times (-1) = -0.032 - 0.004 - 0.1 = -0.136\]

East: intended \((4,2)\), drift-N \(\to (3,3)\), drift-S \(\to (3,1)\): \[0.8 \times (-1) + 0.1 \times 0.76 + 0.1 \times (-0.04) = -0.8 + 0.076 - 0.004 = -0.728\]

West: intended stays (wall at \((2,2)\)), drift-N \(\to (3,3)\), drift-S \(\to (3,1)\): \[0.8 \times (-0.04) + 0.1 \times 0.76 + 0.1 \times (-0.04) = -0.032 + 0.076 - 0.004 = 0.040\]

Best action: North with value 0.504.

\[V_2((3,2)) = -0.04 + 0.504 = 0.464\]

Iteration 2 for \((3,1)\)

\[V_2((3,1)) = -0.04 + \max_a \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid (3,1), a) \, V_1(s')\]

North: intended \((3,2)\), drift-W \(\to (2,1)\), drift-E \(\to (4,1)\): \[0.8 \times (-0.04) + 0.1 \times (-0.04) + 0.1 \times (-0.04) = -0.04\]

South: hits wall, stay. Drift-W \(\to (2,1)\), drift-E \(\to (4,1)\): \[0.8 \times (-0.04) + 0.1 \times (-0.04) + 0.1 \times (-0.04) = -0.04\]

East: intended \((4,1)\), drift-N \(\to (3,2)\), drift-S hits wall, stay: \[0.8 \times (-0.04) + 0.1 \times (-0.04) + 0.1 \times (-0.04) = -0.04\]

West: intended \((2,1)\), drift-N \(\to (3,2)\), drift-S hits wall, stay: \[0.8 \times (-0.04) + 0.1 \times (-0.04) + 0.1 \times (-0.04) = -0.04\]

All actions are tied at \(-0.04\) because \((3,1)\) is surrounded by states that all have \(V_1 = -0.04\). The high value at \((3,3)\) hasn't propagated this far yet.

\[V_2((3,1)) = -0.04 + (-0.04) = -0.08\]

Part 5: Qualitative Policy Sketch

+------+------+------+------+
|  →   |  →   |  →   | GOAL |
+------+------+------+------+
|  ↑   | WALL |  ↑   | HAZD |
+------+------+------+------+
|  ↑   |  →   |  ↑   |  ←   |
+------+------+------+------+

Reasoning:

  • Top row \((y = 3)\): Move East toward the goal. These states are safe (no risk of drifting into the hazard from the top row).
  • \((1,2)\): Move North to reach the safe top row. The wall at \((2,2)\) blocks eastward progress, so the robot must go around.
  • \((3,2)\): This is the most dangerous state. East goes directly to the hazard. North goes toward \((3,3)\), which is near the goal, but drifting East from North leads to the hazard with 10% probability. The optimal policy likely chooses North (accepting the 10% hazard risk) because the alternative paths are much longer.
  • \((4,1)\): North goes to the hazard with 80% probability. The robot should move West to retreat from the hazard column before heading north.
  • \((3,1)\): The robot should go North toward \((3,2)\), which despite its proximity to the hazard, is the most direct route.

Where the policy differs from the shortest path: At \((4,1)\), the shortest path to the goal is North then North-then-East, but the stochastic transitions make this extremely dangerous (80% chance of hitting the hazard on the first step). The optimal policy retreats West first. This is the same safety-vs-efficiency tradeoff we see in the \(4 \times 4\) warehouse MDP.

Most cautious states: \((3,2)\) and \((4,1)\), both of which are adjacent to the hazard at \((4,2)\).
exe:mdp-formulation.title: Formulating an MDP

exe:mdp-agent.content:
This solution builds on the MDP code from Section 4.4, adapted for the 3×4 grid from Problem 4.3 (with a wall at \((2,2)\)). We add an environment simulator, an agent loop, and experiments.

Parts 1–2: Environment Simulator and Agent Loop

MDP Agent: Environment Simulator and Agent Loop

This script builds on the MDP code from Section 4.4. We adapt the 4×4 warehouse MDP to the 3×4 grid from Problem 4.3 (with a wall at \((2,2)\)), then add an environment simulator and an agent loop.

MDP Setup (3×4 Grid)

We redefine the MDP for the 3×4 grid with a wall at \((2,2)\), goal at \((4,3)\), and hazard at \((4,2)\).

import random
from collections import Counter

# Grid dimensions
WIDTH, HEIGHT = 4, 3

# Terminal states and their rewards
GOAL = (4, 3)
HAZARD = (4, 2)
TERMINALS = {GOAL: +1.0, HAZARD: -1.0}

# Living reward for non-terminal states
LIVING_REWARD = -0.04

# Wall position
WALL = (2, 2)

# All valid states: every grid cell except the wall
STATES = [
    (x, y)
    for x in range(1, WIDTH + 1)
    for y in range(1, HEIGHT + 1)
    if (x, y) != WALL
]

# Actions and their (dx, dy) displacements
ACTIONS = {
    "North": (0, 1),
    "South": (0, -1),
    "East": (1, 0),
    "West": (-1, 0),
}

ARROWS = {"North": "\u2191", "South": "\u2193", "East": "\u2192", "West": "\u2190"}

def reward(state):
    """R(s): immediate reward for being in state s."""
    if state in TERMINALS:
        return TERMINALS[state]
    return LIVING_REWARD

def get_perpendicular(action):
    """Return the two actions perpendicular to the given action."""
    if action in ("North", "South"):
        return ["West", "East"]
    else:
        return ["North", "South"]

def attempt_move(state, action):
    """Return the state that results from attempting to move in the
    given direction. If the move would leave the grid or hit a wall,
    return the original state."""
    dx, dy = ACTIONS[action]
    nx, ny = state[0] + dx, state[1] + dy
    if 1 <= nx <= WIDTH and 1 <= ny <= HEIGHT and (nx, ny) != WALL:
        return (nx, ny)
    return state

def transitions(state, action):
    """T(s' | s, a): return a dict {s': probability}."""
    if state in TERMINALS:
        return {}

    outcomes = {}
    intended = attempt_move(state, action)
    outcomes[intended] = outcomes.get(intended, 0) + 0.8

    for perp in get_perpendicular(action):
        drifted = attempt_move(state, perp)
        outcomes[drifted] = outcomes.get(drifted, 0) + 0.1

    return outcomes

def value_iteration(gamma=0.99, epsilon=1e-6):
    """Run value iteration and return the converged value function
    and the number of iterations."""
    V = {s: 0.0 for s in STATES}

    iteration = 0
    while True:
        V_new = {}
        delta = 0

        for s in STATES:
            if s in TERMINALS:
                V_new[s] = reward(s)
                continue

            best_value = float("-inf")
            for a in ACTIONS:
                expected = sum(
                    prob * V[s_next]
                    for s_next, prob in transitions(s, a).items()
                )
                best_value = max(best_value, expected)

            V_new[s] = reward(s) + gamma * best_value
            delta = max(delta, abs(V_new[s] - V[s]))

        V = V_new
        iteration += 1

        if delta < epsilon:
            break

    return V, iteration

def extract_policy(V, gamma=0.99):
    """Compute the optimal policy from a converged value function."""
    policy = {}
    for s in STATES:
        if s in TERMINALS:
            policy[s] = None
            continue

        best_action = None
        best_value = float("-inf")
        for a in ACTIONS:
            expected = sum(
                prob * V[s_next]
                for s_next, prob in transitions(s, a).items()
            )
            value = reward(s) + gamma * expected
            if value > best_value:
                best_value = value
                best_action = a

        policy[s] = best_action
    return policy

Part 1: Environment Simulator

The simulate_step function samples a next state from the transition distribution \(T(s' \mid s, a)\) using random.choices.

def simulate_step(state, action):
    """Sample a next state from T(s' | s, a)."""
    dist = transitions(state, action)
    states = list(dist.keys())
    probs = list(dist.values())
    return random.choices(states, weights=probs, k=1)[0]

Verification

Call simulate_step((3, 1), "North") 10,000 times and check that the empirical frequencies approximate 80/10/10.

random.seed(42)
counts = Counter()
for _ in range(10_000):
    counts[simulate_step((3, 1), "North")] += 1

print("Empirical transition frequencies from (3,1), action North:")
for s, c in sorted(counts.items()):
    print(f"  {s}: {c/10_000:.3f}")
Empirical transition frequencies from (3,1), action North:
  (2, 1): 0.099
  (3, 2): 0.803
  (4, 1): 0.098

Part 2: Agent Loop

The run_episode function simulates a full episode: the agent follows the policy, accumulates reward, and stops at a terminal state or after max_steps.

def run_episode(policy, start=(1, 1), max_steps=100):
    """Simulate one episode following the given policy.

    Returns:
        trajectory: list of states visited (including start)
        total_reward: sum of R(s) over all visited states
        outcome: "goal", "hazard", or "timeout"
    """
    state = start
    trajectory = [state]
    total_reward = reward(state)

    for step in range(max_steps):
        if state in TERMINALS:
            break
        action = policy[state]
        state = simulate_step(state, action)
        trajectory.append(state)
        total_reward += reward(state)

    if state == GOAL:
        outcome = "goal"
    elif state == HAZARD:
        outcome = "hazard"
    else:
        outcome = "timeout"

    return trajectory, total_reward, outcome

Running 1000 Episodes with the Optimal Policy

random.seed(42)
V, num_iters = value_iteration(gamma=0.99)
optimal_policy = extract_policy(V, gamma=0.99)

print(f"Value iteration converged in {num_iters} iterations.\n")

results = [run_episode(optimal_policy) for _ in range(1000)]
outcomes = [r[2] for r in results]
rewards = [r[1] for r in results]

goal_rate = outcomes.count("goal") / 1000
hazard_rate = outcomes.count("hazard") / 1000
avg_reward = sum(rewards) / 1000

print(f"Goal reached:  {goal_rate:.3f}")
print(f"Hazard hit:    {hazard_rate:.3f}")
print(f"Avg reward:    {avg_reward:.3f}")
Value iteration converged in 27 iterations.

Goal reached:  0.982
Hazard hit:    0.018
Avg reward:    0.697

The optimal policy reaches the goal about 98% of the time, hits the hazard about 2% of the time (due to unlucky drift sequences), and never times out. The average total reward is positive, reflecting that the goal’s \(+1\) reward outweighs the accumulated living penalties and occasional hazard hits.

Parts 3–5: Greedy Comparison, Discount Factor, and Harder Warehouse

MDP Experiments: Greedy Comparison, Discount Factor, and Harder Warehouse

This script runs the experiments from Parts 3–5 of the MDP Agent exercise, using the simulator and agent loop from mdp_agent.py.

import random

from mdp_agent import (
    ACTIONS, ARROWS, GOAL, HAZARD, HEIGHT, STATES, TERMINALS, WIDTH,
    WALL, extract_policy, reward, run_episode, value_iteration,
)
Empirical transition frequencies from (3,1), action North:
  (2, 1): 0.099
  (3, 2): 0.803
  (4, 1): 0.098
Value iteration converged in 27 iterations.

Goal reached:  0.982
Hazard hit:    0.018
Avg reward:    0.697

Part 3: Comparison with a Naive Greedy Policy

The greedy policy always moves in the direction of the goal, ignoring the hazard entirely.

def greedy_policy_action(state):
    """Move toward the goal, ignoring hazards."""
    gx, gy = GOAL
    sx, sy = state
    if sx < gx:
        return "East"
    elif sx > gx:
        return "West"
    elif sy < gy:
        return "North"
    else:
        return "South"

greedy_policy = {s: greedy_policy_action(s) for s in STATES if s not in TERMINALS}
greedy_policy[GOAL] = None
greedy_policy[HAZARD] = None

Running 1000 Episodes with Each Policy

random.seed(42)
V, _ = value_iteration(gamma=0.99)
optimal_policy = extract_policy(V, gamma=0.99)

opt_results = [run_episode(optimal_policy) for _ in range(1000)]
opt_outcomes = [r[2] for r in opt_results]
opt_rewards = [r[1] for r in opt_results]

greedy_results = [run_episode(greedy_policy) for _ in range(1000)]
greedy_outcomes = [r[2] for r in greedy_results]
greedy_rewards = [r[1] for r in greedy_results]

print("Optimal policy:")
print(f"  Goal reached:  {opt_outcomes.count('goal') / 1000:.3f}")
print(f"  Hazard hit:    {opt_outcomes.count('hazard') / 1000:.3f}")
print(f"  Avg reward:    {sum(opt_rewards) / 1000:.3f}")

print("\nGreedy policy:")
print(f"  Goal reached:  {greedy_outcomes.count('goal') / 1000:.3f}")
print(f"  Hazard hit:    {greedy_outcomes.count('hazard') / 1000:.3f}")
print(f"  Avg reward:    {sum(greedy_rewards) / 1000:.3f}")
Optimal policy:
  Goal reached:  0.982
  Hazard hit:    0.018
  Avg reward:    0.697

Greedy policy:
  Goal reached:  0.053
  Hazard hit:    0.947
  Avg reward:    -1.114

The greedy policy is catastrophic on this grid: it reaches the goal only ~5% of the time and hits the hazard ~95% of the time. The reason is structural: the greedy policy sends the robot East along the bottom row to \((4,1)\), then North—directly into the hazard at \((4,2)\) with 80% probability. The optimal policy avoids the hazard column entirely by routing up the left side and across the top row, reaching the goal ~98% of the time.

Key insight: The MDP-optimal policy sacrifices short-term efficiency (taking longer paths) for dramatically better outcomes. The greedy policy optimizes for distance to the goal but ignores both the stochastic transition model and the hazard.

Part 4: Discount Factor Experiment

We compute optimal policies for several values of \(\gamma\) and compare their performance.

random.seed(42)
print("Discount factor experiment (living reward = -0.04):\n")
for gamma in [0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 0.99]:
    V, _ = value_iteration(gamma=gamma)
    policy = extract_policy(V, gamma=gamma)
    results = [run_episode(policy) for _ in range(1000)]
    outcomes = [r[2] for r in results]
    rewards = [r[1] for r in results]

    goal_rate = outcomes.count("goal") / 1000
    hazard_rate = outcomes.count("hazard") / 1000
    avg_reward = sum(rewards) / 1000

    print(f"gamma={gamma:.2f}  goal={goal_rate:.3f}  "
          f"hazard={hazard_rate:.3f}  avg_reward={avg_reward:.3f}")
Discount factor experiment (living reward = -0.04):

gamma=0.10  goal=1.000  hazard=0.000  avg_reward=0.614
gamma=0.50  goal=0.965  hazard=0.035  avg_reward=0.670
gamma=0.90  goal=0.978  hazard=0.022  avg_reward=0.700
gamma=0.99  goal=0.984  hazard=0.016  avg_reward=0.704

Analysis: On this compact 3×4 grid, the hazard’s immediate reward of \(-1\) is severe enough that even a myopic agent avoids it. All four discount factors produce policies that reach the goal at high rates (97–100%). The variation is modest because the grid is small: the optimal path is only a few steps long regardless of how far ahead the agent plans.

  • \(\gamma = 0.1\): Despite extreme myopia, the agent avoids the hazard because its \(-1\) reward dominates the discounted future at any horizon. The 100% goal rate in this run reflects the short path and favorable random seed.
  • \(\gamma = 0.5\): Slightly lower goal rate (~97%) as the agent weighs the living penalty more against longer detours.
  • \(\gamma = 0.9\) and \(\gamma = 0.99\): Nearly identical performance (~98% goal rate). With enough foresight the policy stabilizes.

On a larger grid (like the 4×4 warehouse in Section 4.4), the discount factor has a more dramatic effect: a myopic agent cannot “see” distant hazards and takes riskier shortcuts.

Part 5: A Harder Warehouse

We add a second hazard at \((2,3)\) with reward \(-1\), recompute the optimal policy, and evaluate it.

random.seed(42)
TERMINALS[(2, 3)] = -1.0

V, _ = value_iteration(gamma=0.99)
policy = extract_policy(V, gamma=0.99)

print("Policy with second hazard at (2,3):\n")
for y in range(HEIGHT, 0, -1):
    row = []
    for x in range(1, WIDTH + 1):
        s = (x, y)
        if s == GOAL:
            row.append(" GOAL")
        elif s in TERMINALS and TERMINALS[s] < 0:
            row.append(" HAZD")
        elif s not in STATES:
            row.append(" WALL")
        else:
            row.append(f"  {ARROWS[policy[s]]} ")
    print("".join(row))

results = [run_episode(policy) for _ in range(1000)]
outcomes = [r[2] for r in results]
rewards = [r[1] for r in results]
print(f"\nGoal reached:  {outcomes.count('goal') / 1000:.3f}")
print(f"Hazard hit:    {outcomes.count('hazard') / 1000:.3f}")
print(f"Avg reward:    {sum(rewards) / 1000:.3f}")
Policy with second hazard at (2,3):

  ↓  HAZD  →  GOAL
  ↓  WALL  ↑  HAZD
  →   →   ↑   ← 

Goal reached:  0.856
Hazard hit:    0.144
Avg reward:    0.458

Analysis: The second hazard at \((2,3)\) blocks the upper-left corridor that the original policy used. The robot can no longer go East from \((1,3)\) since that enters the new hazard with 80% probability. The bottom-left states now point East along the bottom row, feeding into the \(x=3\) column which routes North to \((3,3)\) and then East to the goal. States \((1,2)\) and \((1,3)\) point South to escape the now-dead-end left column. The goal-reach rate drops from ~98% to ~86% and the hazard-hit rate increases from ~2% to ~14% because there are now two hazards to accidentally drift into and the safe corridor is narrower.

exe:final-uncertainty.content:
(a) Numerator: \(0.90 \times 0.05 = 0.045\). Posterior: \(0.045 / 0.14 \approx 0.321\). After one alarm, the probability of low battery rises from 5% to about 32%.

(b) New prior: \(P(\text{low}) = 0.321\), \(P(\text{ok}) = 0.679\). New denominator: \(0.90 \times 0.321 + 0.10 \times 0.679 = 0.289 + 0.068 = 0.357\). Posterior: \(0.289 / 0.357 \approx 0.81\). Yes — after two alarms, the belief has risen dramatically from 5% → 32% → 81%.

(c) \(V_2(M) = R(M) + \gamma \max_a V_1(\text{next})\). The best action is East (to G): \(V_2(M) = -0.04 + 0.9 \times 1 = -0.04 + 0.9 = 0.86\).

(d) Greedy policy at M: East (toward G, which has \(V_1 = +1\), the highest value of any neighbor).

At S: the greedy policy uses \(V_2\) values of neighbors. East from S goes to M, and we just computed \(V_2(M) = 0.86\). All other neighbors of S (South, North=wall, West=wall) have \(V_2 = -0.04 + 0.9 \times (-0.04) = -0.076\). Since \(0.86 \gg -0.076\), the policy at S is also East (toward M, toward the goal).
exe:final-uncertainty.title: Bayesian Reasoning and MDP Policy

exe:bayes-sensor.content:
Goal: Apply Bayes' rule to reason about hazards in the warehouse with noisy sensors.

Setup: A warehouse robot is at position \((1,1)\) in a \(3 \times 3\) grid. Its creaking sensor has a true-positive rate of 85% and a false-positive rate of 8%. The prior probability of damaged floor at any given square is 0.15.

The robot's adjacent squares from \((1,1)\) are \((2,1)\) and \((1,2)\).

Simplification: For parts 1–3, consider the creaking sensor's response to a single adjacent square (i.e., treat the sensor as reporting on one square at a time). Part 4 considers the multi-square case.

Tasks:

  1. No creaking observed: The robot hears no creaking at \((1,1)\). Using Bayes' rule, compute the posterior probability that \((2,1)\) has damaged floor. Show all steps, clearly labeling the prior, likelihood, evidence, and posterior.

  2. Creaking observed: Now suppose the robot does hear creaking at \((1,1)\). Compute the posterior probability that \((2,1)\) has damaged floor.

  3. Sensor comparison: A newer sensor model has a true-positive rate of 95% and a false-positive rate of 2%. Repeat parts 1 and 2 with this sensor. How does sensor quality affect the posterior?

  4. Multiple adjacent squares: In reality, creaking at \((1,1)\) means damage at \((2,1)\) or \((1,2)\) (or both). Assume floor damage at different squares is independent with prior probability 0.15 each. Define:

    • \(C\): creaking detected at \((1,1)\)
    • \(D_1\): damage at \((2,1)\)
    • \(D_2\): damage at \((1,2)\)

    The sensor detects creaking iff at least one adjacent square is damaged, subject to the noise model: \(P(C = 1 \mid \text{at least one damaged}) = 0.85\) and \(P(C = 1 \mid \text{none damaged}) = 0.08\).

    Compute \(P(D_1 = 1 \mid C = 0)\). (Hint: first compute \(P(\text{at least one damaged})\) using independence, then apply the law of total probability.)
exe:bayes-sensor.title: Bayesian Sensor Reasoning

exe:belief-update.content:
Goal: Track a probability distribution over multiple hypotheses as evidence accumulates.

Setup: A warehouse has four rooms: A, B, C, D. A high-value package is hidden in exactly one room. The prior is uniform: \(P(\text{Package in } X) = 0.25\) for each room \(X\).

The robot has a package scanner with the following characteristics:

  • When the robot is in the room with the package: scanner beeps with probability 0.9
  • When the robot is in a room without the package: scanner beeps with probability 0.05

Tasks:

  1. The robot enters Room A and the scanner does not beep. Update the belief state over all four rooms. (Hint: compute the posterior for each room. The posteriors should sum to 1.)

  2. The robot then enters Room B and the scanner beeps. Starting from the belief state computed in part 1, update again. Show the new belief state.

  3. How many rooms must the robot visit (in the worst case) before it can identify the package location with at least 99% confidence?

  4. Suppose the scanner is perfect (\(P(\text{beep} \mid \text{package here}) = 1\), \(P(\text{beep} \mid \text{no package}) = 0\)). How does the belief update simplify? Connect this to the logical agent from Chapter 3.
exe:belief-update.title: Belief State Tracking

exe:mdp-formulation.content:
Goal: Practice defining MDPs for different problems.

Setup: A delivery robot operates on the following \(3 \times 4\) grid:

+------+------+------+------+
|      |      |      | +1   |
+------+------+------+------+
|      | XXXX |      | -1   |
+------+------+------+------+
|Start |      |      |      |
+------+------+------+------+
  • The robot starts at the bottom-left cell.
  • The cell marked XXXX is a wall (the robot cannot enter it).
  • The top-right cell has reward \(+1\) (goal, terminal).
  • The cell at row 2, column 4 has reward \(-1\) (hazard, terminal).
  • All other cells have reward \(-0.04\).
  • Actions: North, South, East, West.
  • Transitions: 80% intended direction, 10% each perpendicular direction. If the resulting cell is a wall or outside the grid, the robot stays in place.

Tasks:

  1. State and action spaces: List all states and actions. How many non-terminal states are there?

  2. Transition probabilities: Compute the full transition distribution \(T(s' \mid s, a)\) for the robot at \((1,2)\) taking action East. List every reachable state and its probability. (Remember the wall at \((2,2)\).)

  3. Bellman equation: Write the Bellman optimality equation for state \((3,2)\). Expand the equation for at least two actions (e.g., North and East), listing all terms.

  4. Value iteration by hand: Initialize \(V_0(s) = 0\) for all non-terminal states and \(V_0 = R(s)\) for terminal states. Compute \(V_1(s)\) for every state. Then compute \(V_2(s)\) for states \((3,2)\) and \((3,1)\). Use \(\gamma = 1\) for simplicity.

  5. Qualitative policy: Without running value iteration to full convergence, sketch the optimal policy. Which states should the robot be most cautious in? Where might the policy differ from the shortest path?
exe:mdp-formulation.title: Formulating an MDP

exe:mdp-agent.content:
Goal: Design a complete warehouse agent that uses value iteration to plan offline, then executes its optimal policy in a stochastic environment. This bridges the MDP theory from [@m1] and the implementation from [@vi] with the agent framework from Chapter 3.

Setup: Use the MDP code from [@vi] (states, actions, transitions, rewards, value_iteration, extract_policy). You will add an environment simulator and an agent that interacts with it.

Tasks:

  1. Environment simulator: Write a function simulate_step(state, action) that returns a next state sampled from the transition distribution \(T(s' \mid s, a)\). Use Python's random.choices (or equivalent) to sample according to the probabilities returned by transitions(state, action). Verify your function by calling simulate_step((3, 1), "North") many times and checking that the empirical frequencies approximate 80/10/10.

  2. Agent loop: Write a function run_episode(policy, start=(1, 1), max_steps=100) that simulates a full episode:

    • Start at start.
    • At each step, look up \(\pi^*(s)\) in the policy, call simulate_step, accumulate the (undiscounted) reward, and record the trajectory.
    • Stop when a terminal state is reached or max_steps is exceeded.
    • Return the trajectory (list of states visited), the total reward, and whether the agent reached the goal, hit the hazard, or timed out.

    Run 1000 episodes with the optimal policy from [@vi]. Report: (a) the fraction of episodes that reach the goal, (b) the fraction that hit the hazard, (c) the average total reward.

  3. Comparison with a naive policy: Define a greedy policy that always moves in the direction of the goal (East if the goal is east of the robot, North if the goal is north, etc.), without considering the hazard. Run 1000 episodes with this policy and report the same three statistics. How does the MDP-optimal policy compare?

  4. Discount factor experiment: Compute optimal policies for \(\gamma \in \{0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 0.99\}\) (with living reward \(-0.04\)). For each, run 1000 episodes and report the goal-reach rate and average reward. At what value of \(\gamma\) does the agent first consistently avoid the hazard?

  5. A harder warehouse: Add a second hazard at \((2, 3)\) with reward \(-1\). Recompute the optimal policy and run 1000 episodes. Display the new policy. In 2–3 sentences, describe how the agent's behavior changed and whether the goal-reach rate decreased.
exe:mdp-agent.title: Building an MDP Agent (Guided)

exe:naive-bayes-classifier.content:
Goal: Build a Naive Bayes classifier to classify warehouse zones as safe or hazardous based on sensor features.

Setup: A warehouse inspection robot collects the following features at each location:

Feature Values Description
Vibration Low, Medium, High Floor vibration level
Temperature Normal, Elevated Surface temperature
Sound Quiet, Creaking, Loud Ambient sound level

Historical inspection data provides the following statistics:

Class priors: \(P(\text{Safe}) = 0.75\), \(P(\text{Hazardous}) = 0.25\)

Likelihoods (conditional probabilities of each feature given the class):

Feature Value \(P(\cdot \mid \text{Safe})\) \(P(\cdot \mid \text{Hazardous})\)
Vibration Low 0.7 0.1
Vibration Medium 0.2 0.3
Vibration High 0.1 0.6
Temperature Normal 0.85 0.4
Temperature Elevated 0.15 0.6
Sound Quiet 0.6 0.1
Sound Creaking 0.3 0.5
Sound Loud 0.1 0.4

Tasks:

  1. Classify a new observation: The robot observes Vibration=High, Temperature=Elevated, Sound=Creaking. Compute the posterior probability of each class using Naive Bayes. Show the numerator computation for each class and the final normalized posteriors. What is the classification?

  2. Classify an ambiguous case: The robot observes Vibration=Medium, Temperature=Normal, Sound=Quiet. Compute the posteriors. Is this a clear classification or is there significant uncertainty?

  3. Missing features: Suppose the temperature sensor fails and the robot can only observe Vibration and Sound. How does the Naive Bayes computation change? Classify the observation Vibration=High, Sound=Loud with and without the temperature feature.

  4. Conditional independence assumption: Give one concrete example where the conditional independence assumption might be violated for these warehouse features (i.e., where knowing one feature value would change your estimate of another, even after conditioning on the class). How might this affect classification accuracy?
exe:naive-bayes-classifier.title: Naive Bayes for Warehouse Classification

exe:expected-utility.content:
Goal: Practice computing expected utility and making rational decisions under uncertainty.

Setup: The warehouse robot is at position \((2,2)\) and must choose one of three actions:

  • Action A (Move North to \((2,3)\)): Safe with probability 0.9, leads to damaged floor with probability 0.1
  • Action B (Move East to \((3,2)\)): Safe with probability 0.7, leads to the forklift with probability 0.3
  • Action C (Stay and scan): Always safe, but costs time (one action penalty)

Utility values: - Reaching a safe square and advancing toward goal: \(U = +5\) - Being destroyed by damaged floor: \(U = -100\) - Being destroyed by the forklift: \(U = -100\) - Staying and scanning (gaining information): \(U = -1\)

Tasks:

  1. Compute the expected utility of each action. Which action should a rational (MEU) agent choose?

  2. Suppose after scanning (Action C), the robot updates its beliefs: the probability of damage at \((2,3)\) drops to 0.02 and the probability of the forklift at \((3,2)\) drops to 0.05. Now compute EU(A) and EU(B) with the updated probabilities. Was scanning worth it?

  3. Risk sensitivity: At what probability of damage \(p\) does Action A have zero expected utility? What does this tell us about the threshold where the agent should become cautious?

  4. Value of information: Compute the expected utility of the strategy "scan first, then choose the better of A or B with updated probabilities" and compare it to the best single-action expected utility from part 1. The difference is the value of information from scanning.
exe:expected-utility.title: Expected Utility and Decision Making

exe:final-uncertainty.content:
Part A — Bayesian Update

A warehouse robot has a battery sensor that triggers an alarm when the battery is low. The sensor is not perfect:

  • \(P(\text{alarm} \mid \text{low}) = 0.90\) (90% true-positive rate)
  • \(P(\text{alarm} \mid \text{ok}) = 0.10\) (10% false-positive rate)
  • \(P(\text{low}) = 0.05\) (prior: 5% of the time the battery is actually low)

(a) The alarm triggers. Compute the posterior \(P(\text{low} \mid \text{alarm})\) using Bayes' rule ([@def:bayes-rule]):

\[P(\text{low} \mid \text{alarm}) = \frac{P(\text{alarm} \mid \text{low}) \cdot P(\text{low})}{P(\text{alarm})}\]

The denominator is: \(P(\text{alarm}) = 0.90 \times 0.05 + 0.10 \times 0.95 = 0.14\). Compute the numerator and the final posterior.

(b) A second independent sensor also triggers. Using your answer from (a) as the new prior, apply Bayes' rule again. Has the belief changed substantially?

Part B — Markov Decision Process

\(3 \times 2\) grid MDP. Deterministic transitions (moving into a wall stays in place). \(\gamma = 0.9\).

Col 1 Col 2 Col 3
Row 2 S (\(-0.04\)) M (\(-0.04\)) G (\(+1\), terminal)
Row 1 \(-0.04\) \(-0.04\) H (\(-1\), terminal)

After iteration 1 (from \(V_0 = 0\)): \(V_1(s) = R(s)\) for all non-terminal states, so \(V_1(S) = V_1(M) = -0.04\). Terminal values: \(V_1(G) = +1\), \(V_1(H) = -1\).

(c) Perform the second iteration for state M. M can go East to G (\(V_1 = +1\)), South (\(V_1 = -0.04\)), West to S (\(V_1 = -0.04\)), or North (hits wall, stays at M, \(V_1 = -0.04\)). Compute \(V_2(M) = R(M) + \gamma \max_a V_1(\text{next state})\) ([@def:bellman-optimal]).

(d) What is the greedy policy at M after iteration 2? What about at S? Draw arrows on the grid.
exe:final-uncertainty.title: Bayesian Reasoning and MDP Policy

sections.title: Learning from Examples
sections.html:
In Chapter 4, we built agents that make sequential decisions under uncertainty using Markov decision processes. The MDP framework requires a transition model \(T(s' \mid s, a)\) and a reward function \(R(s)\)—but where do these come from? In the warehouse MDP of [@m1], we specified these components by hand: we declared that the robot drifts with probability 0.1, that the goal has reward \(+1\), and so on. For simple, well-understood environments, this works. But for complex real-world systems, the dynamics are too complicated to specify manually.

Machine learning provides the answer: instead of programming an agent's knowledge by hand, we give it data and let it learn. This chapter develops the foundational ideas of machine learning that underlie both the deep learning methods of Chapter 6 and the reinforcement learning algorithms of Chapter 7.

Forms of Learning

Machine learning algorithms differ primarily in the type of feedback available to the learner {% cite 'russell2020' note='sec. 19.1' %}. Three major paradigms have emerged:

Supervised Learning

In supervised learning, the agent is given a training set of input-output pairs \(\{(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^N\) and must learn a function \(h\) that maps inputs to outputs. The "supervision" is the known correct output \(y_i\) for each input \(\mathbf{x}_i\).

Unsupervised Learning

In unsupervised learning, the agent is given inputs \(\{\mathbf{x}_i\}_{i=1}^N\) without corresponding outputs. The goal is to discover structure in the data—clusters, latent factors, density estimates—without being told what to look for.

Reinforcement Learning

In reinforcement learning, the agent learns from a sequence of rewards received after taking actions in an environment. Unlike supervised learning, the agent is never told the correct action—it must discover which actions yield high reward through trial and error.

Paradigm Feedback Example
Supervised Labeled input-output pairs Predicting whether a warehouse location is high-risk from sensor and incident data
Unsupervised Unlabeled inputs only Grouping warehouse incidents into clusters to discover failure modes
Reinforcement Reward signals after actions A robot learning to navigate the warehouse by trial and error

Roadmap: How the Paradigms Connect

This chapter and Chapter 6 focus on supervised learning: given labeled examples, learn a function. In Chapter 7, we return to the MDP framework from Chapter 4, but now the agent learns the transition model and optimal policy from experience—that is reinforcement learning. Unsupervised learning is beyond the scope of these notes, though many of its tools (gradient descent, neural network architectures) overlap with what we cover here.

Beyond the Three Paradigms

Modern practice also recognizes semi-supervised learning (a small labeled set plus a large unlabeled set) and self-supervised learning (the model generates its own supervision from the data's structure—for instance, predicting the next word in a sentence). Large language models like GPT and Claude are trained with self-supervised objectives. These approaches blend the paradigms above rather than defining wholly new ones.

Supervised Learning Framework

Supervised learning is the most mature and widely used paradigm. We formalize it here because the concepts—hypothesis spaces, loss functions, empirical risk—recur throughout deep learning and beyond {% cite 'russell2020' note='sec. 19.2' %}.

The Setup

We are given a training set of \(N\) examples:

\[ \mathcal{D} = \{(\mathbf{x}_1, y_1), (\mathbf{x}_2, y_2), \ldots, (\mathbf{x}_N, y_N)\} \]

Each \(\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathcal{X}\) is a feature vector (also called an input or instance) and each \(y_i \in \mathcal{Y}\) is the corresponding label (or target, or output). The examples are assumed to be drawn independently from some unknown distribution \(P(\mathbf{x}, y)\).

Hypothesis

A hypothesis \(h: \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}\) is a function that maps inputs to predicted outputs. A hypothesis space \(\mathcal{H}\) is the set of all hypotheses the learning algorithm considers.

The choice of hypothesis space is a fundamental design decision. A hypothesis space that is too small may not contain a good approximation of the true relationship; one that is too large may contain many hypotheses that fit the training data but fail on new inputs. This tension is the bias-variance tradeoff, which we formalize in [@ml2].

Classification and Regression

Supervised learning problems fall into two categories based on the output space \(\mathcal{Y}\):

Classification

In classification, the output \(y\) takes values from a finite set of classes (or categories). Binary classification has \(\mathcal{Y} = \{0, 1\}\); multiclass classification has \(\mathcal{Y} = \{1, 2, \ldots, K\}\).

Regression

In regression, the output \(y\) is a real number: \(\mathcal{Y} = \mathbb{R}\) (or \(\mathbb{R}^d\) for multi-output regression).

Warehouse examples:

  • Classification: Given a storage location's features (zone, load weight, time since last inspection, number of sensors), predict whether it is high-risk or low-risk for structural failure. Here \(\mathcal{Y} = \{0, 1\}\).
  • Regression: Given the same features plus distance to the retrieval point, predict the time to complete a retrieval in seconds. Here \(\mathcal{Y} = \mathbb{R}\).

Loss Functions and Empirical Risk

To choose among hypotheses, we need a way to measure how wrong a prediction is.

Loss Function

A loss function \(L(y, \hat{y})\) quantifies the cost of predicting \(\hat{y}\) when the true label is \(y\). The loss is zero when the prediction is perfect and positive otherwise.

Common loss functions include:

Setting Loss Formula
Regression Mean squared error (MSE) \(L(y, \hat{y}) = (y - \hat{y})^2\)
Binary classification 0-1 loss \(L(y, \hat{y}) = \mathbb{1}[y \neq \hat{y}]\)
Binary classification Cross-entropy (log loss) \(L(y, \hat{y}) = -[y \log \hat{y} + (1-y)\log(1-\hat{y})]\)

[@Fig:loss-functions-comparison] visualizes these loss functions. The MSE (left) penalizes errors quadratically—large errors are much more costly than small ones. For classification (right), the 0-1 loss is intuitive but flat everywhere except the threshold, giving gradient-based methods nothing to work with. Cross-entropy provides a smooth, convex alternative: it penalizes confident wrong predictions severely (the loss grows without bound as \(\hat{y} \to 0\) when \(y = 1\)) while remaining differentiable everywhere.

We will return to MSE and cross-entropy in [@ml3], where they serve as the objective functions for gradient descent.

Empirical Risk

The empirical risk of a hypothesis \(h\) on training set \(\mathcal{D}\) is the average loss over all training examples: \[ \hat{R}(h) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} L(y_i, h(\mathbf{x}_i)) \]

The learning problem is then: find the hypothesis that minimizes empirical risk:

\[ h^* = \arg\min_{h \in \mathcal{H}} \hat{R}(h) \]

This is called empirical risk minimization (ERM). It is the foundation of most supervised learning algorithms. However, minimizing training error alone is not enough—we will see in [@ml2] why an algorithm that achieves zero training error can still fail badly on new data.

Decision Trees: A First Learning Algorithm

To make the supervised learning framework concrete, we study decision trees—a simple, interpretable learning algorithm that illustrates both the power and the pitfalls of learning from data {% cite 'russell2020' note='sec. 19.3' %}.

The Warehouse Risk Dataset

Suppose we have collected data on 12 warehouse storage locations and whether each experienced a structural incident:

Location Zone Load (kg) Inspection (days ago) Sensors High-Risk?
A1 East 450 10 3 No
A2 East 800 45 1 Yes
A3 West 300 5 4 No
A4 West 900 60 1 Yes
B1 East 700 30 2 Yes
B2 East 350 15 3 No
B3 West 600 50 2 Yes
B4 West 200 8 4 No
C1 East 500 25 2 No
C2 East 750 55 1 Yes
C3 West 400 20 3 No
C4 West 850 40 1 Yes

The features are: Zone (East/West), Load (weight in kg), Inspection (days since last inspection), and Sensors (number of monitoring sensors). The label is High-Risk (Yes/No).

How Decision Trees Work

Decision Tree

A decision tree is a tree-structured hypothesis where each internal node tests a feature, each branch corresponds to a test outcome, and each leaf node assigns a class label (classification) or a numeric prediction (regression).

To classify a new location, we start at the root and follow the branch corresponding to the test outcome at each node until we reach a leaf. For example, a tree might first ask "Is Load \(\geq 600\)?", then "Is Inspection \(\geq 35\) days?", arriving at a prediction in two or three tests. [@fig:decision-tree-warehouse] shows a decision tree for the warehouse risk dataset that we will build in this section.

The key question is: how do we choose which feature to test at each node? We want splits that separate the classes as cleanly as possible.

Entropy and Information Gain

Entropy

The entropy of a random variable \(Y\) with \(K\) possible values is: \[ H(Y) = -\sum_{k=1}^{K} P(Y = k) \log_2 P(Y = k) \] Entropy measures the uncertainty or impurity of a distribution. It is 0 when all examples belong to one class (no uncertainty) and maximal when examples are evenly split.

For binary classification with \(p\) positive examples and \(q\) negative examples out of \(N = p + q\) total:

\[ H = -\frac{p}{N}\log_2\frac{p}{N} - \frac{q}{N}\log_2\frac{q}{N} \]

[@Fig:binary-entropy] plots this function. Entropy is maximized at \(p/N = 0.5\) (a perfectly balanced dataset, maximum uncertainty) and equals zero when all examples belong to one class (no uncertainty at all). A good split drives the entropy in each child toward zero.

In our dataset, 6 of 12 locations are high-risk, so the entropy at the root is:

\[ H = -\frac{6}{12}\log_2\frac{6}{12} - \frac{6}{12}\log_2\frac{6}{12} = -\frac{1}{2}\log_2\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2}\log_2\frac{1}{2} = 1.0 \text{ bit} \]

Maximum uncertainty—the dataset is perfectly balanced.

Information Gain

The information gain of splitting on feature \(A\) is the reduction in entropy: \[ \text{Gain}(A) = H(Y) - \sum_{v \in \text{Values}(A)} \frac{|S_v|}{|S|} H(Y \mid A = v) \] where \(S_v\) is the subset of examples with \(A = v\).

Worked example: splitting on "Load \(\geq 600\)":

  • Load \(\geq 600\) (6 examples): A2, A4, B1, B3, C2, C4 → all 6 are high-risk. Entropy = 0.
  • Load \(< 600\) (6 examples): A1, A3, B2, B4, C1, C3 → all 6 are low-risk. Entropy = 0.

\[ \text{Gain}(\text{Load} \geq 600) = 1.0 - \left(\frac{6}{12} \cdot 0 + \frac{6}{12} \cdot 0\right) = 1.0 \text{ bit} \]

A perfect split! In practice, data is rarely this clean. Let us compute the gain for splitting on Zone:

  • East (6 examples): A1, A2, B1, B2, C1, C2 → 3 high-risk, 3 low-risk. Entropy = 1.0.
  • West (6 examples): A3, A4, B3, B4, C3, C4 → 3 high-risk, 3 low-risk. Entropy = 1.0.

\[ \text{Gain}(\text{Zone}) = 1.0 - \left(\frac{6}{12} \cdot 1.0 + \frac{6}{12} \cdot 1.0\right) = 0 \text{ bits} \]

Zone provides no information about risk—it splits the data without reducing uncertainty.

The Learning Algorithm

The decision tree learning algorithm recursively selects the feature with highest information gain at each node {% cite 'russell2020' note='sec. 19.3' %}:

function LearnDecisionTree(examples, features):
    if all examples have the same label:
        return Leaf(that label)
    if no features remain:
        return Leaf(majority label)
    A* ← feature in features with highest Gain(A)
    tree ← new decision node testing A*
    for each value v of A*:
        subset ← examples where A* = v
        if subset is empty:
            add Leaf(majority label of examples) as child
        else:
            add LearnDecisionTree(subset, features - {A*}) as child
    return tree

The pseudocode above is written for categorical features, where each value \(v\) produces a branch. For continuous features like Load and Inspection, the algorithm must also choose a threshold \(t\) that defines a binary split "\(A \geq t\)?" vs. "\(A < t\)". The threshold is learned as follows:

  1. Sort the \(N\) examples by the feature value.
  2. Consider every midpoint between consecutive distinct values as a candidate threshold. For example, if the sorted Load values are \(200, 300, 350, 400, \ldots\), the candidates are \(t \in \{250, 325, 375, \ldots\}\).
  3. Evaluate the information gain for each candidate: split the examples into "\(\text{Load} \geq t\)" and "\(\text{Load} < t\)", compute the weighted child entropies, and subtract from the parent entropy.
  4. Select the threshold with the highest information gain.

The algorithm evaluates every feature–threshold combination at each node and picks the overall best. This is why the "Load \(\geq 600\)" split emerged in our worked example: among all features and all thresholds, it produced the largest information gain (1.0 bit). In practice, this exhaustive search is efficient because there are at most \(N - 1\) candidate thresholds per feature.

Decision Trees in Python with scikit-learn

To implement decision trees, we use scikit-learn (sklearn), the standard Python library for machine learning. scikit-learn provides a consistent interface for dozens of learning algorithms: you create a model object, call .fit(X, y) to train it on data, and call .predict(X_new) to make predictions. We will use scikit-learn throughout this chapter and in later chapters for baseline models and utilities.

The scikit-learn API Pattern

Nearly every scikit-learn model follows the same three-step pattern:

  1. Instantiate: model = SomeModel(hyperparameters...)
  2. Fit: model.fit(X_train, y_train) — learn parameters from data
  3. Predict: model.predict(X_new) — apply the learned model to new inputs

This uniform interface makes it easy to swap one algorithm for another (e.g., replacing a decision tree with logistic regression) with minimal code changes.

We use only the three numeric features (Load, Inspection, Sensors), dropping Zone because the information gain calculation above showed it provides no useful information. (In general, categorical features can be included via one-hot encoding, but we omit that here for simplicity.)

The following script trains a DecisionTreeClassifier with criterion="entropy" (matching our information gain formulation) and displays both a text and graphical representation of the learned tree:

Train a decision tree on the warehouse risk dataset and visualize the result.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Dataset

We use three numeric features from the warehouse risk dataset. Zone is omitted because it has zero information gain (see text).

# Features: Load (kg), Inspection (days ago), Sensors
X = np.array([
    [450, 10, 3], [800, 45, 1], [300,  5, 4], [900, 60, 1],
    [700, 30, 2], [350, 15, 3], [600, 50, 2], [200,  8, 4],
    [500, 25, 2], [750, 55, 1], [400, 20, 3], [850, 40, 1],
])
y = np.array([0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1])  # 0=low-risk, 1=high-risk
feature_names = ["Load_kg", "Inspection_days", "Sensors"]
class_names = ["Low-Risk", "High-Risk"]

Train the tree

DecisionTreeClassifier implements the recursive splitting algorithm from the text. We use criterion="entropy" to match our information gain formulation.

tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion="entropy", random_state=42)
tree.fit(X, y)

Text representation

print(export_text(tree, feature_names=feature_names))
|--- Inspection_days <= 27.50
|   |--- class: 0
|--- Inspection_days >  27.50
|   |--- class: 1

Graphical visualization

We render the tree using plot_tree, which shows split conditions, entropy, sample counts, and class labels at each node.

Strengths and Limitations of Decision Trees

Decision trees have genuine strengths:

  • Interpretability: You can read the tree and understand why a prediction was made. Each path from root to leaf is a human-readable rule (e.g., "if Load \(\geq 600\) and Sensors \(\leq 1\), predict High-Risk").
  • Minimal preprocessing: They handle numeric features directly, require no feature normalization, and naturally accommodate missing values in some implementations.
  • Nonlinearity: They can capture nonlinear relationships and feature interactions through recursive splitting.

However, they have three significant limitations that motivate the models we develop in the rest of this chapter:

  1. Overfitting. A deep tree can create a unique leaf for every training example, achieving perfect training accuracy while failing on new data. We address this with regularization and cross-validation in [@ml2].

  2. Axis-aligned boundaries. Each split tests a single feature against a threshold, producing decision boundaries that are parallel to the feature axes. If the true boundary is diagonal—say, risk depends on a combination of load and inspection recency rather than either alone—a decision tree must approximate it with a staircase of many splits. This is inherently inefficient. Linear models ([@ml3]) can learn diagonal and oblique boundaries directly as \(w_1 \cdot \text{Load} + w_2 \cdot \text{Inspection} + b = 0\).

  3. No notion of "closeness". A decision tree treats Load = 599 and Load = 601 as completely different if the split threshold is 600, but treats Load = 601 and Load = 999 as identical (they land in the same leaf). The predictions are discontinuous: small changes in input can produce large jumps in output. Linear models, by contrast, produce smooth, continuous predictions: a small change in features produces a proportionally small change in the output. This smoothness is what makes gradient descent possible—the loss changes gradually as the parameters change, so we can follow the gradient downhill. With decision trees, there is no gradient to follow.

Why These Limitations Matter

The limitations above are not just theoretical concerns—they explain why modern machine learning has moved beyond decision trees for most tasks. The axis-alignment and discontinuity problems grow worse in high dimensions. And the lack of smooth, differentiable predictions means decision trees cannot be trained with gradient descent, which is the optimization engine behind deep learning (Chapter 6). The linear models of [@ml3] resolve all three issues: they produce smooth predictions, support oblique boundaries, and are trained by gradient descent. Their limitation—they can only learn linear boundaries—is then addressed by neural networks, which compose many linear models with nonlinear activations.
