sections.title: From Linear Models to Neural Networks
sections.html:
Chapter 5 ended with a fundamental limitation: linear models cannot learn nonlinear decision boundaries. The XOR problem ([@ml3:xor-problem]) showed that no single hyperplane separates the four points correctly, and we outlined two ways forward—hand-crafted nonlinear features or learned nonlinear features. This chapter takes the second path. A neural network is a composition of linear transformations and nonlinear activations that learns its own features from data. Everything from Chapter 5—loss functions, gradient descent, regularization, the bias-variance tradeoff—carries forward unchanged. The only new ingredient is the architecture {% cite 'russell2020' note='ch. 21' %}.

From Neurons to Layers

Neurons

The basic computational unit of a neural network is the neuron (also called a unit or node). Historically, a neuron with a hard threshold activation (\(g(z) = 1\) if \(z > 0\), else \(0\)) is called a perceptron {% cite 'russell2020' note='sec. 21.1' %}. Modern networks replace the threshold with smooth activations (sigmoid, ReLU), but the term persists in names like "multilayer perceptron."

Neuron (Unit)

A neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs and applies a nonlinear activation function: \[ z = \bm{w}^\top \bm{x} + b, \qquad a = g(z) \] where \(\bm{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is the input vector, \(\bm{w} \in \mathbb{R}^d\) are the weights, \(b \in \mathbb{R}\) is the bias, and \(g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) is the activation function. The quantity \(z\) is called the pre-activation and \(a\) is the activation (or output) of the neuron.

This is exactly the logistic regression model from [@ml3:logistic-regression] with \(g = \sigma\). The following diagram shows the computation of a single neuron:

graph LR
    x1(("$$x_1$$")) -- "$$w_1$$" --> sum["$$\sum + b$$"]
    x2(("$$x_2$$")) -- "$$w_2$$" --> sum
    x3(("$$x_3$$")) -- "$$w_3$$" --> sum
    sum -- "$$z$$" --> act["$$g$$"]
    act -- "$$a$$" --> out((" "))

    style sum fill:#e8f0fe,stroke:#4285f4
    style act fill:#fce8e6,stroke:#ea4335

The inputs \(x_1, \ldots, x_d\) are multiplied by weights, summed with a bias to produce the pre-activation \(z\) (blue), and passed through the activation function \(g\) (red) to produce the output \(a\). A single neuron is just a linear classifier followed by a nonlinearity—it cannot solve XOR any better than logistic regression. The power of neural networks comes from grouping many neurons into layers.

Layers

A layer groups \(d\) neurons that all receive the same input vector but each have their own weights and bias. The layer as a whole transforms an input vector into an output vector.

Layer

A layer of \(d\) neurons transforms an input vector \(\bm{a}_\text{in} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_\text{in}}\) into an output vector \(\bm{a}_\text{out} \in \mathbb{R}^d\) via a linear transformation followed by an element-wise nonlinearity: \[ \bm{z} = \bm{W} \bm{a}_\text{in} + \bm{b}, \qquad \bm{a}_\text{out} = g(\bm{z}) \] where \(\bm{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d_\text{in}}\) is the weight matrix, \(\bm{b} \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is the bias vector, \(\bm{z} \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is the pre-activation vector, and \(g\) is the activation function applied element-wise. The \(j\)-th row of \(\bm{W}\) and the \(j\)-th entry of \(\bm{b}\) are the weights and bias of the \(j\)-th neuron.

The linear part \(\bm{z} = \bm{W}\bm{a}_\text{in} + \bm{b}\) is a direct generalization of the single-neuron computation from [@eq:neuron]—instead of one weight vector \(\bm{w}\) producing one scalar \(z\), a weight matrix \(\bm{W}\) produces a vector \(\bm{z}\) of \(d\) pre-activations (one per neuron). The activation function \(g\) then applies independently to each component:

\[ \bm{a}_\text{out} = g(\bm{z}) = \bigl(g(z_1), \, g(z_2), \, \ldots, \, g(z_d)\bigr)^\top \]

This is also a generalization of the linear regression model from [@ml3:linear-regression-model]: a single neuron with identity activation is linear regression; a layer of \(d\) neurons produces \(d\) outputs from the same input. The following diagram shows a layer of 3 neurons, each computing its linear combination (blue) followed by the activation function (red), all inside the layer box:

graph LR
    x1(("$$x_1$$")) --> n1
    x1 --> n2
    x1 --> n3
    x2(("$$x_2$$")) --> n1
    x2 --> n2
    x2 --> n3

    subgraph "Layer (3 neurons, activation g)"
        n1["$$\bm w_1^\top \bm x + b_1$$"] --> g1["$$g$$"]
        n2["$$\bm w_2^\top \bm x + b_2$$"] --> g2["$$g$$"]
        n3["$$\bm w_3^\top \bm x + b_3$$"] --> g3["$$g$$"]
    end

    g1 -- "$$a_1$$" --> r1[ ]
    g2 -- "$$a_2$$" --> r2[ ]
    g3 -- "$$a_3$$" --> r3[ ]

    style n1 fill:#e8f0fe,stroke:#4285f4
    style n2 fill:#e8f0fe,stroke:#4285f4
    style n3 fill:#e8f0fe,stroke:#4285f4
    style g1 fill:#fce8e6,stroke:#ea4335
    style g2 fill:#fce8e6,stroke:#ea4335
    style g3 fill:#fce8e6,stroke:#ea4335
    style r1 fill:none,stroke:none
    style r2 fill:none,stroke:none
    style r3 fill:none,stroke:none

Each neuron in the layer receives the same input vector \((x_1, x_2)\) but applies its own weights and bias, producing a pre-activation \(z_j\) (blue). The activation function \(g\) (red) then applies independently to each \(z_j\) to produce the layer's output activations \(a_1, a_2, a_3\). Both stages—the linear part \(\bm{z} = \bm{W}\bm{a}_\text{in} + \bm{b}\) and the nonlinear part \(\bm{a}_\text{out} = g(\bm{z})\)—are part of the layer.

Activation Functions

Activation Function

An activation function \(g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) is a (typically nonlinear) function applied element-wise to a layer's pre-activation vector \(\bm{z}\). It introduces nonlinearity: without it, a sequence of layers \(\bm{W}^{(2)}(\bm{W}^{(1)}\bm{x} + \bm{b}^{(1)}) + \bm{b}^{(2)}\) collapses to a single linear transformation \(\bm{W}'\bm{x} + \bm{b}'\), and stacking layers would offer no benefit over a single layer.

We have already encountered one activation function: the sigmoid \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})\) from [@ml3:sigmoid]. Two other activations are widely used:

Hyperbolic tangent (tanh): \[ \tanh(z) = \frac{e^z - e^{-z}}{e^z + e^{-z}} \]

The tanh function is a rescaled sigmoid: \(\tanh(z) = 2\sigma(2z) - 1\). Its output range is \((-1, 1)\) instead of \((0, 1)\), which means it is zero-centered—a property that can improve gradient descent convergence.

Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU):

Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU)

The ReLU activation function is: \[ g(z) = \max(0, z) = \begin{cases} z & \text{if } z > 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } z \leq 0 \end{cases} \]

ReLU is strikingly simple: it passes positive pre-activations unchanged and sets negative pre-activations to zero. Applied to a layer's pre-activation vector, \(g(\bm{z}) = (\max(0, z_1), \ldots, \max(0, z_d))^\top\). Despite this simplicity, it has become the default activation for hidden layers in modern deep networks.

Why ReLU Dominates

ReLU has two practical advantages over sigmoid and tanh. First, its gradient is either 0 or 1—it does not saturate for large positive inputs, which prevents the vanishing gradient problem (discussed in [@dl2:vanishing-gradients]). Second, it produces sparse activations: for any input, roughly half of the neurons in a layer output zero, which makes the network more efficient and can act as a form of implicit regularization. The main drawback is "dead neurons": if a neuron's pre-activation is always negative (due to a large negative bias), it always outputs zero and receives no gradient, so it can never recover. Variants like Leaky ReLU (\(g(z) = \max(0.01z, z)\)) address this, but standard ReLU works well in most settings.

Activation Formula Range Derivative Used In
Sigmoid \(\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\) \((0, 1)\) \(\sigma(z)(1 - \sigma(z))\) Output layer (binary classification)
Tanh \(\tanh(z)\) \((-1, 1)\) \(1 - \tanh^2(z)\) RNNs ([@dl4])
ReLU \(\max(0, z)\) \([0, \infty)\) \(\begin{cases}1 & z > 0 \\ 0 & z \leq 0\end{cases}\) Hidden layers (default)

[@fig:activation-functions] plots all three activation functions. The sigmoid and tanh both saturate (their outputs flatten) for large \(|z|\), which causes vanishing gradients ([@dl2:vanishing-gradients]). ReLU avoids saturation for positive inputs but has a "dead region" for \(z < 0\) where the gradient is zero.

Multilayer Networks

A single layer can only learn a linear decision boundary (followed by a fixed nonlinearity). The power of neural networks comes from stacking layers, so that the output of one layer becomes the input to the next. Each successive layer transforms the representation, learning increasingly abstract features.

Feedforward Neural Network

A feedforward neural network (also called a multilayer perceptron, or MLP) is a function defined by a sequence of layers. For a network with \(L\) layers:

  • Layer 0 (input): the raw feature vector \(\bm{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_0}\), with \(\bm{a}^{(0)} = \bm{x}\)
  • Layer \(\ell\) (\(\ell = 1, \ldots, L\)): takes the previous layer's output as input and computes \[ \bm{z}^{(\ell)} = \bm{W}^{(\ell)} \bm{a}^{(\ell-1)} + \bm{b}^{(\ell)}, \qquad \bm{a}^{(\ell)} = g^{(\ell)}(\bm{z}^{(\ell)}) \] where \(\bm{W}^{(\ell)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_\ell \times d_{\ell-1}}\) is the weight matrix, \(\bm{b}^{(\ell)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_\ell}\) is the bias vector, and \(g^{(\ell)}\) is the activation function for layer \(\ell\)—each exactly as defined in [@eq:layer-computation].
  • Layer \(L\) (output): produces the final prediction \(\hat{\bm{y}} = \bm{a}^{(L)}\)

Hidden Layer

A hidden layer is any layer between the input and output layers. The activations of hidden layers are intermediate representations of the data—features that the network has learned. A network with \(L\) layers has \(L - 1\) hidden layers.

Depth and Width

The depth of a network is the number of layers \(L\) (counting the output layer but not the input). The width of a layer is the number of neurons \(d_\ell\) in that layer. "Deep learning" refers to networks with many layers (large depth).

The following diagram shows a complete feedforward network with 2 inputs, one hidden layer of 3 neurons with ReLU activation, and an output layer of 1 neuron with sigmoid activation. As above, the activation functions are shown inside each layer box.

graph LR
    subgraph "Layer 0: Input"
        x1(("$$x_1$$"))
        x2(("$$x_2$$"))
    end

    x1 --> h1
    x1 --> h2
    x1 --> h3
    x2 --> h1
    x2 --> h2
    x2 --> h3

    subgraph "Layer 1: Hidden, ReLU"
        h1["$$\bm w_1^\top \bm x + b_1$$"] --> r1["$$\text{ReLU}$$"]
        h2["$$\bm w_2^\top \bm x + b_2$$"] --> r2["$$\text{ReLU}$$"]
        h3["$$\bm w_3^\top \bm x + b_3$$"] --> r3["$$\text{ReLU}$$"]
    end

    r1 -- "$$a_1^{(1)}$$" --> o1
    r2 -- "$$a_2^{(1)}$$" --> o1
    r3 -- "$$a_3^{(1)}$$" --> o1

    subgraph "Layer 2: Output, sigmoid"
        o1["$$\bm w^{(2)\top} \bm a^{(1)} + b^{(2)}$$"] --> sig["$$\sigma$$"]
    end

    sig -- "$$\hat y$$" --> out[ ]

    style h1 fill:#e8f0fe,stroke:#4285f4
    style h2 fill:#e8f0fe,stroke:#4285f4
    style h3 fill:#e8f0fe,stroke:#4285f4
    style r1 fill:#fce8e6,stroke:#ea4335
    style r2 fill:#fce8e6,stroke:#ea4335
    style r3 fill:#fce8e6,stroke:#ea4335
    style o1 fill:#e8f0fe,stroke:#4285f4
    style sig fill:#fce8e6,stroke:#ea4335
    style out fill:none,stroke:none

The computation flows left to right. Each layer box contains both the linear transformation (blue: \(\bm{z} = \bm{W}\bm{a}_\text{in} + \bm{b}\)) and the activation function (red: \(g(\bm{z})\)). The hidden layer computes \(\bm{a}^{(1)} = \text{ReLU}(\bm{W}^{(1)}\bm{x} + \bm{b}^{(1)})\); the output layer computes \(\hat{y} = \sigma(\bm{w}^{(2)\top}\bm{a}^{(1)} + b^{(2)})\). This is depth \(L = 2\), with hidden width 3 and output width 1.

Solving XOR

Let us build a concrete network that solves XOR. The input is \(\bm{x} = (x_1, x_2)^\top\) and the target is \(y = x_1 \oplus x_2\) (1 if exactly one input is 1, else 0). We use a network with one hidden layer of 2 neurons and one output neuron.

Architecture: Input (2) → Hidden (2, ReLU) → Output (1, sigmoid)

Weights (chosen by hand to illustrate the idea; in practice, these would be learned):

Hidden layer (\(\ell = 1\)): \[ \bm{W}^{(1)} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \bm{b}^{(1)} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} \]

Output layer (\(\ell = 2\)): \[ \bm{w}^{(2)} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -4 \end{pmatrix}, \quad b^{(2)} = -1 \]

Forward pass for each XOR input:

\(\bm{x}\) \(\bm{z}^{(1)}\) \(\bm{a}^{(1)}\) (ReLU) \(z^{(2)}\) \(\hat{y} = \sigma(z^{(2)})\) Target
\((0, 0)\) \((0, -1)\) \((0, 0)\) \(-1\) \(0.27\) 0
\((0, 1)\) \((1, 0)\) \((1, 0)\) \(1\) \(0.73\) 1
\((1, 0)\) \((1, 0)\) \((1, 0)\) \(1\) \(0.73\) 1
\((1, 1)\) \((2, 1)\) \((2, 1)\) \(-1\) \(0.27\) 0

A threshold at 0.5 gives the correct classification 0, 1, 1, 0. The confidence is moderate because these hand-picked weights are illustrative rather than optimal—gradient descent would refine them to produce sharper predictions.

The following two diagrams trace the forward pass for inputs \((0, 1)\) and \((1, 1)\), showing the numerical value at each stage. Green nodes indicate active/positive outputs; red nodes indicate inactive or negative outputs. Comparing the two reveals how the hidden layer's two features interact to produce the XOR decision.

Forward pass for input \((0, 1)\) — neuron 1 fires, neuron 2 does not, output is positive (class 1):

graph LR
    subgraph Input
        x1(("$$0$$"))
        x2(("$$1$$"))
    end

    x1 --> z1
    x2 --> z1
    x1 --> z2
    x2 --> z2

    subgraph "Hidden layer (ReLU)"
        z1["$$1(0) + 1(1) + 0$$"] -- "$$z_1 = 1$$" --> r1["$$\max(0, 1)$$"]
        z2["$$1(0) + 1(1) - 1$$"] -- "$$z_2 = 0$$" --> r2["$$\max(0, 0)$$"]
    end

    r1 -- "$$a_1 = 1$$" --> z3
    r2 -- "$$a_2 = 0$$" --> z3

    subgraph "Output layer (sigmoid)"
        z3["$$2(1) - 4(0) - 1$$"] -- "$$z = 1$$" --> sig["$$\sigma(1)$$"]
    end

    sig -- "$$\hat y = 0.73$$" --> out[ ]

    style r1 fill:#c6efce,stroke:#006100
    style r2 fill:#fce4ec,stroke:#b71c1c
    style sig fill:#c6efce,stroke:#006100
    style out fill:none,stroke:none

Forward pass for input \((1, 1)\) — both neurons fire, the large negative weight \(-4\) overwhelms, output is negative (class 0):

graph LR
    subgraph Input
        x1(("$$1$$"))
        x2(("$$1$$"))
    end

    x1 --> z1
    x2 --> z1
    x1 --> z2
    x2 --> z2

    subgraph "Hidden layer (ReLU)"
        z1["$$1(1) + 1(1) + 0$$"] -- "$$z_1 = 2$$" --> r1["$$\max(0, 2)$$"]
        z2["$$1(1) + 1(1) - 1$$"] -- "$$z_2 = 1$$" --> r2["$$\max(0, 1)$$"]
    end

    r1 -- "$$a_1 = 2$$" --> z3
    r2 -- "$$a_2 = 1$$" --> z3

    subgraph "Output layer (sigmoid)"
        z3["$$2(2) - 4(1) - 1$$"] -- "$$z = -1$$" --> sig["$$\sigma(-1)$$"]
    end

    sig -- "$$\hat y = 0.27$$" --> out[ ]

    style r1 fill:#c6efce,stroke:#006100
    style r2 fill:#c6efce,stroke:#006100
    style sig fill:#fce4ec,stroke:#b71c1c
    style out fill:none,stroke:none

The key insight is structural: the hidden layer computes two features—\(a_1^{(1)} = \text{ReLU}(x_1 + x_2)\) detects "at least one input is 1" and \(a_2^{(1)} = \text{ReLU}(x_1 + x_2 - 1)\) detects "both inputs are 1." When both features fire (as for input \((1,1)\)), the \(-4\) weight on the second neuron overwhelms the \(+2\) weight on the first, driving the output negative. The output layer combines them: \(2 a_1 - 4 a_2 - 1\) is positive only when the first feature fires but the second does not—exactly the XOR condition.

This is the core idea: hidden layers learn features. In [@ml3:xor-problem], we noted that manually adding \(x_3 = x_1 \cdot x_2\) makes XOR linearly separable. A neural network discovers such features automatically during training.

Universal Approximation

The XOR example is a special case of a much more general result:

Universal Approximation Theorem (Informal)

A feedforward network with a single hidden layer containing a sufficient number of neurons, using any "squashing" activation function (such as sigmoid or tanh), can approximate any continuous function on a compact domain to any desired accuracy {% cite 'russell2020' note='sec. 21.1' %}.

This theorem guarantees that the hypothesis space of single-hidden-layer networks is rich enough to contain a good approximation of any target function. However, it says nothing about:

  • How many neurons are needed—the required width may be exponentially large
  • Whether gradient descent can find the right weights—the loss surface is non-convex
  • Whether the approximation generalizes—fitting the training data is not the same as generalizing

Why Depth Matters

The universal approximation theorem shows that width alone is sufficient in theory. In practice, depth is far more efficient. Deep networks can represent certain functions with exponentially fewer parameters than shallow ones. Intuitively, depth enables compositional computation: layer 1 learns simple features (edges, trends), layer 2 combines them into patterns (shapes, motifs), layer 3 composes patterns into objects or decisions. This hierarchical structure mirrors the way many real-world processes are organized, which is why deep networks are so effective on natural data. The theoretical result says "a solution exists"; the empirical finding is that depth makes it findable by gradient descent.

Warehouse Application Preview

The neural networks of this chapter will be applied to two warehouse tasks that demand the representational power linear models lack:

Control task: picking-time prediction. Given a feature vector describing the current warehouse state—robot position, distances to pending orders, aisle congestion levels, battery status—predict the time to fulfill the next order. This is a regression problem like the retrieval-time prediction of [@ml3:linear-regression-warehouse], but with more features and nonlinear interactions (congestion has a different effect depending on the robot's current aisle, for instance). A feedforward network can learn these interactions automatically.

Vision task: shelf condition classification. A camera mounted on the warehouse robot captures images of storage shelves. Each image must be classified as normal, damaged (structural cracks, bent supports), or overloaded (items stacked beyond capacity). A 64×64 grayscale image has 4096 pixel values—far too high-dimensional for a decision tree or logistic regression to handle effectively. Moreover, the relevant features (crack patterns, load distributions) are spatial and hierarchical, which motivates the convolutional architectures of [@dl3].

Both tasks build on the warehouse domain from previous chapters but raise the stakes: the inputs are richer, the patterns are nonlinear, and the models must be correspondingly more powerful.

sections.title: Training Deep Networks
sections.html:
In [@dl1], we built feedforward networks and showed that they can represent nonlinear functions. But how do we find the right weights? For linear regression, the gradient of the MSE has a clean closed form ([@ml3:mse-gradient]). For a network with multiple layers, the loss is a composition of many functions, and we need a systematic way to compute gradients through the entire chain. That method is backpropagation—the chain rule applied to computational graphs—and it is the engine that makes deep learning possible {% cite 'russell2020' note='sec. 21.3' %}.

The Computational Graph

A neural network's forward pass can be represented as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of operations. Each node performs a simple computation (matrix multiply, add bias, apply activation), and edges carry intermediate values from one operation to the next.

Computational Graph

A computational graph is a directed acyclic graph where each node represents a mathematical operation and each edge carries a value called a tensor (the general term for a scalar, vector, or matrix—a \(d\)-dimensional array of numbers). The forward pass evaluates the graph from inputs to outputs, computing the loss. The backward pass traverses the graph in reverse, computing gradients of the loss with respect to every intermediate value and parameter.

Consider a 2-layer network for the warehouse picking-time predictor. The input is \(\bm{x} \in \mathbb{R}^4\) (robot position, distance, congestion, battery), the hidden layer has 3 neurons with ReLU activation, and the output is a single predicted time \(\hat{y}\). The forward pass as a computational graph:

\[ \xrightarrow{\bm{x}} \boxed{\bm{W}^{(1)}\bm{x} + \bm{b}^{(1)}} \xrightarrow{\bm{z}^{(1)}} \boxed{\text{ReLU}} \xrightarrow{\bm{a}^{(1)}} \boxed{\bm{w}^{(2)\top}\bm{a}^{(1)} + b^{(2)}} \xrightarrow{\hat{y}} \]

Each box is a node (an operation); each arrow carries the value produced by one operation and consumed by the next. The input \(\bm{x}\) enters on the left edge, flows through the hidden layer's linear transformation and ReLU activation, then through the output layer's linear transformation, producing \(\hat{y}\) on the right edge. During training, the loss \(\mathcal{L} = (y - \hat{y})^2\) is computed from \(\hat{y}\), but the loss is not part of the network itself. The graph makes the dependencies explicit, which is exactly what we need to apply the chain rule.

Why Tensors?

In the graph above, \(\bm{x}\) is a vector (a 1-dimensional array), \(\bm{W}^{(1)}\) is a matrix (a 2-dimensional array), and \(\hat{y}\) is a scalar (a 0-dimensional array). The umbrella term for all of these is tensor: a \(d\)-dimensional array of numbers, where \(d\) is the rank (or order). A scalar has rank 0, a vector rank 1, a matrix rank 2, and so on.

In practice, the values flowing through a network are almost always tensors of rank 2 or higher, because we process mini-batches of examples simultaneously ([@dl2:sgd-revisited]). A single input \(\bm{x} \in \mathbb{R}^4\) is a vector, but a mini-batch of 32 inputs is a \(32 \times 4\) matrix. After the hidden layer, the activations \(\bm{a}^{(1)}\) become a \(32 \times 3\) matrix—one row per example, one column per neuron. For image inputs ([@dl3]), a single example is already a 3-dimensional tensor (height \(\times\) width \(\times\) channels), and a mini-batch is a 4-dimensional tensor.

Deep learning frameworks like PyTorch represent everything as tensors and implement all operations (matrix multiplication, element-wise activation, loss computation) as tensor operations. This is why the field uses the term "tensor" rather than "vector" or "matrix"—it is the natural generalization that covers all cases.

Backpropagation

Backpropagation

Backpropagation (backprop) is an algorithm for computing the gradient of the loss with respect to every parameter in the network. It applies the chain rule of calculus in reverse order through the computational graph: starting from the loss, it propagates gradients backward through each operation, layer by layer.

The Chain Rule for Composed Functions

Recall the chain rule from calculus: if \(y = f(u)\) and \(u = g(x)\), then \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du} \cdot \frac{du}{dx}\). A neural network is a long chain of such compositions, and the chain rule applies to each link.

For a network with \(L\) layers, the loss \(\mathcal{L}\) depends on the output \(\bm{a}^{(L)}\), which depends on \(\bm{z}^{(L)}\), which depends on \(\bm{a}^{(L-1)}\), and so on back to the input. The gradient of the loss with respect to any parameter \(\bm{W}^{(\ell)}\) is:

\[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \bm{W}^{(\ell)}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \bm{z}^{(\ell)}} \cdot \frac{\partial \bm{z}^{(\ell)}}{\partial \bm{W}^{(\ell)}} \]

where \(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \bm{z}^{(\ell)}}\) is computed by chaining backward from the loss through all layers above \(\ell\).

Worked Example: Backprop Through Two Layers

Let us compute the gradients for the 2-layer picking-time predictor, using a single training example \((\bm{x}, y)\) with MSE loss \(\mathcal{L} = (y - \hat{y})^2\).

Step 1: Forward pass (compute and store all intermediate values).

Suppose \(\bm{x} = (2, 5, 1, 0.8)^\top\), \(y = 35\) seconds, and after the forward pass we obtain:

\[ \bm{z}^{(1)} = (-0.3, 1.2, 0.7)^\top, \quad \bm{a}^{(1)} = (0, 1.2, 0.7)^\top, \quad \hat{y} = z^{(2)} = 28.0 \]

So \(\mathcal{L} = (35 - 28)^2 = 49\).

Step 2: Backward pass (apply the chain rule from the loss back to each parameter).

Output layer gradient: \[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{y}} = -2(y - \hat{y}) = -2(35 - 28) = -14 \]

Since the output layer has no activation (identity), \(\hat{y} = z^{(2)}\), so \(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z^{(2)}} = -14\) as well. Now we need the gradient with respect to the output weights \(\bm{w}^{(2)}\). The output pre-activation is \(z^{(2)} = \bm{w}^{(2)\top}\bm{a}^{(1)} + b^{(2)}\), which is a dot product: \(z^{(2)} = w_1^{(2)} a_1^{(1)} + w_2^{(2)} a_2^{(1)} + w_3^{(2)} a_3^{(1)} + b^{(2)}\). Differentiating with respect to \(w_j^{(2)}\) gives \(\partial z^{(2)} / \partial w_j^{(2)} = a_j^{(1)}\)—the activation of the \(j\)-th hidden neuron. Collecting these into a vector: \(\partial z^{(2)} / \partial \bm{w}^{(2)} = \bm{a}^{(1)}\). By the chain rule:

\[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \bm{w}^{(2)}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z^{(2)}} \cdot \frac{\partial z^{(2)}}{\partial \bm{w}^{(2)}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z^{(2)}} \cdot \bm{a}^{(1)} = -14 \cdot (0, 1.2, 0.7)^\top = (0, -16.8, -9.8)^\top \]

Similarly, \(\partial z^{(2)} / \partial b^{(2)} = 1\), so:

\[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial b^{(2)}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z^{(2)}} \cdot 1 = -14 \]

Hidden layer gradient (propagating through the output weights and the ReLU): \[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \bm{a}^{(1)}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z^{(2)}} \cdot \bm{w}^{(2)} \]

The ReLU derivative is \(g'(z) = \mathbb{1}[z > 0]\) (1 if the pre-activation was positive, 0 otherwise): \[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \bm{z}^{(1)}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \bm{a}^{(1)}} \odot g'(\bm{z}^{(1)}) \]

where \(\odot\) denotes element-wise multiplication. Since \(\bm{z}^{(1)} = (-0.3, 1.2, 0.7)^\top\), the ReLU mask is \((0, 1, 1)^\top\), so the gradient through the first neuron is zeroed out (it was inactive during the forward pass).

Finally: \[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \bm{W}^{(1)}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \bm{z}^{(1)}} \cdot \bm{x}^\top \]

Each element of this matrix tells us how to adjust one weight in the first layer to reduce the loss.

Backprop Is Just the Chain Rule

Backpropagation can seem mysterious when described abstractly, but it is nothing more than the chain rule applied methodically. The "forward pass" computes and stores intermediate values; the "backward pass" multiplies local derivatives in reverse order. Every deep learning framework (PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX) implements this automatically: you define the forward computation, and the framework builds the computational graph and computes all gradients for you. The worked example above is what loss.backward() does internally.

Stochastic Gradient Descent Revisited

In [@ml3:sgd], we introduced stochastic gradient descent for linear models. The same algorithm trains neural networks, but the setting is fundamentally different: the loss surface is non-convex, with many local minima, saddle points, and flat regions.

Mini-Batch SGD

Mini-batch stochastic gradient descent updates parameters using the average gradient over a random subset (mini-batch) of the training data: \[ \bm{\theta} \leftarrow \bm{\theta} - \alpha \cdot \frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}} \nabla_{\bm{\theta}} \mathcal{L}(\bm{x}_i, y_i; \bm{\theta}) \] where \(\bm{\theta}\) denotes all network parameters, \(\mathcal{B}\) is the mini-batch, and \(\alpha\) is the learning rate.

Epoch

An epoch is one complete pass through the entire training set. If the training set has \(N\) examples and the mini-batch size is \(m\), each epoch consists of \(\lceil N/m \rceil\) parameter updates.

Learning Rate Schedules

A fixed learning rate works for convex problems (like linear regression), but deep networks often benefit from reducing \(\alpha\) during training. Common schedules include:

  • Step decay: reduce \(\alpha\) by a factor (e.g., \(\times 0.1\)) at predetermined epochs
  • Cosine annealing: smoothly decrease \(\alpha\) following a cosine curve from the initial value to near zero over the training run

The intuition is that large steps are useful early (to make rapid progress) but harmful late (when the optimizer should settle into a minimum).

Why SGD Works on Non-Convex Losses

The loss surface of a deep network has many local minima and saddle points. In principle, gradient descent could get stuck. In practice, several factors conspire to make SGD effective: (1) the noise from mini-batch sampling helps escape shallow local minima, (2) most local minima in high-dimensional loss surfaces have similar loss values to the global minimum, and (3) saddle points (where the gradient is zero but the point is not a minimum) are more common than true local minima, and SGD's noise naturally pushes it off saddle points. Understanding why SGD works so well for deep learning remains an active area of research.

Weight Initialization and Batch Normalization

The Vanishing Gradient Problem

Vanishing Gradient Problem

The vanishing gradient problem occurs when gradients become exponentially small as they are propagated backward through many layers. Each layer multiplies the gradient by its local derivative; if these derivatives are consistently less than 1 (as happens with sigmoid activations for large or small inputs), the gradient reaching early layers is negligibly small, and those layers stop learning.

Consider a network with \(L\) layers using sigmoid activations. The maximum value of \(\sigma'(z)\) is \(0.25\) (at \(z = 0\)). In the worst case, the gradient at layer \(\ell\) is scaled by a factor of roughly \(0.25^{L - \ell}\) relative to the output layer. For a 10-layer network, the gradient reaching the first layer is \(0.25^9 \approx 4 \times 10^{-6}\) of the output gradient—effectively zero.

The reverse problem also exists: if the local derivatives are consistently greater than 1, gradients explode, leading to numerical overflow and unstable training.

Weight Initialization

Proper initialization of the weight matrices can prevent vanishing and exploding gradients at the start of training. The key idea is to choose initial weights so that the variance of activations remains approximately constant across layers:

  • Xavier initialization (for sigmoid/tanh): draw weights from \(\mathcal{N}(0, 1/d_{\ell-1})\) or \(\mathcal{U}(-\sqrt{3/d_{\ell-1}}, \sqrt{3/d_{\ell-1}})\), where \(d_{\ell-1}\) is the number of inputs to the layer (both give variance \(1/d_{\ell-1}\))
  • He initialization (for ReLU): draw weights from \(\mathcal{N}(0, 2/d_{\ell-1})\), accounting for the fact that ReLU zeros out half the activations

These are the defaults in PyTorch and work well for most architectures.

Batch Normalization

Batch Normalization

Batch normalization normalizes the pre-activations of each layer across a mini-batch: \[ \hat{z}_j = \frac{z_j - \mu_\mathcal{B}}{\sqrt{\sigma^2_\mathcal{B} + \epsilon}}, \qquad \tilde{z}_j = \gamma \hat{z}_j + \beta \] where \(\mu_\mathcal{B}\) and \(\sigma^2_\mathcal{B}\) are the mean and variance of \(z_j\) computed over the mini-batch, \(\epsilon\) is a small constant for numerical stability, and \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) are learnable parameters that allow the network to undo the normalization if needed.

Batch normalization stabilizes training by keeping the distribution of each layer's inputs roughly constant during training. This reduces the dependence of later layers on the initialization of earlier layers, enabling higher learning rates and faster convergence. It has become a standard component of deep network architectures.

Optimizers Beyond SGD

Plain SGD can oscillate in ravine-like loss landscapes, where the gradient alternately points steeply across the ravine and gently along it. Two ideas address this:

Momentum

SGD with momentum maintains a running average of past gradients and uses it to update the parameters: \[ \bm{v} \leftarrow \beta \bm{v} + \nabla_{\bm{\theta}} \mathcal{L}, \qquad \bm{\theta} \leftarrow \bm{\theta} - \alpha \bm{v} \] where \(\beta \in [0, 1)\) is the momentum coefficient (typically 0.9). The velocity \(\bm{v}\) accumulates gradients over time, smoothing out oscillations and accelerating movement in consistent directions.

Adam Optimizer

Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation) combines momentum with per-parameter adaptive learning rates. It maintains running estimates of both the first moment (mean) and second moment (uncentered variance) of the gradient: \[ \bm{m} \leftarrow \beta_1 \bm{m} + (1 - \beta_1)\nabla\mathcal{L}, \qquad \bm{v} \leftarrow \beta_2 \bm{v} + (1 - \beta_2)(\nabla\mathcal{L})^2 \] \[ \bm{\theta} \leftarrow \bm{\theta} - \alpha \cdot \frac{\hat{\bm{m}}}{\sqrt{\hat{\bm{v}}} + \epsilon} \] where \(\hat{\bm{m}}\) and \(\hat{\bm{v}}\) are bias-corrected estimates. Default hyperparameters are \(\beta_1 = 0.9\), \(\beta_2 = 0.999\), \(\epsilon = 10^{-8}\).

Adam as the Default

Adam is the most widely used optimizer in deep learning practice. It adapts the learning rate for each parameter individually, which is especially useful when different parameters have gradients of very different magnitudes (common in deep networks). When in doubt, start with Adam at its default learning rate (\(\alpha = 0.001\)). SGD with momentum can sometimes achieve better final performance (especially for image classification), but it requires more careful tuning of the learning rate and schedule.

Training in Python

The following script trains a 3-layer feedforward network on the warehouse shelf-condition dataset using PyTorch. We demonstrate the training loop, visualize the loss curve, compare learning rates, and show the effect of batch normalization on convergence.

sections.title: Implementation: XOR from Scratch and in PyTorch
sections.html:
The previous two sections developed the building blocks—neurons, layers, activation functions ([@dl1])—and the training algorithm—backpropagation and SGD ([@dl2]). In this section, we bring them together by implementing a complete neural network that learns XOR. We first build the network from scratch in NumPy, making every computation (forward pass, loss, backpropagation, parameter update) explicit. We then replicate the result in PyTorch to introduce the framework used for the rest of the chapter.

From Scratch in NumPy

The architecture is:

\[ \text{Input (2)} \to \text{Hidden (4, ReLU)} \to \text{Output (1, sigmoid)} \]

We use 4 hidden neurons rather than the 2 from the hand-constructed XOR example in [@dl1:solving-xor]—with random initialization, 4 neurons converge more reliably. The loss function is binary cross-entropy ([@ml3:cross-entropy]), and the optimizer is plain gradient descent.

The implementation translates the equations from [@dl1] and [@dl2] directly into code:

  • Forward pass: compute \(\bm{z}^{(1)} = \bm{W}^{(1)}\bm{x} + \bm{b}^{(1)}\), \(\bm{a}^{(1)} = \text{ReLU}(\bm{z}^{(1)})\), \(z^{(2)} = \bm{w}^{(2)\top}\bm{a}^{(1)} + b^{(2)}\), \(\hat{y} = \sigma(z^{(2)})\)
  • Backward pass: compute gradients using the chain rule ([@dl2:backpropagation]), starting from \(\partial \mathcal{L}/\partial \hat{y}\) and propagating back through the sigmoid, the output weights, the ReLU, and the hidden weights
  • Update: \(\bm{\theta} \leftarrow \bm{\theta} - \alpha \nabla_{\bm{\theta}} \mathcal{L}\)

XOR from scratch

We implement a 2-layer neural network trained with backpropagation entirely in NumPy—no deep learning framework. Every computation (forward pass, loss, backward pass, parameter update) is explicit, so we can see exactly what PyTorch does under the hood.

Architecture: Input (2) → Hidden (4, ReLU) → Output (1, sigmoid)

We use 4 hidden neurons rather than the 2 from the hand-constructed XOR example in [@dl1:solving-xor]. With random initialization, 2 neurons frequently get stuck in local minima; 4 neurons converge reliably.

A note on the dataset. XOR is unusual: the labels are exact (there is no noise), and the entire dataset has only 4 examples. In real applications, datasets are noisy and much larger, and the model cannot memorize the training set without overfitting. We use XOR here because its simplicity makes every step of training visible, not because it is representative of real problems. The same code structure—forward, loss, backward, update—scales directly to large, noisy datasets.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Activation functions

We need the activations from [@dl1:activation-functions] and their derivatives for backpropagation ([@dl2:backpropagation]). The sigmoid is used at the output (producing a probability for binary classification), and ReLU is used in the hidden layer.

def sigmoid(z):
    """Sigmoid activation (Section 6.1): maps any real z to (0, 1)."""
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

def relu(z):
    """ReLU activation (Section 6.1): max(0, z), applied element-wise."""
    return np.maximum(0, z)

def relu_grad(z):
    """Derivative of ReLU w.r.t. the pre-activation z.

    Returns 1 where z > 0 (the linear region) and 0 where z <= 0
    (the dead region discussed in Section 6.1).
    """
    return (z > 0).astype(float)

Forward pass

This is the layer computation from [@eq:layer-computation], applied twice: once for the hidden layer and once for the output layer.

\[ \bm{z}^{(1)} = \bm{W}^{(1)}\bm{x} + \bm{b}^{(1)}, \qquad \bm{a}^{(1)} = \text{ReLU}(\bm{z}^{(1)}) \] \[ z^{(2)} = \bm{w}^{(2)\top}\bm{a}^{(1)} + b^{(2)}, \qquad \hat{y} = \sigma(z^{(2)}) \]

We store all intermediate values in a cache dictionary because backpropagation needs them to compute gradients ([@dl2:backpropagation]).

def forward(x, W1, b1, W2, b2):
    """Forward pass through both layers. Returns prediction and cache."""
    # --- Hidden layer (layer 1) ---
    z1 = W1 @ x + b1       # linear: weight matrix times input plus bias
    a1 = relu(z1)           # activation: element-wise ReLU

    # --- Output layer (layer 2) ---
    z2 = W2 @ a1 + b2       # linear: weight vector times hidden activations
    a2 = sigmoid(z2)        # activation: sigmoid produces probability in (0,1)

    # Store intermediates for the backward pass
    cache = {"x": x, "z1": z1, "a1": a1, "z2": z2, "a2": a2}
    return a2.item(), cache

Loss function

We use binary cross-entropy (BCE), which we derived in [@ml3:cross-entropy] as the loss for logistic regression. The same loss applies here because our output layer is a sigmoid producing a probability. Recall that BCE avoids the vanishing-gradient problem that MSE causes with sigmoid outputs.

def bce_loss(y_hat, y):
    """Binary cross-entropy for a single example (Section 5.3).

    L = -[y log(y_hat) + (1-y) log(1-y_hat)]
    """
    eps = 1e-12  # prevent log(0)
    return -(y * np.log(y_hat + eps) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - y_hat + eps))

Backward pass (backpropagation)

This is the algorithm from [@dl2:backpropagation]: apply the chain rule in reverse through the computational graph. For each layer, we compute the gradient of the loss with respect to (1) the pre-activations, (2) the weights, and (3) the biases.

A key simplification: the combination of sigmoid activation and BCE loss produces the clean gradient \(\partial L / \partial z^{(2)} = \hat{y} - y\) (the sigmoid derivative cancels with terms in the BCE derivative, as shown in [@ml3:cross-entropy]). This is why cross-entropy is preferred over MSE for classification.

def backward(y, cache, W2):
    """Backpropagation: compute gradients of BCE loss w.r.t. all parameters."""
    x  = cache["x"]
    z1 = cache["z1"]
    a1 = cache["a1"]
    a2 = cache["a2"]

    # --- Output layer gradients ---
    # d(BCE)/d(z2) = a2 - y  (sigmoid + BCE cancellation from Section 5.3)
    dz2 = a2 - y                        # (1,) gradient at output pre-activation
    dW2 = dz2[:, None] @ a1[None, :]   # (1, n_h) outer product: dL/dW2
    db2 = dz2                           # (1,) dL/db2 = dL/dz2

    # --- Hidden layer gradients ---
    # Propagate gradient back through output weights
    da1 = W2.T @ dz2                    # (n_h,) gradient at hidden activations

    # Propagate through ReLU: zero out gradients where z1 <= 0
    dz1 = da1 * relu_grad(z1)          # (n_h,) element-wise mask

    # Gradient w.r.t. hidden weights and biases
    dW1 = dz1[:, None] @ x[None, :]    # (n_h, 2) outer product: dL/dW1
    db1 = dz1                           # (n_h,) dL/db1 = dL/dz1

    return dW1, db1, dW2, db2

XOR dataset

The XOR function outputs 1 when exactly one of the two inputs is 1, and 0 otherwise. As shown in [@ml3:xor-problem], no linear model can learn this function—the positive and negative examples are not linearly separable. This is the problem that motivated neural networks in [@dl1].

Note that this is a noise-free, complete dataset: all four possible inputs are present, and the labels are exact. In the warehouse applications later in this chapter, datasets will be noisy and much larger, requiring regularization ([@dl5]) and train/test splits ([@ml2:train-val-test]).

X = np.array([[0, 0], [0, 1], [1, 0], [1, 1]], dtype=float)
Y = np.array([0, 1, 1, 0], dtype=float)

Weight initialization

We use He initialization ([@dl2:weight-initialization]): weights are drawn from \(\mathcal{N}(0, 2/d_{\text{in}})\), which keeps the variance of activations roughly constant across layers when using ReLU. Biases are initialized to zero.

n_hidden = 4   # width of the hidden layer
lr = 0.1       # learning rate (alpha)
epochs = 5000  # number of full passes through the dataset
seed = 0       # for reproducibility

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)

# He initialization: variance = 2 / fan_in
W1 = rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(2 / 2), size=(n_hidden, 2))        # (4, 2)
b1 = np.zeros(n_hidden)                                        # (4,)
W2 = rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(2 / n_hidden), size=(1, n_hidden))  # (1, 4)
b2 = np.zeros(1)                                                # (1,)

Training loop

Each epoch loops over all 4 examples. For each example we perform four steps:

  1. Forward pass — compute the prediction
  2. Loss — compute how wrong the prediction is
  3. Backward pass — compute gradients via backpropagation
  4. Update — adjust weights in the direction that reduces loss

This is online (single-example) gradient descent rather than mini-batch SGD. With only 4 examples, there is no practical difference; for larger datasets, mini-batching ([@dl2:sgd-revisited]) is essential for efficiency.

losses = []

for epoch in range(epochs):
    epoch_loss = 0.0

    for i in range(len(X)):
        # 1. Forward pass
        y_hat, cache = forward(X[i], W1, b1, W2, b2)

        # 2. Accumulate loss for monitoring
        epoch_loss += bce_loss(y_hat, Y[i])

        # 3. Backward pass: compute all gradients
        dW1, db1_grad, dW2, db2_grad = backward(
            np.array([Y[i]]), cache, W2
        )

        # 4. Gradient descent update: theta <- theta - alpha * grad
        W1 -= lr * dW1
        b1 -= lr * db1_grad
        W2 -= lr * dW2
        b2 -= lr * db2_grad

    # Average loss over the 4 examples
    losses.append(epoch_loss / len(X))

Results

After training, the network should predict values close to 0 for inputs \((0,0)\) and \((1,1)\), and close to 1 for \((0,1)\) and \((1,0)\).

print("Final predictions:")
print(f"{'Input':>10s}  {'Target':>6s}  {'Predicted':>9s}")
for i in range(len(X)):
    y_hat, _ = forward(X[i], W1, b1, W2, b2)
    print(f"  {X[i]}     {Y[i]:.0f}      {y_hat:.4f}")
Final predictions:
     Input  Target  Predicted
  [0. 0.]     0      0.0027
  [0. 1.]     1      0.9996
  [1. 0.]     1      0.9996
  [1. 1.]     0      0.0003

Loss curve

The BCE loss decreases steadily on a log scale, confirming that gradient descent is finding a good solution despite the non-convex loss landscape ([@dl2:sgd-revisited]). The loss does not reach exactly zero because the sigmoid output asymptotically approaches 0 and 1 but never reaches them.

After 5000 epochs with learning rate \(\alpha = 0.1\), the network correctly classifies all four XOR inputs with high confidence (predictions near 0.00 and 1.00). The loss drops steadily, confirming that gradient descent finds a good solution despite the non-convex loss surface.

The Same Network in PyTorch

The PyTorch version produces the same result with significantly less code. The key differences:

  • No manual gradient computation: loss.backward() computes all gradients automatically via automatic differentiation—the same backpropagation algorithm, but handled by the framework
  • No manual parameter management: nn.Module tracks all weights and biases; optimizer.step() updates them
  • Batched computation: all 4 examples are processed in a single matrix multiplication rather than looped one at a time

XOR in PyTorch

We now replicate the from-scratch XOR network using PyTorch. The architecture, dataset, and hyperparameters are identical:

Architecture: Input (2) → Hidden (4, ReLU) → Output (1, sigmoid)

Comparing the two implementations reveals what a deep learning framework handles automatically:

  • Gradient computation: loss.backward() runs the same backpropagation algorithm we coded by hand, but PyTorch derives and applies the chain rule automatically for any computational graph—not just the 2-layer case.
  • Parameter management: nn.Module tracks all weights and biases; we never manually index into arrays.
  • Batched computation: all 4 examples are processed in a single matrix multiplication, rather than looped one at a time.

The from-scratch version is essential for understanding what happens inside backward() and step(). From here on, we use PyTorch and focus on architecture and training decisions rather than gradient arithmetic.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Dataset

Same XOR dataset as the from-scratch version. PyTorch uses tensors (GPU-acceleratable arrays) instead of NumPy arrays. Note that Y is shaped (4, 1) rather than (4,) so it matches the network’s (batch, 1) output shape.

As noted in the from-scratch version, XOR is noise-free and tiny—a pedagogical tool, not a realistic dataset.

X = torch.tensor(
    [[0, 0], [0, 1], [1, 0], [1, 1]],
    dtype=torch.float32,
)
Y = torch.tensor(
    [[0], [1], [1], [0]],
    dtype=torch.float32,
)

Model definition

We define the same 2-layer architecture as a nn.Module. Each nn.Linear(d_in, d_out) creates a layer with a \(d_\text{out} \times d_\text{in}\) weight matrix and a \(d_\text{out}\)-dimensional bias vector—exactly the \(\bm{W}\) and \(\bm{b}\) from [@def:layer]. The forward method chains the layers, applying ReLU after the hidden layer and sigmoid after the output layer.

class XORNet(nn.Module):
    """Input(2) -> Hidden(4, ReLU) -> Output(1, sigmoid)."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        # Layer 1: 2 inputs -> 4 hidden neurons
        self.hidden = nn.Linear(2, 4)
        # Layer 2: 4 hidden -> 1 output
        self.output = nn.Linear(4, 1)

    def forward(self, x):
        # Hidden layer: linear transform + ReLU activation
        a1 = torch.relu(self.hidden(x))
        # Output layer: linear transform + sigmoid activation
        y_hat = torch.sigmoid(self.output(a1))
        return y_hat

Training setup

  • Loss: nn.BCELoss() is binary cross-entropy, the same loss we implemented by hand (and derived in [@ml3:cross-entropy]).
  • Optimizer: optim.SGD is plain stochastic gradient descent with learning rate \(\alpha = 0.1\), matching the from-scratch version. In later sections we will switch to Adam ([@dl2:optimizers]).
  • Seed: fixed for reproducibility. PyTorch uses its own RNG, separate from NumPy’s, so the initial weights differ from the from-scratch version—but both converge to correct solutions.
torch.manual_seed(0)

model = XORNet()
criterion = nn.BCELoss()                          # binary cross-entropy
optimizer = optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)  # plain gradient descent

epochs = 5000

Training loop

The loop structure mirrors the from-scratch version, but three lines replace all of our manual gradient code:

  1. optimizer.zero_grad() — clear gradients from the previous step
  2. loss.backward() — backpropagation (automatic)
  3. optimizer.step() — parameter update: \(\bm{\theta} \leftarrow \bm{\theta} - \alpha \nabla \mathcal{L}\)

Note that model(X) processes all 4 examples at once as a (4, 2) matrix, producing a (4, 1) output. The from-scratch version looped over examples one at a time. Batched computation is one of the main performance advantages of frameworks.

losses = []

for epoch in range(epochs):
    # Forward pass: all 4 examples in one matrix multiply
    y_hat = model(X)
    loss = criterion(y_hat, Y)

    # Backward pass + update (replaces our manual backward() + -= lr * grad)
    optimizer.zero_grad()   # reset gradients to zero
    loss.backward()         # compute dL/d(all parameters) via chain rule
    optimizer.step()        # W <- W - lr * dW  for every parameter

    losses.append(loss.item())

Results

The predictions should match the from-scratch version: values near 0.00 for \((0,0)\) and \((1,1)\), near 1.00 for \((0,1)\) and \((1,0)\).

print("Final predictions:")
print(f"{'Input':>10s}  {'Target':>6s}  {'Predicted':>9s}")
with torch.no_grad():  # disable gradient tracking for inference
    preds = model(X)
    for i in range(len(X)):
        print(
            f"  {X[i].tolist()}     {Y[i].item():.0f}      "
            f"{preds[i].item():.4f}"
        )
Final predictions:
     Input  Target  Predicted
  [0.0, 0.0]     0      0.0015
  [0.0, 1.0]     1      0.9988
  [1.0, 0.0]     1      0.9897
  [1.0, 1.0]     0      0.0015

Loss curve

Compare to the from-scratch version: both show steady convergence on a log scale, reaching similar final loss values. The curves may differ in detail because the random seeds (and thus initial weights) are different, but the qualitative behavior—rapid initial decrease followed by slow refinement—is the same.

Why PyTorch?

We use PyTorch for the remainder of this chapter because it provides automatic differentiation (computing gradients without manual derivation), GPU acceleration, and a large ecosystem of pre-built layers and optimizers. The from-scratch implementation above is essential for understanding what PyTorch does under the hood; from here forward, we focus on using the framework to build and train networks. Other popular frameworks include TensorFlow and JAX, but the concepts are identical across all of them.
