sections.title: Active Reinforcement Learning: Q-Learning
sections.html:
In [@rl2], the agent followed a fixed policy and learned value estimates. Now the agent must do both: learn and decide. The agent no longer receives a policy to follow—it must discover the optimal policy through its own actions. This is the full reinforcement learning problem {% cite 'russell2020' note='sec. 22.3' %}.

The central algorithm of this section is Q-learning, which learns the optimal action-value function \(Q^*\) directly from experience, without ever constructing a model of the environment.

From Values to Action-Values

In [@rl2], we learned \(V^\pi(s)\). Could we use TD learning to learn \(V^*(s)\) directly and then extract the optimal policy? In principle, yes—but extracting the policy from \(V^*\) requires the transition model:

\[ \pi^*(s) = \arg\max_a \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, a) \, V^*(s') \]

Without \(T\), we cannot compute this argmax. The solution is to learn the action-value function \(Q^*(s, a)\) instead. Given \(Q^*\), the optimal policy is:

\[ \pi^*(s) = \arg\max_a Q^*(s, a) \]

No model needed—we simply pick the action with the highest Q-value.

Why Q-Functions Are Central to Model-Free RL

The shift from \(V\) to \(Q\) is the key insight that makes model-free RL practical. With \(V^*\) alone, the agent needs \(T\) to act; with \(Q^*\), the agent can act optimally using only a table lookup (or, as we will see in [@rl4], a function approximation). Every model-free RL algorithm in this chapter learns some form of \(Q\).

Q-Learning

Q-Learning

Q-learning updates the action-value estimate after each transition \((s, a, r, s')\): \[ Q(s, a) \leftarrow Q(s, a) + \alpha \bigl[r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a') - Q(s, a)\bigr] \] where \(\alpha\) is the learning rate and the target \(r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a')\) uses the maximum Q-value at the next state.

The update closely resembles TD(0) ([@eq:td-update]), but with two differences:

  1. We learn \(Q(s, a)\) instead of \(V(s)\)—one value per state-action pair instead of per state
  2. The target uses \(\max_{a'} Q(s', a')\) instead of \(Q(s', \pi(s'))\)—we bootstrap from the best action, regardless of which action the agent actually takes next

Behavior Policy and Target Policy

In RL, the behavior policy \(\mu(a \mid s)\) is the policy the agent actually uses to select actions (which generates the \((s, a, r, s')\) transitions stored in experience). The target policy \(\pi(a \mid s)\) is the policy the algorithm is trying to evaluate or improve. When \(\mu = \pi\) the algorithm is on-policy; when they differ it is off-policy.

Off-Policy Learning

An off-policy algorithm learns about a target policy \(\pi\) while following a different behavior policy \(\mu\). Q-learning is off-policy: the target \(\max_{a'} Q(s', a')\) corresponds to the greedy (target) policy, but the behavior policy can be any exploration strategy (e.g., \(\varepsilon\)-greedy) during data collection.

This separation between the behavior policy (which generates data) and the target policy (which is being evaluated) is powerful: it allows the agent to explore freely while still learning about the optimal policy.

Algorithm

The full Q-learning algorithm with \(\varepsilon\)-greedy exploration:

Initialize \(Q(s, a) = 0\) for all \(s \in \mathcal{S}\), \(a \in \mathcal{A}\)

For each episode:

  1. Initialize state \(s\) (e.g., start at \((1,1)\))
  2. Repeat until \(s\) is terminal:
    • Choose action \(a\) using \(\varepsilon\)-greedy: with probability \(\varepsilon\) select a random action, otherwise \(a = \arg\max_{a'} Q(s, a')\)
    • Take action \(a\), observe reward \(r\) and next state \(s'\)
    • Update: \(Q(s, a) \leftarrow Q(s, a) + \alpha [r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a') - Q(s, a)]\)
    • \(s \leftarrow s'\)
  3. Decay \(\varepsilon\)

Worked Example: Q-Learning on the Warehouse Grid

Initialize \(Q(s, a) = 0\) for all state-action pairs. Set \(\alpha = 0.1\), \(\gamma = 0.99\), \(\varepsilon = 0.3\).

Episode 1, Step 1: State \((1,1)\). The \(\varepsilon\)-greedy policy selects North (randomly, since all Q-values are 0). The environment transitions to \((1,2)\) with reward \(-0.04\).

\[ Q((1,1), \text{N}) \leftarrow 0 + 0.1[-0.04 + 0.99 \cdot \max_a Q((1,2), a) - 0] = 0.1(-0.04) = -0.004 \]

Step 2: State \((1,2)\). Select East (random exploration). Transition to \((2,2)\), reward \(-0.04\).

\[ Q((1,2), \text{E}) \leftarrow 0 + 0.1[-0.04 + 0.99(0) - 0] = -0.004 \]

Step 3: State \((2,2)\). Select North. Transition to \((2,3)\), reward \(-0.04\).

\[ Q((2,2), \text{N}) \leftarrow 0 + 0.1[-0.04 + 0.99(0) - 0] = -0.004 \]

After many steps of random exploration, the agent eventually reaches the goal at \((4,4)\) and receives reward \(+1\). Suppose this happens on a transition from \((3,4)\) via East. Under the reward convention \(r_{t+1} = R(s_{t+1})\) ([@rl1:returns-value-functions]), the observed reward for this transition is \(r = R((4,4)) = +1\). Since \((4,4)\) is terminal, \(\max_{a'} Q((4,4), a') = 0\) ([@cmt:terminal-handling]), and the Q-learning update gives

\[ Q((3,4), \text{E}) \leftarrow 0 + 0.1[1.0 + 0.99(0) - 0] = 0.1. \]

This is the first positive Q-value in the table — the goal reward has entered the agent's estimate. In subsequent episodes, when the agent reaches \((3,4)\), this positive Q-value propagates backward:

\[ Q((2,4), \text{E}) \leftarrow 0 + 0.1[-0.04 + 0.99 \cdot 0.1 - 0] = 0.1(0.059) = 0.0059 \]

Over hundreds of episodes, the positive values propagate from the goal back to the start state, gradually shaping the Q-table to reflect the optimal policy. The convergence is slow at first (most episodes explore randomly) but accelerates as the Q-values improve and the \(\varepsilon\)-greedy policy becomes more informed.

SARSA: An On-Policy Alternative

SARSA (State-Action-Reward-State-Action)

SARSA updates the action-value estimate using the action actually taken at the next state: \[ Q(s, a) \leftarrow Q(s, a) + \alpha \bigl[r + \gamma Q(s', a') - Q(s, a)\bigr] \] where \(a'\) is the action chosen by the current policy at state \(s'\) (including exploration). The name comes from the quintuple \((s, a, r, s', a')\) used in each update.

On-Policy Learning

An on-policy algorithm evaluates and improves the same policy that is used to generate data. SARSA is on-policy: the target \(r + \gamma Q(s', a')\) uses the action \(a'\) that the agent actually takes, which includes exploratory actions.

Q-Learning vs. SARSA

The difference between Q-learning and SARSA is a single symbol: \(\max_{a'} Q(s', a')\) vs. \(Q(s', a')\).

Property Q-Learning SARSA
Target \(r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a')\) \(r + \gamma Q(s', a')\)
Policy type Off-policy On-policy
Learns about Optimal policy \(\pi^*\) Current (exploring) policy
Near hazards Aggressive (ignores exploration risk) Conservative (accounts for exploration)

The practical difference is clearest near dangerous states. Consider state \((3,3)\) in the warehouse, which is adjacent to the hazard at \((4,3)\). Suppose the greedy action at \((3,3)\) is North. With \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), the agent still takes East (toward the hazard) with probability \(\varepsilon / |\mathcal{A}| = 0.1/4 = 2.5\%\) at any given step. Q-learning ignores this: its target assumes the agent will act optimally from \(s'\). SARSA accounts for it: its target includes the possibility that the agent will occasionally blunder into the hazard due to exploration.

As a result, SARSA learns to give states near hazards lower Q-values than Q-learning does, because its policy includes exploratory (potentially dangerous) actions. This makes SARSA's learned policy more conservative—it avoids paths that are near hazards, even if those paths are optimal under the greedy policy.

SARSA and Safety

SARSA's conservatism near hazards is sometimes desirable. In the warehouse, if the robot's actuators are noisy (beyond the 80/10/10 transition model), the path that skirts the hazard at \((4,3)\) is genuinely risky. SARSA's learned policy accounts for the actual behavior of the agent—including its mistakes—and avoids the riskiest paths. Q-learning's policy is optimal under perfect execution but dangerous if the agent occasionally explores. The choice between Q-learning and SARSA depends on whether safety during learning matters.

Expected SARSA

Between Q-learning (maximum over next actions) and SARSA (a single sampled next action) sits a natural hybrid:

Expected SARSA

Expected SARSA replaces the sampled \(Q(s', a')\) of SARSA with the expectation over the current policy: \[ Q(s, a) \leftarrow Q(s, a) + \alpha \Bigl[r + \gamma \sum_{a'} \pi(a' \mid s') \, Q(s', a') - Q(s, a)\Bigr] \] where \(\pi\) is the current \(\varepsilon\)-greedy policy.

Expected SARSA has lower variance than SARSA (it averages out the randomness in \(a'\)) and is typically more stable, at the cost of computing the sum \(\sum_{a'} \pi(a'|s') Q(s', a')\) each step. When \(\pi\) is the greedy policy, Expected SARSA coincides with Q-learning; when \(\pi\) is the behavior policy (e.g., \(\varepsilon\)-greedy), it retains the on-policy safety properties of SARSA. It is a useful reference point for thinking about the Q-learning–SARSA spectrum.

Convergence and the Exploration Schedule

Convergence Guarantees

Q-learning converges to \(Q^*\) under the same conditions as TD(0):

  1. Every state-action pair \((s, a)\) is visited infinitely often
  2. The learning rate satisfies the Robbins-Monro conditions (\(\sum \alpha_t = \infty\), \(\sum \alpha_t^2 < \infty\))

The first condition requires sufficient exploration. With \(\varepsilon\)-greedy and \(\varepsilon > 0\), every action has a nonzero probability of being selected, so condition 1 is satisfied in any communicating MDP.

SARSA converges to \(Q^\pi\) (the Q-function of the current policy, not \(Q^*\)) under similar conditions. If \(\varepsilon \to 0\) as \(t \to \infty\), the policy converges to greedy and \(Q^\pi \to Q^*\).

Exploration Schedules

Common strategies for decaying \(\varepsilon\):

  • Linear decay: \(\varepsilon_t = \max(\varepsilon_{\min}, \varepsilon_0 - t \cdot \Delta)\), where \(\Delta\) is the decay rate per episode
  • Exponential decay: \(\varepsilon_t = \max(\varepsilon_{\min}, \varepsilon_0 \cdot \rho^t)\), where \(\rho \in (0, 1)\) is the decay factor

Both start with high exploration (\(\varepsilon_0 \approx 1.0\)) and gradually reduce to a small minimum (\(\varepsilon_{\min} \approx 0.01\)) to maintain a small amount of residual exploration.

Warehouse Q-Learning: From Scratch to Optimal Policy

We now train Q-learning on the full \(4 \times 4\) warehouse grid. The agent starts with no knowledge—all Q-values are zero—and must discover the optimal policy entirely through trial and error.

After training for 1000 episodes, the Q-table encodes the value of every state-action pair. The learned policy is extracted as \(\pi(s) = \arg\max_a Q(s, a)\) and can be visualized as arrows on the grid.

Convergence check: the learned policy should match the value iteration solution from [@m1:optimal-policy-result]. In particular:

  • At \((3,3)\): the policy should prefer North over East (avoiding the hazard)
  • At \((4,2)\): the policy should prefer West (retreating from the hazard column)
  • The reward-per-episode curve should rise from negative values (random wandering) to values near the optimal expected return

Q-Learning and SARSA in Python

The following script implements both Q-learning and SARSA on the warehouse MDP. We train both agents for 1000 episodes, compare their learned policies to the value iteration solution, and visualize the Q-table, policy arrows, and learning curves.

Q-Learning and SARSA on the Warehouse Grid

We implement both Q-learning ([@def:q-learning]) and SARSA ([@def:sarsa]) on the \(4 \times 4\) warehouse MDP. Both agents start with no knowledge and must discover the optimal policy entirely through trial and error.

After training, we compare the learned policies to the value iteration solution from Chapter 4 and visualize the difference in behavior near the hazard cell ([@rl3:q-vs-sarsa]).

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Warehouse Environment

Same grid as [@rl2:td-python], but now the agent chooses its own actions rather than following a fixed policy.

GRID_W, GRID_H = 4, 4
GOAL = (3, 3)
HAZARD = (3, 2)
TERMINALS = {GOAL, HAZARD}
ACTIONS = [(0, 1), (0, -1), (-1, 0), (1, 0)]  # N, S, W, E
ACTION_NAMES = ['N', 'S', 'W', 'E']
N_ACTIONS = len(ACTIONS)
LIVING_REWARD = -0.04
GOAL_REWARD = 1.0
HAZARD_REWARD = -1.0
GAMMA = 0.99

ALL_STATES = [(x, y) for x in range(GRID_W) for y in range(GRID_H)
              if (x, y) not in TERMINALS]

def step(state, action_idx):
    """Take action with 80/10/10 stochastic transitions."""
    if state in TERMINALS:
        return state, 0.0, True

    intended = ACTIONS[action_idx]
    if action_idx in (0, 1):
        perpendiculars = [ACTIONS[2], ACTIONS[3]]
    else:
        perpendiculars = [ACTIONS[0], ACTIONS[1]]

    r = np.random.random()
    if r < 0.8:
        move = intended
    elif r < 0.9:
        move = perpendiculars[0]
    else:
        move = perpendiculars[1]

    nx = max(0, min(GRID_W - 1, state[0] + move[0]))
    ny = max(0, min(GRID_H - 1, state[1] + move[1]))
    next_state = (nx, ny)

    if next_state == GOAL:
        return next_state, GOAL_REWARD, True
    elif next_state == HAZARD:
        return next_state, HAZARD_REWARD, True
    else:
        return next_state, LIVING_REWARD, False

\(\varepsilon\)-Greedy Action Selection

The agent selects the greedy action with probability \(1 - \varepsilon\) and a uniformly random action with probability \(\varepsilon\) ([@def:epsilon-greedy]).

def epsilon_greedy(Q, state, epsilon):
    """Select action using epsilon-greedy policy."""
    if np.random.random() < epsilon:
        return np.random.randint(N_ACTIONS)
    else:
        q_values = [Q.get((state, a), 0.0) for a in range(N_ACTIONS)]
        return int(np.argmax(q_values))

Q-Learning

The Q-learning update ([@eq:q-learning]) uses \(\max_{a'} Q(s', a')\) as the bootstrap target — the agent learns about the optimal policy regardless of which action it actually takes next (off-policy, [@def:off-policy]).

def q_learning(n_episodes=1000, alpha=0.1, gamma=GAMMA,
               epsilon_start=1.0, epsilon_decay=0.995,
               epsilon_min=0.01, seed=42):
    """Train Q-learning on the warehouse grid."""
    np.random.seed(seed)
    Q = {}
    epsilon = epsilon_start
    rewards_per_episode = []

    for episode in range(n_episodes):
        state = (0, 0)
        done = False
        total_reward = 0

        while not done:
            action = epsilon_greedy(Q, state, epsilon)
            next_state, reward, done = step(state, action)
            total_reward += reward

            # Q-learning update: max over next actions
            if done:
                target = reward
            else:
                max_q = max(Q.get((next_state, a), 0.0)
                            for a in range(N_ACTIONS))
                target = reward + gamma * max_q

            old_q = Q.get((state, action), 0.0)
            Q[(state, action)] = old_q + alpha * (target - old_q)

            state = next_state

        epsilon = max(epsilon_min, epsilon * epsilon_decay)
        rewards_per_episode.append(total_reward)

    return Q, rewards_per_episode

SARSA

SARSA ([@eq:sarsa]) uses \(Q(s', a')\) where \(a'\) is the action actually taken at the next state — on-policy learning ([@def:on-policy]). The agent accounts for its own exploratory behavior, making it more conservative near hazards.

def sarsa(n_episodes=1000, alpha=0.1, gamma=GAMMA,
          epsilon_start=1.0, epsilon_decay=0.995,
          epsilon_min=0.01, seed=42):
    """Train SARSA on the warehouse grid."""
    np.random.seed(seed)
    Q = {}
    epsilon = epsilon_start
    rewards_per_episode = []

    for episode in range(n_episodes):
        state = (0, 0)
        action = epsilon_greedy(Q, state, epsilon)
        done = False
        total_reward = 0

        while not done:
            next_state, reward, done = step(state, action)
            total_reward += reward

            # SARSA update: use the action actually taken at s'
            if done:
                target = reward
            else:
                next_action = epsilon_greedy(Q, next_state, epsilon)
                target = reward + gamma * Q.get(
                    (next_state, next_action), 0.0)

            old_q = Q.get((state, action), 0.0)
            Q[(state, action)] = old_q + alpha * (target - old_q)

            if not done:
                state = next_state
                action = next_action
            else:
                state = next_state

        epsilon = max(epsilon_min, epsilon * epsilon_decay)
        rewards_per_episode.append(total_reward)

    return Q, rewards_per_episode

Train Both Agents

Q_ql, rewards_ql = q_learning(n_episodes=1000)
Q_sarsa, rewards_sarsa = sarsa(n_episodes=1000)

Learning Curves

Rolling average reward over the last 50 episodes. Both algorithms climb from negative values (random wandering) toward the optimal return, with Q-learning converging slightly faster.

def rolling_avg(data, window=50):
    return np.convolve(data, np.ones(window)/window, mode='valid')

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(8, 4))
ax.plot(rolling_avg(rewards_ql), label='Q-Learning', alpha=0.8)
ax.plot(rolling_avg(rewards_sarsa), label='SARSA', alpha=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel('Episode')
ax.set_ylabel('Reward (rolling avg, window=50)')
ax.set_title('Q-Learning vs. SARSA: Learning Curves')
ax.legend()
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('q_learning_curves.svg', bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

Extract and Visualize Learned Policies

The learned policy is \(\pi(s) = \arg\max_a Q(s, a)\). We compare both algorithms to the value iteration solution.

# Optimal policy from value iteration
OPTIMAL_POLICY = {
    (0, 0): 0, (1, 0): 3, (2, 0): 3, (3, 0): 0,
    (0, 1): 0, (1, 1): 0, (2, 1): 0, (3, 1): 2,
    (0, 2): 0, (1, 2): 0, (2, 2): 0,
    (0, 3): 3, (1, 3): 3, (2, 3): 3,
}

def extract_policy(Q):
    """Extract greedy policy from Q-table."""
    policy = {}
    for state in ALL_STATES:
        q_vals = [Q.get((state, a), 0.0) for a in range(N_ACTIONS)]
        policy[state] = int(np.argmax(q_vals))
    return policy

policy_ql = extract_policy(Q_ql)
policy_sarsa = extract_policy(Q_sarsa)

def plot_policy(ax, policy, title):
    """Plot policy arrows on the warehouse grid."""
    arrow_map = {0: (0, 0.3), 1: (0, -0.3), 2: (-0.3, 0), 3: (0.3, 0)}
    ax.set_xlim(-0.5, GRID_W - 0.5)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.5, GRID_H - 0.5)

    # Draw grid
    for x in range(GRID_W + 1):
        ax.axvline(x - 0.5, color='gray', linewidth=0.5)
    for y in range(GRID_H + 1):
        ax.axhline(y - 0.5, color='gray', linewidth=0.5)

    # Goal and hazard
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((GOAL[0]-0.5, GOAL[1]-0.5), 1, 1,
                                color='green', alpha=0.3))
    ax.text(GOAL[0], GOAL[1], '+1', ha='center', va='center',
            fontsize=12, fontweight='bold', color='green')
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((HAZARD[0]-0.5, HAZARD[1]-0.5), 1, 1,
                                color='red', alpha=0.3))
    ax.text(HAZARD[0], HAZARD[1], '-1', ha='center', va='center',
            fontsize=12, fontweight='bold', color='red')

    # Policy arrows
    for state, action in policy.items():
        dx, dy = arrow_map[action]
        ax.annotate('', xy=(state[0]+dx, state[1]+dy),
                    xytext=(state[0], state[1]),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', lw=1.5,
                                    color='#333333'))

    ax.set_xticks(range(GRID_W))
    ax.set_xticklabels([f'x={i+1}' for i in range(GRID_W)])
    ax.set_yticks(range(GRID_H))
    ax.set_yticklabels([f'y={i+1}' for i in range(GRID_H)])
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_aspect('equal')

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4))
plot_policy(axes[0], OPTIMAL_POLICY, 'Value Iteration (Ch 4)')
plot_policy(axes[1], policy_ql, 'Q-Learning')
plot_policy(axes[2], policy_sarsa, 'SARSA')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('q_policies.svg', bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

Policy Comparison

Q-learning typically matches the optimal policy at most states. SARSA may differ near the hazard at \((4,3)\): it tends to route the agent further from the hazard column, reflecting its conservative treatment of exploration risk ([@cmt:sarsa-conservative]).

matches_ql = sum(1 for s in ALL_STATES
                 if policy_ql[s] == OPTIMAL_POLICY.get(s, -1))
matches_sarsa = sum(1 for s in ALL_STATES
                    if policy_sarsa[s] == OPTIMAL_POLICY.get(s, -1))

print(f"Q-Learning matches optimal: {matches_ql}/{len(ALL_STATES)} states")
print(f"SARSA matches optimal:      {matches_sarsa}/{len(ALL_STATES)} states")

# Show differences
for s in ALL_STATES:
    opt = OPTIMAL_POLICY.get(s)
    ql = policy_ql[s]
    sa = policy_sarsa[s]
    if ql != opt or sa != opt:
        label = f"({s[0]+1},{s[1]+1})"
        opt_name = ACTION_NAMES[opt] if opt is not None else '?'
        print(f"  {label}: VI={opt_name}, Q-L={ACTION_NAMES[ql]}, "
              f"SARSA={ACTION_NAMES[sa]}")
Q-Learning matches optimal: 9/14 states
SARSA matches optimal:      9/14 states
  (1,3): VI=N, Q-L=N, SARSA=E
  (2,1): VI=E, Q-L=N, SARSA=N
  (3,1): VI=E, Q-L=N, SARSA=W
  (3,2): VI=N, Q-L=N, SARSA=W
  (3,3): VI=N, Q-L=W, SARSA=N
  (4,1): VI=N, Q-L=W, SARSA=W
  (4,2): VI=W, Q-L=S, SARSA=W

sections.title: Continuous State Spaces and Function Approximation
sections.html:
The Q-table from [@rl3] stores one value per state-action pair. For the \(4 \times 4\) warehouse with 4 actions, the table has \(16 \times 4 = 64\) entries—trivially small. But a real warehouse robot has a continuous position \((x, y) \in [0, L] \times [0, W]\), a heading \(\theta \in [0, 2\pi)\), and a velocity \(v \geq 0\). The state space is \(\mathbb{R}^4\)—no table can enumerate it. This section addresses the central question: how do we apply RL when the state space is continuous? {% cite 'russell2020' note='sec. 22.4' %}

We progress through three approaches of increasing power: discretization, linear function approximation, and deep Q-networks. Each builds on the tools from previous chapters—the function approximation ideas of Chapter 5 and the neural network architectures of Chapter 6.

From Grids to Continuous Spaces

Continuous State Space

A continuous state space is a state space \(\mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) where states are real-valued vectors rather than discrete labels. The number of possible states is uncountably infinite.

The shift from discrete to continuous states creates three problems:

  1. Representation: a Q-table with one entry per \((s, a)\) pair is impossible when \(\mathcal{S}\) is continuous
  2. Generalization: the agent visits each exact state at most once, so it must generalize from nearby states it has visited
  3. Sample efficiency: with infinite states, the agent cannot explore every region of the state space

The solution is function approximation: replace the Q-table with a parameterized function \(\hat{Q}(s, a; \mathbf{w})\) that maps any state-action pair to an estimated Q-value, and learn the parameters \(\mathbf{w}\) from experience.

Warehouse Upgrade: Continuous Floor

For the remainder of this section, we replace the \(4 \times 4\) grid with a continuous warehouse floor:

  • State: \((x, y) \in [0, 4] \times [0, 4]\) — the robot's real-valued position on the floor
  • Actions: discrete \(\{\)North, South, East, West\(\}\) — the same four directions as the grid MDP (continuous actions come in [@rl5])
  • Dynamics: each action moves the robot by a fixed step in the intended direction, plus Gaussian noise on both axes. The noise models real actuator imprecision — unlike the grid, the robot is no longer snapped to cell centers and can land anywhere on the continuous floor
  • Rewards: \(-0.01\) per step, \(+1\) for reaching the goal region (a circle around \((3.5, 3.5)\)), \(-1\) for entering the hazard region (around \((3.5, 2.5)\))

The task is the same as the grid MDP — navigate to the goal while avoiding the hazard — but now the agent must generalize to states it has never visited before (every position is unique). Later, the 6D extension ([@rl4:warehouse-dqn]) adds heading, velocity, payload weight, and battery to the state, demonstrating how higher-dimensional state spaces break tabular methods.

Discretization and Tile Coding

State Discretization

State Discretization

State discretization converts a continuous state space into a discrete one by partitioning each dimension into bins. A state \((x, y)\) is mapped to a bin index \((i, j)\) where \(i = \lfloor x / \Delta_x \rfloor\) and \(j = \lfloor y / \Delta_y \rfloor\), and the Q-table stores values per bin.

For the 2D position \((x, y) \in [0, 4] \times [0, 4]\) with bin width \(\Delta = 1.0\), we recover the original \(4 \times 4\) grid. Finer bins (\(\Delta = 0.5\)) give an \(8 \times 8\) grid with 64 states—more resolution but more entries to learn.

The fundamental problem is the curse of dimensionality: the number of bins grows exponentially with the number of dimensions. With 4 continuous dimensions and 10 bins per dimension, the state space has \(10^4 = 10{,}000\) bins, each requiring a Q-value for every action. With 20 bins, it becomes \(20^4 = 160{,}000\). Worse, most bins are never visited, so their Q-values remain at their initial (uninformative) values.

Fine bins give good resolution but sparse visits; coarse bins give dense visits but poor resolution. No single bin width works well for all regions of the state space.

Tile Coding

Tile Coding

Tile coding overlays multiple offset grids (tilings) over the continuous state space. Each tiling partitions the space into tiles, and each state activates exactly one tile per tiling. The state is represented as a binary feature vector \(\boldsymbol{\phi}(s) \in \{0, 1\}^{n_\text{tilings} \times n_\text{tiles}}\) where each entry is 1 if the corresponding tile contains \(s\) and 0 otherwise.

The key idea: by offsetting the tilings, nearby states share most of their active tiles, creating smooth generalization. A small shift in position changes only the tile assignment in the tilings where the state crosses a boundary, while all other tilings remain unchanged. [@fig:tile-coding] illustrates this for two tilings.

Worked example: Consider the two tilings in [@fig:tile-coding]: each is a \(4 \times 4\) grid with tile width \(\Delta = 1.0\) over \([0, 4] \times [0, 4]\). Tiling 1 has its origin at \((0, 0)\); tiling 2 is offset by \((\Delta/2, \Delta/2) = (0.5, 0.5)\). For state A \(= (2.3, 1.7)\):

  • Tiling 1: \(\lfloor 2.3 / 1.0 \rfloor = 2\), \(\lfloor 1.7 / 1.0 \rfloor = 1\) → tile \((2, 1)\)
  • Tiling 2: \(\lfloor (2.3 + 0.5) / 1.0 \rfloor = 2\), \(\lfloor (1.7 + 0.5) / 1.0 \rfloor = 2\) → tile \((2, 2)\)

Now consider nearby state B \(= (2.6, 1.7)\): in tiling 1 it also maps to tile \((2, 1)\) (same tile as A), but in tiling 2 it maps to tile \((3, 2)\) (different tile, because \(\lfloor 3.1 / 1.0 \rfloor = 3\)). The feature vectors for A and B share one of their two active entries — they have 50% overlap.

Why does overlap matter? The Q-function is linear in the feature vector: \(\hat{Q}(s, a) = \mathbf{w}^\top \boldsymbol{\phi}(s)\). When the agent visits state A and updates the weight for the shared tile, that update automatically changes the Q-value at state B (and every other state that activates the same tile). States that share more tiles are more strongly coupled. This is the generalization mechanism: nearby states influence each other's values, while distant states (which share no tiles) do not.

Scaling to more tilings: With \(n\) tilings, each offset by \(\Delta / n\) from the previous one, two states that differ by less than \(\Delta / n\) in every dimension share all \(n\) tiles. States one step apart (like A and B above, separated by \(0.3\) in \(x\)) typically share \(n - 1\) of \(n\) tiles. With the standard choice of 8 tilings, that means 7 out of 8 active features are shared — 87.5% overlap — so updating A transfers most of the learning to B. This smooth, distance-dependent generalization is what makes tile coding effective without requiring every state to be visited individually.

Warehouse example: tile-code the \((x, y)\) position with 8 tilings, each offset by \((\Delta / 8, \Delta / 8)\) from the previous one. Each offset tiling needs one extra tile per dimension at the boundary (so that edge tiles have their natural width, not a clamped double-width), giving \(5 \times 5 = 25\) tiles per tiling. With 8 tilings, each state activates 8 tiles, producing a \(8 \times 25 = 200\)-dimensional binary feature vector. The Q-function is \(\hat{Q}(s, a; \mathbf{w}_a) = \mathbf{w}_a^\top \boldsymbol{\phi}(s)\), where \(\mathbf{w}_a \in \mathbb{R}^{200}\) are learned weights for action \(a\).

Tile coding has three advantages over naive discretization:

  1. Smooth generalization: nearby states share tiles, so updating one state also affects nearby states
  2. Linear scaling: the number of features is \(n_\text{tilings} \times n_\text{tiles}\), not \(n_\text{tiles}^d\) (no curse of dimensionality)
  3. Fast computation: each state activates exactly \(n_\text{tilings}\) features, so the Q-value is a sum of \(n_\text{tilings}\) weights

Tile Coding in Practice

Tile coding was the standard approach for continuous RL before deep learning and remains a strong baseline for problems with fewer than 5–10 continuous dimensions. It was used extensively in the RL textbook by Sutton and Barto and powered many early successes in robot control. For higher-dimensional problems (raw images, complex sensor suites), tile coding becomes impractical and neural network approximation is needed.

Linear Function Approximation

Tile coding is a special case of a broader framework: linear function approximation.

Function Approximation in RL

Function approximation replaces the Q-table with a parameterized function \(\hat{Q}(s, a; \mathbf{w})\) that generalizes across states. The parameters \(\mathbf{w}\) are learned from experience using gradient-based updates.

For linear function approximation, the Q-function is:

\[ \hat{Q}(s, a; \mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{w}^\top \boldsymbol{\phi}(s, a) \]

where \(\boldsymbol{\phi}(s, a) \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is a hand-designed feature vector. The features encode relevant properties of the state-action pair. For the warehouse robot, natural features might include:

Feature Formula Intuition
Distance to goal \(\|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{g}\|\) Closer to goal is better
Distance to hazard \(\|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{h}\|\) Farther from hazard is better
Heading alignment \(\cos(\theta - \theta_\text{goal})\) Facing the goal is better
Wall proximity \(\min(x, 4-x, y, 4-y)\) Avoid getting stuck at walls

Semi-Gradient TD Update

To learn \(\mathbf{w}\), we apply the Q-learning update using gradient descent. The loss for a single transition is:

\[ L = \frac{1}{2}\bigl[r + \gamma \max_{a'} \hat{Q}(s', a'; \mathbf{w}) - \hat{Q}(s, a; \mathbf{w})\bigr]^2 \]

Taking the gradient with respect to \(\mathbf{w}\) (treating the target \(r + \gamma \max_{a'} \hat{Q}(s', a'; \mathbf{w})\) as a constant—hence "semi-gradient"):

\[ \mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} + \alpha \, \delta \, \nabla_\mathbf{w} \hat{Q}(s, a; \mathbf{w}) \]

where \(\delta = r + \gamma \max_{a'} \hat{Q}(s', a'; \mathbf{w}) - \hat{Q}(s, a; \mathbf{w})\) is the TD error. Because \(\hat{Q}\) is linear in \(\mathbf{w}\) ([@eq:linear-q]), \(\nabla_\mathbf{w} \hat{Q} = \boldsymbol{\phi}(s, a)\), giving the simple update:

\[ \mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} + \alpha \, \delta \, \boldsymbol{\phi}(s, a) \]

Why Semi-Gradient?

Why do we treat the target \(r + \gamma \max_{a'} \hat{Q}(s', a'; \mathbf{w})\) as a constant when computing the gradient, even though it depends on \(\mathbf{w}\)? In the tabular case ([@rl3]), each Q-table entry is an independent parameter, so the target and the prediction share no parameters and the distinction is moot. With function approximation, \(\mathbf{w}\) is shared across all states: changing \(\mathbf{w}\) to improve \(\hat{Q}(s, a)\) simultaneously changes the target \(\hat{Q}(s', a')\) that we are trying to match. Taking the full gradient would chase a target that moves with every update, often leading to oscillation or divergence. The semi-gradient approach freezes the target for each update step, trading theoretical rigor for practical stability. This is also why the target network ([@def:target-network]) is needed for DQN — it freezes the target for many steps at a time.

The Deadly Triad

The tabular convergence guarantees of [@rl2:td-convergence] and [@rl3:convergence-guarantees] do not carry over to function approximation. {% cite 'sutton2018' note='ch. 11' %} identifies the deadly triad — three individually useful ingredients that, combined, can cause divergence:

  1. Function approximation (generalizing across states with shared parameters)
  2. Bootstrapping (using the current estimate \(\hat{Q}(s', a')\) in the TD target rather than waiting for the observed return \(G_t\); see [@cmt:bootstrapping])
  3. Off-policy learning (learning about one policy while following another; see [@def:off-policy])

Any two of the three are safe; all three together can diverge even with linear approximation. Q-learning with function approximation has all three (off-policy, bootstrapping, linear/neural approximator), so convergence is not guaranteed in general. DQN's experience replay and target network mitigate divergence in practice but do not eliminate it theoretically. For on-policy methods like SARSA with linear features, convergence is guaranteed. This tradeoff between off-policy flexibility and on-policy stability is a recurring theme in RL algorithm design.

Connection to Chapter 5

This update is the same gradient descent rule from [@ml3:gradient-descent] — the TD error plays the role of the residual, and the feature vector plays the role of the input. Linear RL function approximation is linear regression applied incrementally, with the Bellman target replacing the true label. The difference is that the target itself changes as learning progresses.

Deep Q-Networks

Linear function approximation requires hand-designed features—the agent can only generalize as well as the features allow. The promise of deep learning (Chapter 6) is to learn the features end-to-end. A Deep Q-Network replaces the linear Q-function with a neural network.

Deep Q-Network (DQN)

A Deep Q-Network uses a neural network \(\hat{Q}(s, a; \boldsymbol{\theta})\) to approximate the action-value function. The network takes the state \(s\) as input and outputs Q-values for all actions simultaneously: \(\hat{Q}(s, \cdot; \boldsymbol{\theta}) \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{A}|}\). The parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) are trained by minimizing the TD error using gradient descent.

Naively applying the semi-gradient update ([@eq:semi-gradient]) with a neural network is unstable. Two innovations are needed:

Experience Replay

Experience Replay

Experience replay stores transitions \((s, a, r, s')\) in a fixed-size buffer \(\mathcal{D}\). At each training step, a random mini-batch of transitions is sampled from \(\mathcal{D}\) and used to compute the gradient update, rather than using only the most recent transition.

Why replay helps:

  1. Breaks temporal correlations: consecutive transitions are highly correlated (the next state of one transition is the current state of the next). Training on correlated data causes the network to overfit to recent experience and forget earlier lessons. Random sampling from the buffer decorrelates the training data.
  2. Reuses data: each transition can be used in multiple updates, improving sample efficiency.

Target Network

Target Network

A target network is a separate copy of the Q-network, with parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}^-\), used to compute the TD target: \[ y = r + \gamma \max_{a'} \hat{Q}(s', a'; \boldsymbol{\theta}^-) \] The target network parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}^-\) are updated periodically (e.g., every \(C\) steps) by copying the current parameters: \(\boldsymbol{\theta}^- \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta}\). Between updates, \(\boldsymbol{\theta}^-\) is fixed.

Why a target network helps: without it, the target \(r + \gamma \max_{a'} \hat{Q}(s', a'; \boldsymbol{\theta})\) changes at every gradient step (because \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) changes). This creates a "moving target" problem—the network is chasing a target that moves as fast as the network itself. The target network freezes the target for \(C\) steps, giving the network a stable objective to train against.

The DQN Algorithm

Initialize Q-network \(\hat{Q}(s, a; \boldsymbol{\theta})\) with random weights, target network \(\hat{Q}(s, a; \boldsymbol{\theta}^-) \leftarrow \hat{Q}(s, a; \boldsymbol{\theta})\), replay buffer \(\mathcal{D}\)

For each episode:

  1. Initialize state \(s\)
  2. Repeat until \(s\) is terminal:
    • Choose \(a\) via \(\varepsilon\)-greedy on \(\hat{Q}(s, \cdot; \boldsymbol{\theta})\)
    • Take action \(a\), observe \(r\), \(s'\)
    • Store \((s, a, r, s')\) in \(\mathcal{D}\)
    • Sample mini-batch \(\mathcal{B} = \{(s_i, a_i, r_i, s'_i)\}\) from \(\mathcal{D}\)
    • Compute targets: \(y_i = r_i + \gamma \max_{a'} \hat{Q}(s'_i, a'; \boldsymbol{\theta}^-)\) (or \(y_i = r_i\) if \(s'_i\) is terminal)
    • Update \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) by gradient descent on \(\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_i (y_i - \hat{Q}(s_i, a_i; \boldsymbol{\theta}))^2\)
    • Every \(C\) total steps: \(\boldsymbol{\theta}^- \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta}\)
    • \(s \leftarrow s'\)
  3. Decay \(\varepsilon\)

Feature Normalization for DQN

Neural networks are sensitive to input scale ([@ml3:gradient-descent-python], [@dl2:optimizers]). Before passing the state to the Q-network, normalize each component to roughly \([0, 1]\): divide \((x, y)\) by the floor dimensions, \(\theta\) by \(2\pi\), and \(v\) by its maximum. Without normalization, the network's early layers see inputs on wildly different scales, slowing learning and causing instability.

The DQN Breakthrough

DQN was introduced by {% cite 'mnih2015' %} at DeepMind, demonstrating that a single neural network architecture could learn to play dozens of Atari video games at human or superhuman level, directly from raw pixel inputs. The combination of experience replay and target networks made training stable enough for the first time. DQN connects Chapter 6's neural networks (the function approximator) with Chapter 7's Q-learning (the RL algorithm) into a unified deep RL system.

Overestimation and Double DQN

DQN's target uses \(\max_{a'} \hat{Q}(s', a'; \boldsymbol{\theta}^-)\), which systematically overestimates Q-values: the \(\max\) operator picks the action with the highest estimated value, and any estimation noise biases this upward. Double DQN fixes this by decoupling action selection from action evaluation: select the action using the online network, but evaluate it using the target network: \(y = r + \gamma \hat{Q}(s', \arg\max_{a'} \hat{Q}(s', a'; \boldsymbol{\theta}); \boldsymbol{\theta}^-)\). This simple change reduces overestimation and often improves performance.

Warehouse DQN on the Continuous Floor

We apply all three approaches to the continuous warehouse:

Approach State Representation Parameters (2D) Generalization
Discretized Q-learning Bin indices \(n_\text{bins}^2 \times |\mathcal{A}|\) None (each bin independent)
Tile-coded linear Binary tile features \(n_\text{tilings} \times n_\text{tiles} \times |\mathcal{A}|\) Smooth (nearby states share tiles)
DQN Raw state vector \((x, y)\) Neural network weights Learned (network discovers features)

Expected results on 2D:

  • Discretized Q-learning learns quickly in visited bins but has limited resolution
  • Tile coding achieves smooth generalization and good performance
  • DQN achieves comparable final performance, converging more slowly due to the overhead of training a neural network

All three methods perform similarly on the 2D warehouse because the state space is small enough that even coarse discretization covers it. This is the expected outcome for low-dimensional problems — and it illustrates an important engineering principle: use the simplest method that works.

Expected results on 6D: The script also tests a higher-dimensional warehouse with state \((x, y, \theta, v, \text{load}, \text{battery})\). With 6 continuous dimensions, discretization at 10 bins per dimension requires 4 million Q-values — and after 1,000 episodes, less than 2% of bins have been visited. The discretized agent fails to learn. DQN, with only about 1,500 network parameters, generalizes across the full 6D space and solves the task. This is where DQN's advantage becomes clear: the curse of dimensionality makes tabular and tile-coded methods impractical, but the neural network discovers the relevant structure automatically.

When Does DQN Shine?

DQN's advantage emerges in problems where discretization and hand-designed features fail:

  • High-dimensional states: a warehouse robot with position, heading, velocity, battery, arm joint angles, and load weight might have 10+ continuous dimensions. Discretizing with 10 bins per dimension produces \(10^{10} = 10\) billion bins — no Q-table can store this. Tile coding scales linearly with dimension but requires careful manual design.
  • Complex feature interactions: if the optimal action depends on subtle nonlinear relationships between state variables (e.g., "speed up when the heading aligns with the goal and no obstacle is within 0.5 meters and battery is above 20%"), hand-designed linear features will miss these interactions. A neural network discovers them automatically.
  • Rich sensory inputs: if the state is a camera image rather than a position vector, no hand-designed feature set can capture the relevant information. DQN with convolutional layers (the original Atari setup) learns directly from pixels.

The 2D warehouse demo keeps the problem simple so that all three methods are comparable and the visualizations are clear. In the exercises ([@rx:function-approx-showdown]), students explore the tradeoffs with the full 4D state space.

Function Approximation in Python

The following script implements all three approaches on the continuous warehouse environment. We plot learning curves (episode reward vs. episode number) and visualize the learned policies as vector fields over the \((x, y)\) floor.

Function Approximation: Discretized, Tile-Coded, and DQN

We compare three approaches to RL in a continuous-state warehouse environment ([@rl4:grids-to-continuous]):

  1. Discretized Q-learning — partition the floor into bins ([@def:discretization])
  2. Tile-coded linear Q-learning — overlapping offset tilings for smooth generalization ([@def:tile-coding])
  3. Deep Q-Network (DQN) — a neural network learns features end-to-end ([@def:dqn])

All three train on the same continuous warehouse floor and are compared by learning curves and final policy quality.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Continuous Warehouse Environment

The robot has state \((x, y) \in [0, 4]^2\) (we use 2D position for this demonstration, keeping the visualization clear). Actions are discrete: North, South, West, East. Transitions add Gaussian noise to the intended movement.

class ContinuousWarehouse:
    """Continuous 2D warehouse with goal and hazard regions."""

    def __init__(self, goal=(3.5, 3.5), hazard=(3.5, 2.5),
                 region_radius=0.4, step_size=0.5, noise_std=0.1):
        self.goal = np.array(goal)
        self.hazard = np.array(hazard)
        self.radius = region_radius
        self.step_size = step_size
        self.noise_std = noise_std
        # N, S, W, E
        self.action_deltas = np.array([
            [0, 1], [0, -1], [-1, 0], [1, 0]
        ], dtype=float)
        self.n_actions = 4

    def reset(self):
        # Random start near the bottom-left corner
        self.state = np.array([
            np.random.uniform(0.2, 0.8),
            np.random.uniform(0.2, 0.8)])
        return self.state.copy()

    def step(self, action):
        delta = self.action_deltas[action] * self.step_size
        noise = np.random.randn(2) * self.noise_std
        new_state = self.state + delta + noise
        new_state = np.clip(new_state, 0.0, 4.0)

        # Check regions
        if np.linalg.norm(new_state - self.goal) < self.radius:
            self.state = new_state
            return new_state.copy(), 1.0, True
        elif np.linalg.norm(new_state - self.hazard) < self.radius:
            self.state = new_state
            return new_state.copy(), -1.0, True
        else:
            self.state = new_state
            return new_state.copy(), -0.01, False

Approach 1: Discretized Q-Learning

Partition the \((x, y)\) floor into a \(10 \times 10\) grid of bins ([@def:discretization]). Each bin maps to a discrete state, and we apply tabular Q-learning within this discretized space.

class DiscretizedAgent:
    """Q-learning with state discretization."""

    def __init__(self, n_bins=10, n_actions=4, alpha=0.1,
                 gamma=0.99):
        self.n_bins = n_bins
        self.n_actions = n_actions
        self.alpha = alpha
        self.gamma = gamma
        self.Q = np.zeros((n_bins, n_bins, n_actions))

    def discretize(self, state):
        """Map continuous (x,y) to bin indices."""
        bx = min(int(state[0] / 4.0 * self.n_bins), self.n_bins - 1)
        by = min(int(state[1] / 4.0 * self.n_bins), self.n_bins - 1)
        return bx, by

    def select_action(self, state, epsilon):
        bx, by = self.discretize(state)
        if np.random.random() < epsilon:
            return np.random.randint(self.n_actions)
        return int(np.argmax(self.Q[bx, by]))

    def update(self, state, action, reward, next_state, done):
        bx, by = self.discretize(state)
        if done:
            target = reward
        else:
            nbx, nby = self.discretize(next_state)
            target = reward + self.gamma * np.max(self.Q[nbx, nby])
        self.Q[bx, by, action] += self.alpha * (
            target - self.Q[bx, by, action])

Approach 2: Tile-Coded Linear Q-Learning

We overlay 8 offset tilings ([@def:tile-coding]), each a \(4 \times 4\) grid. Each state activates one tile per tiling, producing a sparse binary feature vector. The Q-function is linear: \(\hat{Q}(s, a) = \mathbf{w}_a^\top \boldsymbol{\phi}(s)\) ([@eq:linear-q]).

class TileCodedAgent:
    """Linear Q-learning with tile coding."""

    def __init__(self, n_tilings=8, tiles_per_dim=4, n_actions=4,
                 alpha=0.05, gamma=0.99):
        self.n_tilings = n_tilings
        self.tiles_per_dim = tiles_per_dim
        self.n_actions = n_actions
        self.alpha = alpha / n_tilings  # divide by tilings for stability
        self.gamma = gamma

        # Each offset tiling needs one extra tile per dimension so that
        # boundary tiles have their natural width (not clamped).  Sutton
        # & Barto's reference implementation handles this automatically
        # via hash-based indexing; here we allocate the extra slot
        # explicitly.
        self.ext = tiles_per_dim + 1  # tiles per dim for offset tilings
        self.tiles_per_tiling = self.ext * self.ext
        self.n_features = n_tilings * self.tiles_per_tiling
        self.W = np.zeros((n_actions, self.n_features))

        self.tile_width = 4.0 / tiles_per_dim
        self.offsets = np.array([
            [k * self.tile_width / n_tilings,
             k * self.tile_width / n_tilings]
            for k in range(n_tilings)
        ])

    def get_features(self, state):
        """Compute binary feature vector for a state."""
        phi = np.zeros(self.n_features)
        for k in range(self.n_tilings):
            sx = state[0] + self.offsets[k, 0]
            sy = state[1] + self.offsets[k, 1]
            bx = int(sx / self.tile_width)
            by = int(sy / self.tile_width)
            bx = max(0, min(bx, self.ext - 1))
            by = max(0, min(by, self.ext - 1))
            idx = k * self.tiles_per_tiling + bx * self.ext + by
            phi[idx] = 1.0
        return phi

    def q_values(self, state):
        phi = self.get_features(state)
        return self.W @ phi

    def select_action(self, state, epsilon):
        if np.random.random() < epsilon:
            return np.random.randint(self.n_actions)
        return int(np.argmax(self.q_values(state)))

    def update(self, state, action, reward, next_state, done):
        phi = self.get_features(state)
        q_sa = self.W[action] @ phi
        if done:
            target = reward
        else:
            target = reward + self.gamma * np.max(self.q_values(next_state))
        # Semi-gradient update ([@eq:linear-q-update])
        self.W[action] += self.alpha * (target - q_sa) * phi

Approach 3: Deep Q-Network (DQN)

A neural network \(\hat{Q}(s; \boldsymbol{\theta})\) takes the raw state as input and outputs Q-values for all actions ([@def:dqn]). We use PyTorch (introduced in Chapter 6) with experience replay ([@def:experience-replay]) and a target network ([@def:target-network]) for stability.

The architecture is the same two-hidden-layer ReLU network from Chapter 6, now trained with the Q-learning target instead of supervised labels.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
from collections import deque
import random

class DQNAgent:
    """DQN with experience replay and target network (PyTorch)."""

    def __init__(self, state_dim=2, n_actions=4, hidden=32,
                 lr=1e-3, gamma=0.99, buffer_size=5000,
                 batch_size=32, target_update=100,
                 state_norm=None):
        self.n_actions = n_actions
        self.gamma = gamma
        self.batch_size = batch_size
        self.target_update = target_update
        self.step_count = 0

        # Normalization: divide raw state by this before the network
        if state_norm is None:
            self.state_norm = np.full(state_dim, 4.0, dtype=np.float32)
        else:
            self.state_norm = np.array(state_norm, dtype=np.float32)

        # Q-network: state → 32 → 32 → n_actions  ([@dl1:pytorch-nn])
        self.q_net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(state_dim, hidden),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden, hidden),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden, n_actions),
        )

        # Target network (frozen copy, [@def:target-network])
        self.target_net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(state_dim, hidden),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden, hidden),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden, n_actions),
        )
        self.target_net.load_state_dict(self.q_net.state_dict())
        self.target_net.eval()

        self.optimizer = optim.Adam(self.q_net.parameters(), lr=lr)
        self.buffer = deque(maxlen=buffer_size)

    def select_action(self, state, epsilon):
        if np.random.random() < epsilon:
            return np.random.randint(self.n_actions)
        with torch.no_grad():
            s = torch.FloatTensor(state / self.state_norm).unsqueeze(0)
            return int(self.q_net(s).argmax(dim=1).item())

    def update(self, state, action, reward, next_state, done):
        self.buffer.append((state / self.state_norm, action,
                            reward, next_state / self.state_norm,
                            float(done)))
        self.step_count += 1

        if len(self.buffer) < self.batch_size:
            return

        batch = random.sample(self.buffer, self.batch_size)
        s, a, r, ns, d = zip(*batch)

        states_t = torch.FloatTensor(np.array(s))
        actions_t = torch.LongTensor(a)
        rewards_t = torch.FloatTensor(r)
        next_states_t = torch.FloatTensor(np.array(ns))
        dones_t = torch.FloatTensor(d)

        # Q-values for the actions actually taken
        q_values = self.q_net(states_t).gather(
            1, actions_t.unsqueeze(1)).squeeze(1)

        # TD target: r + gamma * max_a' Q_target(s', a') * (1 - done)
        with torch.no_grad():
            q_next = self.target_net(next_states_t).max(dim=1)[0]
            targets = rewards_t + self.gamma * q_next * (1 - dones_t)

        loss = nn.MSELoss()(q_values, targets)
        self.optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        self.optimizer.step()

        # Sync target network every C steps
        if self.step_count % self.target_update == 0:
            self.target_net.load_state_dict(self.q_net.state_dict())

Training

All three agents train on the same 2D environment for 1,000 episodes with the same \(\varepsilon\)-decay schedule.

def train_on_env(agent, env, n_episodes=1000, epsilon_start=1.0,
                 epsilon_decay=0.995, epsilon_min=0.01, seed=42):
    """Train an agent on any warehouse environment."""
    np.random.seed(seed)
    epsilon = epsilon_start
    rewards = []

    # Pre-fill replay buffer with random experience (DQN only)
    if hasattr(agent, 'buffer'):
        state = env.reset()
        for _ in range(500):
            action = np.random.randint(env.n_actions)
            next_state, reward, done = env.step(action)
            agent.update(state, action, reward, next_state, done)
            state = env.reset() if done else next_state

    for ep in range(n_episodes):
        state = env.reset()
        done = False
        total_reward = 0
        steps = 0

        while not done and steps < 200:
            action = agent.select_action(state, epsilon)
            next_state, reward, done = env.step(action)
            agent.update(state, action, reward, next_state, done)
            state = next_state
            total_reward += reward
            steps += 1

        epsilon = max(epsilon_min, epsilon * epsilon_decay)
        rewards.append(total_reward)

    return rewards

env_2d = ContinuousWarehouse()

print("Training discretized Q-learning...")
agent_disc = DiscretizedAgent()
rewards_disc = train_on_env(agent_disc, env_2d)

print("Training tile-coded linear Q-learning...")
agent_tile = TileCodedAgent()
rewards_tile = train_on_env(agent_tile, env_2d)

print("Training DQN...")
agent_dqn = DQNAgent()
rewards_dqn = train_on_env(agent_dqn, env_2d)

Learning Curves

Rolling average reward (window=100) for all three approaches. Tile coding achieves smooth generalization and good sample efficiency. DQN takes longer to converge but can achieve the best final performance. Discretized Q-learning is limited by its coarse state representation.

def rolling_avg(data, window=100):
    return np.convolve(data, np.ones(window)/window, mode='valid')

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(8, 4))
ax.plot(rolling_avg(rewards_disc), label='Discretized Q', alpha=0.8)
ax.plot(rolling_avg(rewards_tile), label='Tile-coded Linear', alpha=0.8)
ax.plot(rolling_avg(rewards_dqn), label='DQN', alpha=0.8)

Learned Policies as Vector Fields

We evaluate each agent’s greedy policy on a grid of \((x, y)\) positions and plot the resulting action arrows. The goal (green circle) and hazard (red circle) are shown for reference.

                        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', lw=1.0,
                                        color='#333333'))

    # Goal and hazard circles
    goal_c = plt.Circle((3.5, 3.5), 0.4, color='green', alpha=0.3)
    hazard_c = plt.Circle((3.5, 2.5), 0.4, color='red', alpha=0.3)

            color='green')
    ax.text(3.5, 2.5, '-1', ha='center', va='center', fontweight='bold',
            color='red')

    ax.set_xlim(0, 4)

Parameter Count Comparison

The approaches range from simple (400 parameters for discretized) to moderate (1024 for tile-coded) to larger (394 for DQN, with the network learning its own feature representation).

n_disc = agent_disc.Q.size
n_tile = agent_tile.W.size

Higher-Dimensional Challenge: When DQN Shines

The 2D warehouse is simple enough that all three methods work well. A real warehouse robot, however, must account for more than position: how heavy is its payload? How much battery remains? These variables affect optimal behavior — a heavily loaded robot with low battery should take a short, safe path rather than the fastest one.

We extend the state to 6 dimensions: \((x, y, \theta, v, \text{load}, \text{battery})\), where load \(\in [0, 1]\) is the payload weight (heavier loads slow the robot but earn more reward at the goal) and battery \(\in [0, 1]\) depletes over time (lower battery reduces speed).

The curse of dimensionality in action: discretizing 6 dimensions with 10 bins each requires \(10^6 \times 4 = 4{,}000{,}000\) Q-values. With 1,000 episodes of 200 steps each, only about 200,000 transitions are observed — less than 2% coverage. Most bins are never visited, so the Q-table is nearly empty.

DQN uses a neural network with about 1,500 parameters that generalizes across all 6 dimensions. It does not need to visit every region of the state space to learn a useful policy.

class HighDimWarehouse:
    """6D continuous warehouse: (x, y, theta, v, load, battery)."""

    def __init__(self, goal=(3.5, 3.5), hazard=(3.5, 2.5),
                 region_radius=0.4, step_size=0.5, noise_std=0.1):
        self.goal = np.array(goal)
        self.hazard = np.array(hazard)
        self.radius = region_radius
        self.step_size = step_size
        self.noise_std = noise_std
        self.action_deltas = np.array([
            [0, 1], [0, -1], [-1, 0], [1, 0]
        ], dtype=float)
        self.n_actions = 4
        self.state_dim = 6

    def reset(self):
        x, y = 0.5, 0.5
        theta = np.random.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi)
        v = 0.0
        load = np.random.uniform(0, 1)      # item weight
        battery = np.random.uniform(0.5, 1)  # starts partially charged
        self.state = np.array([x, y, theta, v, load, battery])
        return self.state.copy()

    def step(self, action):
        x, y, theta, v, load, battery = self.state

        # Battery depletes; speed depends on load and battery
        battery = max(0.0, battery - 0.002)
        speed_factor = (1 - 0.3 * load) * max(0.2, battery)

        delta = self.action_deltas[action] * self.step_size * speed_factor
        noise = np.random.randn(2) * self.noise_std
        new_xy = np.clip(np.array([x, y]) + delta + noise, 0.0, 4.0)

        # Heading drifts toward movement direction
        if np.linalg.norm(delta) > 0.01:
            theta = np.arctan2(delta[1], delta[0])
        v = np.linalg.norm(delta)

        self.state = np.array([new_xy[0], new_xy[1], theta, v,
                               load, battery])

        if np.linalg.norm(new_xy - self.goal) < self.radius:
            # Heavier loads earn more reward
            return self.state.copy(), 1.0 + 0.5 * load, True
        elif np.linalg.norm(new_xy - self.hazard) < self.radius:
            return self.state.copy(), -1.0, True
        else:
            return self.state.copy(), -0.01, False

Discretization Breaks Down

With 10 bins per dimension, the Q-table has 4 million entries. We can allocate it, but 1,000 episodes of training leave 95% of the bins empty.

class SparseDiscretizedAgent:
    """Discretized Q-learning using a sparse dict (6D state)."""

    def __init__(self, n_bins=10, n_actions=4, alpha=0.1,
                 gamma=0.99, state_ranges=None):
        self.n_bins = n_bins
        self.n_actions = n_actions
        self.alpha = alpha
        self.gamma = gamma
        self.Q = {}  # sparse: only visited bins stored
        self.state_ranges = state_ranges or [
            (0, 4), (0, 4), (0, 2*np.pi), (0, 1), (0, 1), (0, 1)]

    def discretize(self, state):
        bins = []
        for i, (lo, hi) in enumerate(self.state_ranges):
            b = min(int((state[i] - lo) / (hi - lo) * self.n_bins),
                    self.n_bins - 1)
            bins.append(max(0, b))
        return tuple(bins)

    def select_action(self, state, epsilon):
        if np.random.random() < epsilon:
            return np.random.randint(self.n_actions)
        key = self.discretize(state)
        q_vals = [self.Q.get((key, a), 0.0) for a in range(self.n_actions)]
        return int(np.argmax(q_vals))

    def update(self, state, action, reward, next_state, done):
        key = self.discretize(state)
        if done:
            target = reward
        else:
            nkey = self.discretize(next_state)
            target = reward + self.gamma * max(
                self.Q.get((nkey, a), 0.0) for a in range(self.n_actions))
        old_q = self.Q.get((key, action), 0.0)
        self.Q[(key, action)] = old_q + self.alpha * (target - old_q)

print("\n--- 6D Warehouse Challenge ---")

n_bins = 10
q_table_size = n_bins**6 * 4
print(f"Discretized Q-table size: {n_bins}^6 × 4 = "
      f"{q_table_size:,} entries")

print("Training discretized Q-learning (6D)...")
agent_disc_6d = SparseDiscretizedAgent(n_bins=10)
env_6d = HighDimWarehouse()
rewards_disc_6d = train_on_env(agent_disc_6d, env_6d)
bins_visited = len(agent_disc_6d.Q)
print(f"  Bins visited: {bins_visited:,} / {q_table_size:,} "
      f"({100*bins_visited/q_table_size:.2f}%)")

print("Training DQN (6D)...")
norm_6d = [4.0, 4.0, 2*np.pi, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0]
agent_dqn_6d = DQNAgent(state_dim=6, n_actions=4, hidden=32,
                         lr=1e-3, gamma=0.99, buffer_size=5000,
                         batch_size=32, target_update=100,
                         state_norm=norm_6d)
rewards_dqn_6d = train_on_env(agent_dqn_6d, env_6d)

n_dqn_6d = sum(p.numel() for p in agent_dqn_6d.q_net.parameters())
print(f"  DQN parameters: {n_dqn_6d:,}")
--- 6D Warehouse Challenge ---
Discretized Q-table size: 10^6 × 4 = 4,000,000 entries
Training discretized Q-learning (6D)...

  Bins visited: 69,246 / 4,000,000 (1.73%)
Training DQN (6D)...

  DQN parameters: 1,412

6D Comparison: Curse of Dimensionality

With 6 continuous dimensions, the discretized agent visits only a tiny fraction of the Q-table. It cannot generalize to unvisited bins, so its performance is poor. The DQN agent uses a small neural network (< 2,000 parameters) that generalizes across all 6 dimensions.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(8, 4))
ax.plot(rolling_avg(rewards_disc_6d), label='Discretized Q (6D)',
        alpha=0.8)
ax.plot(rolling_avg(rewards_dqn_6d), label='DQN (6D)', alpha=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel('Episode')
ax.set_ylabel('Reward (rolling avg, window=100)')
ax.set_title('6D Warehouse: Curse of Dimensionality')
ax.legend()
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('6d_comparison.svg', bbox_inches='tight')
