sections.title: Policy Search and Actor-Critic Methods
sections.html:
Every algorithm in this chapter so far—TD learning, Q-learning, SARSA, DQN—learns a value function and derives the policy from it. This is the value-based approach: learn \(Q^*(s, a)\), then act greedily. But value-based methods have a fundamental limitation: they require \(\arg\max_a Q(s, a)\) to select actions. For discrete actions (e.g., the 4 directions in the warehouse grid), this is a simple lookup. For continuous actions, it requires solving an optimization problem at every step {% cite 'russell2020' note='sec. 22.5' %}.

This section introduces policy-based methods, which parameterize the policy directly and optimize it using gradient ascent. We then combine the two approaches in actor-critic methods, which are the foundation of modern deep RL.

The Continuous Action Problem

Continuous Action Space

A continuous action space \(\mathcal{A} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m\) contains actions that are real-valued vectors. Each component of the action controls a continuous degree of freedom (e.g., motor torque, steering angle, thrust magnitude).

In [@rl4], we addressed continuous states while keeping actions discrete. But many real-world control problems have continuous actions. Consider the warehouse robot with:

  • Thrust: \(f \in [0, f_{\max}]\)—how hard to drive the wheels
  • Steering angle: \(\delta \in [-\delta_{\max}, \delta_{\max}]\)—which direction to turn

The action is a vector \((f, \delta) \in \mathbb{R}^2\). Q-learning requires \(\pi(s) = \arg\max_{(f,\delta)} Q(s, f, \delta)\), which means solving a continuous optimization problem at every time step. For a neural network \(Q\), this inner optimization has no closed form and is expensive to approximate.

The solution: instead of learning \(Q\) and optimizing over actions, learn the policy directly.

Policy Gradient Methods

Policy Gradient

A policy gradient method parameterizes the policy as \(\pi_\theta(a \mid s)\)—a probability distribution over actions given the state, with learnable parameters \(\theta\)—and optimizes \(\theta\) by gradient ascent on the expected return: \[ J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi_\theta}[G_0] = \mathbb{E}_{\pi_\theta}\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t r_{t+1}\right] \]

We need to choose a family of probability distributions for \(\pi_\theta(a \mid s)\) over the continuous action space. A natural choice is the Gaussian (normal) distribution:

\[ \pi_\theta(a \mid s) = \mathcal{N}\bigl(\mu_\theta(s), \, \sigma_\theta(s)^2\bigr) \]

Why Gaussian? Three reasons: (1) it has support on all of \(\mathbb{R}\), so any action value has nonzero probability — this guarantees exploration; (2) it is fully characterized by just two parameters (mean and standard deviation), which the network can output directly; and (3) its log-probability \(\log \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\) has a simple closed-form derivative with respect to \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\), which makes the policy gradient ([@rl5:reinforce]) easy to compute.

Here \(\mu_\theta(s)\) and \(\sigma_\theta(s)\) are neural networks that output the mean and standard deviation of the action distribution given the state. The action is sampled: \(a \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid s)\). During training, the stochasticity provides exploration; at deployment, the agent can use the mean \(\mu_\theta(s)\) for deterministic control. For vector-valued actions (e.g., thrust and steering), the policy outputs a multivariate Gaussian \(\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_\theta(s), \text{diag}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}_\theta(s)^2))\) with a diagonal covariance — one mean and one standard deviation per action component.

Policy Gradients in Robotics

Policy gradient methods dominate in robotics and continuous control because they naturally output continuous actions. A robot arm with 7 joints needs a 7-dimensional continuous action at each time step—there is no practical way to discretize this space (it would require \(n^7\) bins). Policy gradients handle this by outputting a 7-dimensional Gaussian, making them the natural choice for physical systems.

The REINFORCE Algorithm

The central challenge is computing \(\nabla_\theta J(\theta)\) — the gradient of the expected return with respect to the policy parameters. We cannot differentiate through the environment's dynamics (they are unknown, per [@def:reinforcement-learning]), but we can differentiate through the policy \(\pi_\theta\). The key mathematical tool is the log-derivative trick. Start from the identity \(\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta = \pi_\theta \, \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta\) (which follows from the chain rule: \(\nabla \log f = \nabla f / f\)). When \(J(\theta)\) is written as a sum \(\sum_a \pi_\theta(a \mid s) \, (\cdots)\), substituting \(\pi_\theta = \pi_\theta \cdot 1\) turns the gradient of that sum into

\[\sum_a \pi_\theta(a \mid s) \, \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s) \, (\cdots)\]

which is an expectation under \(\pi_\theta\) — something we can estimate by sampling trajectories, without knowing the dynamics. Applying this to the full objective \(J(\theta)\) yields:

Policy Gradient Theorem

The gradient of the expected return with respect to the policy parameters is: \[ \nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi_\theta}\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{H} \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t) \, G_t\right] \] where \(H\) is the episode length (we use \(H\) rather than \(T\) to avoid confusion with the transition function \(T(s' \mid s, a)\)), \(G_t\) is the return from time step \(t\), and \(\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)\) is the score function — the gradient of the log-probability of the action taken.

The intuition: the score function \(\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)\) points in the direction that increases the probability of action \(a_t\) at state \(s_t\). If the return \(G_t\) from that point onward was high, we move in that direction (reinforcing the action); if \(G_t\) was low, we move away. No model of the environment is needed — only the ability to sample trajectories and differentiate the policy.

REINFORCE

REINFORCE is a Monte Carlo policy gradient algorithm:

  1. Run an episode using policy \(\pi_\theta\), collecting \((s_0, a_0, r_1, s_1, a_1, r_2, \ldots, s_H)\)
  2. Compute returns \(G_t = \sum_{k=0}^{H-t} \gamma^k r_{t+k+1}\) for each time step
  3. Update: \(\theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha \sum_{t=0}^{H} \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t) \, G_t\)

REINFORCE is conceptually simple and general—it works for any differentiable policy—but it has a practical weakness: high variance. The return \(G_t\) is a noisy estimate of the value, and multiplying it by the log-gradient produces gradient estimates that vary enormously from episode to episode. This makes learning slow and unstable.

Variance Reduction and Baselines

The variance of REINFORCE comes from using the full return \(G_t\) as the reinforcement signal. A key insight: we can subtract any baseline \(b(s_t)\) from \(G_t\) without introducing bias, as long as the baseline depends only on the state (not the action):

\[ \nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi_\theta}\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{H} \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t) \, \bigl(G_t - b(s_t)\bigr)\right] \]

The baseline drops out of the expectation because \(\mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi_\theta}[\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s) \cdot b(s)] = b(s) \cdot \nabla_\theta \sum_a \pi_\theta(a \mid s) = b(s) \cdot \nabla_\theta 1 = 0\). Subtracting \(b\) does not change the expected gradient, but it can dramatically reduce its variance.

The variance-minimizing baseline is the value function \(V^\pi(s_t)\) — the expected return from the current state. With this baseline, \(G_t - V^\pi(s_t)\) measures how much better this particular trajectory was than average, which is a much lower-variance signal than \(G_t\) alone. This quantity has a name:

Advantage Function

The advantage function measures how much better action \(a\) is compared to the average action at state \(s\): \[ A^\pi(s, a) = Q^\pi(s, a) - V^\pi(s) \] When \(A^\pi(s, a) > 0\), action \(a\) is better than average; when \(A^\pi(s, a) < 0\), it is worse. Using the advantage as the reinforcement signal tells the gradient "how much to reinforce" without the noise of absolute returns.

We do not know \(V^\pi(s_t)\) — we need to estimate it. This leads to the actor-critic architecture.

Actor-Critic Methods

Actor-Critic

An actor-critic method maintains two components:

  • Actor: the policy \(\pi_\theta(a \mid s)\), which selects actions
  • Critic: a value estimator \(\hat{V}_\mathbf{w}(s)\), which provides the baseline

After each observed transition \((s_t, a_t, r_{t+1}, s_{t+1})\), both are updated using the TD error \(\delta_t\) ([@def:td-error]) as the advantage estimate ([@eq:advantage]):

\[ \delta_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma \hat{V}_\mathbf{w}(s_{t+1}) - \hat{V}_\mathbf{w}(s_t) \]

Critic update (TD learning, pulling \(\hat{V}\) toward the observed target): \[ \mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} + \alpha_\mathbf{w} \, \delta_t \, \nabla_\mathbf{w} \hat{V}_\mathbf{w}(s_t) \]

Actor update (policy gradient, reinforcing actions that did better than expected): \[ \theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha_\theta \, \delta_t \, \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t) \]

The TD error \(\delta_t\) serves as a single-step estimate of the advantage \(A^\pi(s_t, a_t)\) ([@eq:advantage]): if \(\delta_t > 0\), the action led to a better outcome than the critic expected, so the actor increases its probability; if \(\delta_t < 0\), the action was worse than expected, and the actor decreases it. The critic's \(\hat{V}\) serves double duty: it provides the baseline for the actor's gradient and the bootstrap for the critic's own TD update.

The Actor-Critic Algorithm

Initialize actor parameters \(\theta\) (randomly), critic parameters \(\mathbf{w}\) (zeros or randomly)

For each episode:

  1. Initialize state \(s\)
  2. Repeat until \(s\) is terminal:
    • Sample action \(a \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid s)\)
    • Take action \(a\), observe reward \(r\) and next state \(s'\)
    • Compute TD error: \(\delta = r + \gamma \hat{V}_\mathbf{w}(s') - \hat{V}_\mathbf{w}(s)\) (use \(\delta = r\) if \(s'\) is terminal)
    • Update critic: \(\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} + \alpha_\mathbf{w} \, \delta \, \nabla_\mathbf{w} \hat{V}_\mathbf{w}(s)\)
    • Update actor: \(\theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha_\theta \, \delta \, \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\)
    • \(s \leftarrow s'\)

Actor-Critic as Unification

Actor-critic methods unify the value-based and policy-based approaches. The critic learns a value function (like TD learning in [@rl2]), and the actor learns a policy (like REINFORCE). The critic reduces the variance of the actor's gradient estimates, enabling faster and more stable learning. Most state-of-the-art deep RL algorithms are actor-critic variants:

  • PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization): clips the ratio \(\pi_\theta(a|s) / \pi_{\theta_\text{old}}(a|s)\) to prevent the policy from changing too much in a single update, improving stability without the complexity of a trust-region constraint.
  • SAC (Soft Actor-Critic): adds an entropy bonus \(\mathcal{H}[\pi_\theta(\cdot|s)]\) to the objective, encouraging exploration and preventing premature convergence to a deterministic policy.

These algorithms have been used to train simulated robots to walk, fly, and manipulate objects, and are the standard tools for continuous-control deep RL.

Actor-Critic in Python

The following script trains an actor-critic agent on the warehouse floor from [@rl4] with continuous velocity actions \((a_x, a_y) \in [-1, 1]^2\) — the agent directly controls its horizontal and vertical velocity at each step. The hazard is placed in the center of the floor, directly between the start region (bottom-left) and the goal (top-right), so the agent must learn to navigate around the obstacle. The actor and critic share a backbone network: the actor outputs the mean of a Gaussian policy ([@eq:gaussian-policy]) via tanh (bounding actions to \([-1, 1]\)), and the critic outputs \(\hat{V}(s)\).

Actor-Critic on the Continuous Warehouse

We train an actor-critic agent ([@def:actor-critic]) on the warehouse floor from [@rl4] with continuous thrust and steering actions ([@rl5:continuous-actions]). The hazard sits in the center of the floor, directly between the start region (bottom-left) and the goal (top-right), forcing the agent to learn a path around the obstacle.

The actor is a Gaussian policy ([@eq:gaussian-policy]); the critic estimates \(\hat{V}(s)\) and provides the advantage signal ([@eq:advantage-td]).

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
from torch.distributions import Normal
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Warehouse with Center Hazard

The robot controls a continuous 2D action:

  • \(a_x \in [-1, 1]\): horizontal velocity
  • \(a_y \in [-1, 1]\): vertical velocity

This is simpler than thrust/steering and lets the agent move in any direction without trigonometric output layers.

class ContinuousWarehouse:
    """2D warehouse with continuous velocity actions."""

    def __init__(self, goal=(3.5, 3.5), hazard=(2.0, 2.0),
                 goal_radius=0.5, hazard_radius=0.6,
                 step_scale=0.4, noise_std=0.08):
        self.goal = np.array(goal, dtype=np.float32)
        self.hazard = np.array(hazard, dtype=np.float32)
        self.goal_radius = goal_radius
        self.hazard_radius = hazard_radius
        self.step_scale = step_scale
        self.noise_std = noise_std

    def reset(self):
        self.state = np.array([
            np.random.uniform(0.2, 1.2),
            np.random.uniform(0.2, 1.2)], dtype=np.float32)
        return self.state.copy()

    def step(self, action):
        ax = float(np.clip(action[0], -1, 1))
        ay = float(np.clip(action[1], -1, 1))
        delta = np.array([ax, ay], dtype=np.float32) * self.step_scale
        noise = np.random.randn(2).astype(np.float32) * self.noise_std
        new_state = np.clip(self.state + delta + noise, 0.0, 4.0)
        self.state = new_state

        if np.linalg.norm(new_state - self.goal) < self.goal_radius:
            return new_state.copy(), 10.0, True
        elif np.linalg.norm(new_state - self.hazard) < self.hazard_radius:
            return new_state.copy(), -5.0, True
        else:
            return new_state.copy(), -0.05, False

Actor-Critic Network

The actor and critic share hidden layers. The actor outputs the mean of a 2D Gaussian via tanh (bounding actions to \([-1, 1]\)); the standard deviation is a learnable parameter. The critic outputs \(\hat{V}(s)\).

class ActorCritic(nn.Module):
    """Shared-backbone actor-critic with Gaussian policy."""

    def __init__(self, state_dim=2, action_dim=2, hidden=64):
        super().__init__()
        self.shared = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(state_dim, hidden), nn.Tanh(),
            nn.Linear(hidden, hidden), nn.Tanh(),
        )
        self.actor_mean = nn.Linear(hidden, action_dim)
        self.log_std = nn.Parameter(torch.full((action_dim,), -0.5))
        self.critic_head = nn.Linear(hidden, 1)

    def forward(self, state):
        h = self.shared(state)
        mean = torch.tanh(self.actor_mean(h))  # [-1, 1]
        std = self.log_std.exp()
        value = self.critic_head(h).squeeze(-1)
        return mean, std, value

    def get_action(self, state_np):
        s = torch.FloatTensor(state_np / 4.0).unsqueeze(0)
        mean, std, value = self.forward(s)
        dist = Normal(mean, std)
        action = dist.sample()
        log_prob = dist.log_prob(action).sum(dim=-1)
        return (action.squeeze(0).detach().numpy(),
                log_prob.squeeze(0),
                value.squeeze(0))

Training with Generalized Advantage Estimation

We collect full episodes and compute advantages using GAE (a multi-step extension of the single-step TD advantage in [@eq:advantage-td]). GAE smoothly interpolates between single-step TD (\(\lambda = 0\)) and Monte Carlo (\(\lambda = 1\)) by accumulating discounted TD errors:

\[\hat{A}_t = \sum_{k=0}^{H-t} (\gamma\lambda)^k \delta_{t+k}\]

This gives lower-variance advantages than single-step TD while keeping some bias reduction from bootstrapping.

def compute_gae(rewards, values, dones, gamma=0.99, lam=0.95):
    """Compute Generalized Advantage Estimation."""
    advantages = []
    gae = 0
    for t in reversed(range(len(rewards))):
        if t == len(rewards) - 1:
            next_val = 0.0
        else:
            next_val = values[t + 1]
        delta = rewards[t] + gamma * next_val * (1 - dones[t]) - values[t]
        gae = delta + gamma * lam * (1 - dones[t]) * gae
        advantages.insert(0, gae)
    return advantages

def train(n_episodes=800, gamma=0.99, lr=3e-3, seed=42):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)

    env = ContinuousWarehouse()
    model = ActorCritic()
    optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    rewards_history = []

    for ep in range(n_episodes):
        state = env.reset()
        done = False
        total_reward = 0

        states, log_probs, values, rewards, dones = [], [], [], [], []

        while not done and len(rewards) < 80:
            action, log_prob, value = model.get_action(state)
            next_state, reward, done = env.step(action)
            total_reward += reward

            states.append(state / 4.0)
            log_probs.append(log_prob)
            values.append(value.item())
            rewards.append(reward)
            dones.append(float(done))
            state = next_state

        # GAE advantages
        advantages = compute_gae(rewards, values, dones, gamma)
        advantages = torch.FloatTensor(advantages)
        returns = advantages + torch.FloatTensor(values)
        # Normalize advantages
        if len(advantages) > 1:
            advantages = (advantages - advantages.mean()) / (
                advantages.std() + 1e-8)

        log_probs_t = torch.stack(log_probs)
        states_t = torch.FloatTensor(np.array(states))
        _, _, values_t = model(states_t)

        actor_loss = -(log_probs_t * advantages).mean()
        critic_loss = ((values_t - returns) ** 2).mean()
        # Entropy bonus for exploration
        mean_t, std_t, _ = model(states_t)
        entropy = Normal(mean_t, std_t).entropy().mean()
        loss = actor_loss + 0.5 * critic_loss - 0.01 * entropy

        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 0.5)
        optimizer.step()

        rewards_history.append(total_reward)

    return model, rewards_history

print("Training actor-critic...")
model_ac, rewards_ac = train()
Training actor-critic...

Learning Curve

def rolling_avg(data, window=50):
    return np.convolve(data, np.ones(window)/window, mode='valid')

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(8, 4))
ax.plot(rolling_avg(rewards_ac), color='#e08214', alpha=0.9)
ax.set_xlabel('Episode')
ax.set_ylabel('Reward (rolling avg, window=50)')
ax.set_title('Actor-Critic Learning Curve')
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('actor_critic_curve.svg', bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

Learned Policy

Arrows show the mean action (velocity vector) at each position. The policy steers around the hazard to reach the goal.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(5.5, 5.5))
grid_pts = np.linspace(0.3, 3.7, 12)

with torch.no_grad():
    for gx in grid_pts:
        for gy in grid_pts:
            s = torch.FloatTensor([gx / 4.0, gy / 4.0]).unsqueeze(0)
            mean, _, _ = model_ac(s)
            dx = float(mean[0, 0]) * 0.18
            dy = float(mean[0, 1]) * 0.18
            ax.annotate('', xy=(gx + dx, gy + dy), xytext=(gx, gy),
                        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', lw=1.2,
                                        color='#333333'))

goal_c = plt.Circle((3.5, 3.5), 0.5, color='green', alpha=0.3)
hazard_c = plt.Circle((2.0, 2.0), 0.6, color='red', alpha=0.3)
ax.add_patch(goal_c)
ax.add_patch(hazard_c)
ax.text(3.5, 3.5, 'Goal', ha='center', va='center', fontweight='bold',
        fontsize=10, color='green')
ax.text(2.0, 2.0, 'Hazard', ha='center', va='center', fontweight='bold',
        fontsize=10, color='red')
ax.set_xlim(0, 4)
ax.set_ylim(0, 4)
ax.set_aspect('equal')
ax.set_title('Learned Policy (mean action)')
ax.set_xlabel('$x$')
ax.set_ylabel('$y$')
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.2)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('actor_critic_policy.svg', bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

Trajectory Rollouts

30 trajectories from random starts in the bottom-left corner, using the mean action (no sampling).

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=(6, 6))

n_rollouts = 30
env_viz = ContinuousWarehouse()
cmap = plt.cm.viridis(np.linspace(0.1, 0.9, n_rollouts))
goals_reached = 0

for i in range(n_rollouts):
    np.random.seed(i + 300)
    state = np.array([np.random.uniform(0.2, 1.3),
                      np.random.uniform(0.2, 1.3)], dtype=np.float32)
    env_viz.state = state.copy()
    traj = [state.copy()]
    done = False
    steps = 0

    with torch.no_grad():
        while not done and steps < 80:
            s = torch.FloatTensor(state / 4.0).unsqueeze(0)
            mean, _, _ = model_ac(s)
            action = mean.squeeze(0).numpy()
            state, reward, done = env_viz.step(action)
            traj.append(state.copy())
            steps += 1
            if done and reward > 0:
                goals_reached += 1

    traj = np.array(traj)
    ax.plot(traj[:, 0], traj[:, 1], '-', color=cmap[i],
            linewidth=1.5, alpha=0.7)
    ax.plot(traj[0, 0], traj[0, 1], 'o', color=cmap[i],
            markersize=5, zorder=5)

goal_c = plt.Circle((3.5, 3.5), 0.5, color='green', alpha=0.25)
hazard_c = plt.Circle((2.0, 2.0), 0.6, color='red', alpha=0.25)
ax.add_patch(goal_c)
ax.add_patch(hazard_c)
ax.text(3.5, 3.5, 'Goal', ha='center', va='center', fontweight='bold',
        fontsize=11, color='green')
ax.text(2.0, 2.0, 'Hazard', ha='center', va='center', fontweight='bold',
        fontsize=11, color='red')
ax.set_xlim(0, 4)
ax.set_ylim(0, 4)
ax.set_aspect('equal')
ax.set_title(f'Rollouts ({goals_reached}/{n_rollouts} reach goal)')
ax.set_xlabel('$x$')
ax.set_ylabel('$y$')
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.2)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('actor_critic_rollouts.svg', bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

The trajectories start from the bottom-left (circles), navigate around the center hazard, and converge on the goal. The policy was never told where the goal or hazard are — it discovered the layout from the reward signal alone.

Performance

print(f"Actor-Critic last 100 avg: {np.mean(rewards_ac[-100:]):+.3f}")
print(f"Rollout success: {goals_reached}/{n_rollouts}")
Actor-Critic last 100 avg: +2.754
Rollout success: 19/30

The RL Landscape

The algorithms in this chapter can be organized along several axes:

Algorithm Model-Based? Value or Policy? On/Off-Policy
Value iteration (Ch 4) Model-based Value —
Monte Carlo ([@rl2]) Model-free Value On-policy
TD(0) / \(n\)-step TD ([@rl2]) Model-free Value On-policy
Q-learning ([@rl3]) Model-free Value Off-policy
SARSA ([@rl3]) Model-free Value On-policy
Expected SARSA ([@rl3]) Model-free Value Either
DQN ([@rl4]) Model-free Value Off-policy
REINFORCE ([@rl5]) Model-free Policy On-policy
Actor-critic ([@rl5]) Model-free Both On-policy

Open Challenges

Reinforcement learning remains an active research area. Key challenges include:

  • Sample efficiency: deep RL algorithms often require millions of interactions to learn, making them expensive for real-world robotics where each episode takes minutes or hours
  • Stability: training can be sensitive to hyperparameters (learning rates, network architecture, exploration schedules)
  • Reward design: the agent optimizes the reward function it is given, which may not capture the intended behavior (reward hacking)
  • Sim-to-real transfer: policies trained in simulation often fail when deployed on physical robots due to differences between the simulator and reality

For many engineering applications, simpler methods should be tried first. Tabular Q-learning is sufficient for small discrete problems. Linear function approximation handles moderate continuous problems with well-designed features. Deep RL is the tool of last resort—powerful but expensive and difficult to tune.

Closing the Loop

This chapter completes the arc that began in Chapter 1 with the warehouse robot as a rational agent. We have now covered the full stack:

  • Chapter 1: What is an intelligent agent? Rational behavior, agent-environment interaction
  • Chapter 2: How does an agent find solutions? Search algorithms, optimization, constraint satisfaction
  • Chapter 3: How does an agent reason about the world? Propositional and first-order logic, knowledge-based agents
  • Chapter 4: How does an agent handle uncertainty? Probability, Bayesian reasoning, MDPs, value iteration
  • Chapter 5: How does an agent learn from data? Supervised learning, decision trees, linear models, gradient descent
  • Chapter 6: How does an agent learn complex representations? Neural networks, CNNs, RNNs, transformers
  • Chapter 7: How does an agent learn to act? Reinforcement learning, Q-learning, function approximation, policy gradients

Each chapter built on the last. The MDP framework (Ch 4) provided the mathematical foundation for RL (Ch 7). Machine learning (Ch 5) provided the tools for learning from data, and deep learning (Ch 6) provided the function approximators that make RL scale to complex environments.

AI as an Engineering Tool

The warehouse robot is a unifying example, but the real lesson is broader. AI engineering is about choosing the right tool for the problem. Not every problem needs deep RL—and not every problem can be solved with search alone. A linear model may suffice where a neural network is overkill. Tabular Q-learning may solve what DQN would require months to train. The engineer's job is to understand the full toolkit and deploy each tool where it adds genuine value. This chapter—and this course—has aimed to give you that toolkit.

sections.html:
Tabular Q-Learning for Warehouse Navigation

Objective: Implement Q-learning and SARSA from scratch for the \(4 \times 4\) warehouse MDP, compare their learned policies to the value iteration solution from Chapter 4, and investigate the effect of exploration schedules and learning rates on convergence.

Background: In [@rl3], we derived the Q-learning and SARSA update rules and traced several updates by hand. In [@m1:optimal-policy-result] and [@vi], we computed the optimal policy and value function using value iteration. This exercise implements both RL algorithms and verifies that they converge to the same solution that value iteration found—but without access to \(T\) or \(R\).

Task:

  1. Implement the warehouse environment. Write an environment class that takes a state and action, samples the next state from the stochastic transition model (80/10/10), and returns the reward. The agent interacts only through this interface—it never accesses \(T\) or \(R\) directly.

  2. Implement Q-learning with \(\varepsilon\)-greedy exploration. Initialize \(Q(s, a) = 0\) for all state-action pairs. Train for 1000 episodes using \(\alpha = 0.1\), \(\gamma = 0.99\), \(\varepsilon = 1.0\) with exponential decay (\(\rho = 0.995\)).

    • Record the total reward per episode.
    • Extract the learned policy \(\pi(s) = \arg\max_a Q(s, a)\).

  3. Implement SARSA. Use the same hyperparameters and exploration schedule. Compare the learned policies of Q-learning and SARSA. Where do they differ? Does the difference align with the discussion in [@rl3:q-vs-sarsa] about behavior near hazards?

  4. Plot learning curves. On the same axes, plot the rolling average reward (window size 50) for Q-learning and SARSA. Mark the optimal expected return (from value iteration) as a horizontal line.

  5. Compare to value iteration. Load the optimal policy from [@vi] and compare it to the Q-learning and SARSA policies. Report the number of states where the learned policy matches the optimal policy. Visualize all three policies as arrow plots on the grid.

  6. Hyperparameter sensitivity. Experiment with:

    • Learning rates \(\alpha \in \{0.01, 0.1, 0.5\}\)
    • Exploration decay rates \(\rho \in \{0.99, 0.995, 0.999\}\)
    • Plot learning curves for each configuration. Which combination converges fastest? Which fails to converge?

Copilot Coaching:

  • Environment: "Write a Python class for the 4×4 warehouse MDP with stochastic transitions (80/10/10). The step method should take a state and action and return (next_state, reward, done)."
  • Q-learning: "Implement tabular Q-learning with epsilon-greedy exploration and epsilon decay. Track episode rewards."
  • Comparison: "Compare two learned policies (Q-learning and SARSA) to a known optimal policy from value iteration. Report the number of matching actions per state."
  • Visualization: "Plot the learned policy as arrows on a 4×4 grid, with color indicating the Q-value of the chosen action."

Deliverables:

  • warehouse_env_rl.py: warehouse environment class (no model access for the agent)
  • q_learning_sarsa.py: Q-learning and SARSA implementations with training loops
  • exercise_1_report.pdf: 3-page report including learning curves, policy arrow plots (Q-learning, SARSA, value iteration), hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, and discussion of Q-learning vs. SARSA behavior near the hazard

From Discrete to Continuous: Function Approximation Showdown

Objective: Implement three approaches to RL in a continuous-state warehouse environment—discretized Q-learning, tile-coded linear Q-learning, and DQN—and compare their learning efficiency and final policy quality. Then extend the state space to see where DQN's advantage emerges.

Background: In [@rl4], we introduced the continuous warehouse floor and three function approximation strategies. The section demo used a simple 2D state \((x, y)\) with 4 discrete actions to keep visualizations clear. This exercise uses a richer environment: the robot has heading and velocity as additional state variables, and the hazard is placed in the center of the floor (directly in the path from start to goal), making the navigation problem more challenging.

Task:

  1. Implement the continuous warehouse environment. The robot has state \((x, y, \theta, v) \in [0,4]^2 \times [0,2\pi) \times [0,1]\) and 4 discrete actions (North, South, East, West). Add Gaussian noise to transitions; heading and velocity are updated based on the action taken. The goal region is a circle of radius 0.5 around \((3.5, 3.5)\); the hazard region is a circle of radius 0.5 around \((2.0, 2.0)\).

  2. Implement discretized Q-learning. Discretize the \((x, y)\) position into a \(10 \times 10\) grid (ignoring \(\theta\) and \(v\) for simplicity). Train for 2000 episodes. Plot the learning curve.

  3. Implement tile-coded linear Q-learning. Use 8 offset tilings of the \((x, y)\) space, each with a \(4 \times 4\) grid of tiles. Each offset tiling needs one extra tile per dimension so that boundary tiles have their natural width ([@fig:tile-coding]). Use the semi-gradient update from [@eq:linear-q-update]. Train for 2000 episodes. Plot the learning curve.

  4. Implement DQN. Build a neural network in PyTorch with 2 hidden layers (64 units each, ReLU) that takes the full state \((x, y, \theta, v)\) as input and outputs Q-values for all 4 actions. Implement experience replay (buffer size 10,000, batch size 64) and a target network (updated every 100 steps). Normalize state features to \([0, 1]\) before passing to the network ([@cmt:dqn-normalization]). Train for 2000 episodes. Plot the learning curve.

  5. Compare all three approaches. On the same axes, plot learning curves (rolling average reward, window 100) for all three agents. Report:

    • Episodes to reach 80% of optimal performance
    • Final average reward over the last 200 episodes
    • Number of parameters for each approach

  6. Ablation study for DQN. Train three variants:

    • Full DQN (experience replay + target network)
    • DQN without experience replay (train on most recent transition only)
    • DQN without target network (use the online network for targets)
    • Plot all three learning curves. Which component contributes more to stability? Relate your findings to the deadly triad ([@cmt:deadly-triad]).

  7. Bonus: the 6D challenge. Extend the state to \((x, y, \theta, v, \text{load}, \text{battery})\) where load \(\in [0, 1]\) is payload weight (affects speed; heavier loads earn more reward at the goal) and battery \(\in [0, 1]\) depletes over time (lower battery reduces speed). Discretize with 10 bins per dimension and compute the Q-table size (\(10^6 \times 4\) entries). Can the discretized agent fill enough of the table to learn? Compare to DQN on this higher-dimensional problem. This demonstrates the curse of dimensionality discussed in [@rl4:warehouse-dqn].

Copilot Coaching:

  • Continuous environment: "Write a continuous warehouse environment class with state (x, y, theta, v), 4 discrete actions (N/S/E/W), Gaussian noise on transitions, and circular goal/hazard regions at (3.5,3.5) and (2.0,2.0)."
  • Tile coding: "Implement tile coding for a 2D continuous space with 8 offset tilings of 4×4 tiles, allocating one extra tile per dimension for offset tilings. Return a binary feature vector."
  • DQN: "Implement DQN in PyTorch with experience replay buffer and target network. Normalize state features to [0,1]. Use architecture: state → 64 → 64 → 4 actions."
  • Ablation: "Run DQN with and without experience replay, and with and without the target network. Plot all learning curves."

Deliverables:

  • continuous_warehouse.py: continuous environment class
  • discretized_q.py: discretized Q-learning implementation
  • tile_coded_q.py: tile coding + linear Q-learning implementation
  • dqn_agent.py: DQN implementation with replay and target network
  • exercise_2_report.pdf: 3-page report including learning curve comparison, parameter count table, policy visualizations (vector fields over the floor), DQN ablation analysis, and (bonus) 6D comparison

Policy Gradient Control with Continuous Actions

Objective: Implement REINFORCE and an actor-critic method for a continuous-action warehouse environment, and compare their learning efficiency and stability.

Background: In [@rl5], we introduced policy gradient methods for continuous action spaces where Q-learning's \(\arg\max_a Q(s,a)\) is intractable. REINFORCE ([@def:reinforce]) provides a simple Monte Carlo approach, while actor-critic methods ([@def:actor-critic]) reduce variance by learning a value baseline. This exercise implements both and demonstrates the advantage of the critic.

Task:

  1. Implement the continuous-action warehouse. The robot has state \((x, y, \theta, v) \in [0,4]^2 \times [0,2\pi) \times [0,1]\) and continuous actions: thrust \(f \in [0, 1]\) and steering angle \(\delta \in [-\pi/4, \pi/4]\). The goal and hazard regions are the same as Exercise 2.

  2. Implement a Gaussian policy. The policy \(\pi_\theta(a \mid s) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_\theta(s), \sigma_\theta(s)^2)\) ([@eq:gaussian-policy]) outputs mean and standard deviation for both thrust and steering. Use a linear policy (matrix \(W\) mapping state to action means, learnable log-std).

  3. Implement REINFORCE. Collect full episodes, compute returns \(G_t\), and update using the policy gradient theorem ([@eq:policy-gradient-theorem]). Normalize returns per episode for stability. Train for 2000 episodes and plot the learning curve.

  4. Implement actor-critic. Add a linear critic \(\hat{V}_\mathbf{w}(s) = \mathbf{w}^\top s + b\) that estimates the value function. Replace \(G_t\) in the policy gradient with the advantage \(\hat{A}_t = r + \gamma \hat{V}(s') - \hat{V}(s)\) ([@eq:advantage-td]). Train for 2000 episodes.

  5. Compare learning curves. Plot REINFORCE and actor-critic on the same axes. Which converges faster? Which has less variance? Relate your observations to the variance reduction discussion in [@rl5:actor-critic].

  6. Visualize the learned policies. For each agent, plot the action field: at a grid of \((x, y)\) positions, show arrows indicating the thrust direction and magnitude output by the policy (using the mean, not samples).

Copilot Coaching:

  • Environment: "Write a continuous-state, continuous-action warehouse environment. The robot controls thrust and steering angle. Use Gaussian noise on transitions."
  • Gaussian policy: "Implement a linear Gaussian policy that outputs mean and std of a 2D action. Include a sample method and a log-probability method."
  • REINFORCE: "Implement REINFORCE with return normalization. Compute the policy gradient analytically for a Gaussian policy."
  • Actor-Critic: "Add a linear value function critic. Use the TD error as the advantage estimate for the actor update."

Deliverables:

  • continuous_action_warehouse.py: environment class
  • reinforce_agent.py: REINFORCE implementation
  • actor_critic_agent.py: actor-critic implementation
  • exercise_3_report.pdf: 3-page report including learning curves, policy visualizations, variance comparison, and discussion of when policy gradients are preferable to value-based methods ([@rl5:rl-landscape])

RL Formulation and Algorithm Selection

A robotic arm in a warehouse picks items from bins and places them on a conveyor belt. The arm has 6 joints, each with a continuous angle \(\theta_i \in [-\pi, \pi]\). The end-effector position is determined by the joint angles. At each time step, the robot chooses how to adjust all 6 joints simultaneously.

Rewards: \(+1\) for a successful pick-and-place, \(-0.5\) for dropping an item, \(-0.01\) per time step. An episode ends when the item is placed or dropped, or after 200 steps.

(a) Define the states and actions for this MDP. Is the action space discrete or continuous? Is the task episodic or continuing ([@def:episodic-continuing])?

(b) Tabular Q-learning ([@def:q-learning]) stores one value per state-action pair. In 1–2 sentences, explain why it cannot work here.

(c) DQN ([@def:dqn]) outputs Q-values for all actions, then selects \(\arg\max_a Q(s,a)\). In 1–2 sentences, explain why this is problematic when the action space is continuous.

(d) The actor-critic algorithm ([@def:actor-critic]) handles continuous actions: the actor outputs a continuous action, the critic estimates \(\hat{V}(s)\). The TD error \(\delta = r + \gamma \hat{V}(s') - \hat{V}(s)\) tells the actor whether its action was better or worse than expected ([@eq:advantage-td]).

Suppose: \(r = +1\) (successful pick), \(\hat{V}(s) = 0.5\), \(\hat{V}(s') = 0\) (terminal), \(\gamma = 0.99\). Then \(\delta = 1 + 0.99 \times 0 - 0.5 = +0.5\). Since \(\delta > 0\), was this action better or worse than expected? What does the actor do with this positive \(\delta\)?

exe:tabular-q-learning.content:
Key implementation details:

The environment should return rewards according to the convention in [@rl1:agent-environment]: \(r_{t+1} = R(s_{t+1})\). The terminal states (goal and hazard) end the episode and return their rewards (\(+1\) and \(-1\)). Non-terminal states return \(-0.04\).

Common pitfalls:

  • Forgetting to handle terminal states: when \(s'\) is terminal, \(Q(s', a') = 0\) for all \(a'\) (no future rewards). The update should use \(r\) alone as the target.
  • Not decaying \(\varepsilon\): without decay, the agent explores forever and the policy never stabilizes.
  • Initializing \(Q\) optimistically (e.g., \(Q(s,a) = 1.0\)): this encourages early exploration but can slow convergence. Zero initialization works well with \(\varepsilon\)-greedy.

Expected results:

  • Q-learning converges to the optimal policy within 300–500 episodes for \(\alpha = 0.1\), \(\rho = 0.995\)
  • SARSA converges to a slightly different policy near \((3,3)\) and \((4,2)\): it avoids the column adjacent to the hazard more aggressively
  • \(\alpha = 0.5\) converges fastest but with more oscillation; \(\alpha = 0.01\) converges slowly but smoothly
  • Very slow decay (\(\rho = 0.999\)) delays convergence because the agent explores too long

Exercise 1: Warehouse Environment for RL

This module implements the \(4 \times 4\) warehouse MDP for reinforcement learning. The agent interacts only through reset() and step(action) — it never accesses \(T\) or \(R\) directly ([@rl1:warehouse-rl-setup]).

import numpy as np
class WarehouseEnv:
    """4x4 warehouse grid MDP for reinforcement learning.

    The agent does NOT have access to the transition model or
    reward function. It can only observe (state, action, reward,
    next_state, done) tuples through interaction.

    States are (x, y) tuples with x in {0..3}, y in {0..3}.
    Actions: 0=North, 1=South, 2=West, 3=East.
    Transitions: 80% intended direction, 10% each perpendicular.
    """

    GRID_W = 4
    GRID_H = 4
    GOAL = (3, 3)       # +1 reward
    HAZARD = (3, 2)     # -1 reward
    TERMINALS = {(3, 3), (3, 2)}
    ACTIONS = [(0, 1), (0, -1), (-1, 0), (1, 0)]  # N, S, W, E
    ACTION_NAMES = ['N', 'S', 'W', 'E']
    N_ACTIONS = 4
    LIVING_REWARD = -0.04
    START = (0, 0)

    def __init__(self):
        self.state = self.START

    def reset(self):
        """Reset to start state and return it."""
        self.state = self.START
        return self.state

    def get_all_states(self):
        """Return all non-terminal states."""
        return [(x, y) for x in range(self.GRID_W)
                for y in range(self.GRID_H)
                if (x, y) not in self.TERMINALS]

    def step(self, action):
        """Take action, return (next_state, reward, done).

        Reward convention: r = R(s'), the reward for entering the
        next state ([@rl1:returns-value-functions]).
        """
        if self.state in self.TERMINALS:
            return self.state, 0.0, True

        # Stochastic transitions (80/10/10)
        intended = self.ACTIONS[action]
        if action in (0, 1):  # N or S
            perps = [self.ACTIONS[2], self.ACTIONS[3]]
        else:                  # W or E
            perps = [self.ACTIONS[0], self.ACTIONS[1]]

        r = np.random.random()
        if r < 0.8:
            move = intended
        elif r < 0.9:
            move = perps[0]
        else:
            move = perps[1]

        nx = max(0, min(self.GRID_W - 1, self.state[0] + move[0]))
        ny = max(0, min(self.GRID_H - 1, self.state[1] + move[1]))
        next_state = (nx, ny)

        if next_state == self.GOAL:
            reward, done = 1.0, True
        elif next_state == self.HAZARD:
            reward, done = -1.0, True
        else:
            reward, done = self.LIVING_REWARD, False

        self.state = next_state
        return next_state, reward, done

Exercise 1 Solution: Q-Learning and SARSA

Full solution for the tabular Q-learning exercise ([@exe:tabular-q-learning]). Implements Q-learning and SARSA on the warehouse grid, compares to value iteration, and explores hyperparameter sensitivity.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from warehouse_env_rl import WarehouseEnv

Q-Learning Implementation

Off-policy Q-learning ([@def:q-learning]) with \(\varepsilon\)-greedy exploration ([@def:epsilon-greedy]).

def epsilon_greedy(Q, state, epsilon, n_actions):
    """Select action using epsilon-greedy policy."""
    if np.random.random() < epsilon:
        return np.random.randint(n_actions)
    q_vals = [Q.get((state, a), 0.0) for a in range(n_actions)]
    return int(np.argmax(q_vals))

def q_learning(env, n_episodes=1000, alpha=0.1, gamma=0.99,
               epsilon_start=1.0, epsilon_decay=0.995,
               epsilon_min=0.01):
    """Train Q-learning on the warehouse grid.

    Returns the Q-table and per-episode rewards.
    """
    Q = {}
    epsilon = epsilon_start
    rewards = []

    for _ in range(n_episodes):
        state = env.reset()
        done = False
        total_reward = 0

        while not done:
            action = epsilon_greedy(Q, state, epsilon, env.N_ACTIONS)
            next_state, reward, done = env.step(action)
            total_reward += reward

            # Terminal states: Q(s', a') = 0 for all a'
            if done:
                target = reward
            else:
                max_q = max(Q.get((next_state, a), 0.0)
                            for a in range(env.N_ACTIONS))
                target = reward + gamma * max_q

            old_q = Q.get((state, action), 0.0)
            Q[(state, action)] = old_q + alpha * (target - old_q)
            state = next_state

        epsilon = max(epsilon_min, epsilon * epsilon_decay)
        rewards.append(total_reward)

    return Q, rewards

SARSA Implementation

On-policy SARSA ([@def:sarsa]) uses the action actually taken at the next state, making it more conservative near hazards ([@cmt:sarsa-conservative]).

def sarsa(env, n_episodes=1000, alpha=0.1, gamma=0.99,
          epsilon_start=1.0, epsilon_decay=0.995,
          epsilon_min=0.01):
    """Train SARSA on the warehouse grid."""
    Q = {}
    epsilon = epsilon_start
    rewards = []

    for _ in range(n_episodes):
        state = env.reset()
        action = epsilon_greedy(Q, state, epsilon, env.N_ACTIONS)
        done = False
        total_reward = 0

        while not done:
            next_state, reward, done = env.step(action)
            total_reward += reward

            if done:
                target = reward
            else:
                next_action = epsilon_greedy(
                    Q, next_state, epsilon, env.N_ACTIONS)
                target = reward + gamma * Q.get(
                    (next_state, next_action), 0.0)

            old_q = Q.get((state, action), 0.0)
            Q[(state, action)] = old_q + alpha * (target - old_q)

            if not done:
                state = next_state
                action = next_action
            else:
                state = next_state

        epsilon = max(epsilon_min, epsilon * epsilon_decay)
        rewards.append(total_reward)

    return Q, rewards

Train Both Agents

Key implementation notes:

For the continuous environment, normalize the state features to \([0, 1]\) before passing to the DQN — this is critical for stable training ([@cmt:dqn-normalization]). Divide \((x, y)\) by 4, \(\theta\) by \(2\pi\), and \(v\) by its maximum.

The tile coding implementation should offset each tiling by a fraction of the tile width: tiling \(k\) is offset by \((k \cdot \Delta / n_\text{tilings}, k \cdot \Delta / n_\text{tilings})\). Each offset tiling needs \(n_\text{tiles} + 1\) tiles per dimension so that boundary tiles have symmetric half-widths rather than being clamped to an asymmetric double-width (see [@fig:tile-coding] and [@rl4:tile-coding]). The feature vector is binary with \(n_\text{tilings} \times (n_\text{tiles} + 1)^2\) entries.

For DQN, use Adam optimizer with learning rate \(10^{-3}\) ([@dl2:optimizers]). Start filling the replay buffer with random actions before training begins (at least 500 transitions).

Expected results:

  • All three methods achieve comparable performance on this 4D problem — discretized Q-learning, tile coding, and DQN all learn to navigate to the goal while avoiding the center hazard. This is the expected outcome for low-to-moderate dimensional problems: use the simplest method that works ([@cmt:when-dqn-shines]).
  • Tile-coded Q-learning typically converges fastest due to smooth generalization with low overhead.
  • DQN may converge more slowly (neural network overhead) but handles the full 4D state without ignoring any dimensions.
  • In the ablation study, removing experience replay causes instability (the deadly triad, [@cmt:deadly-triad]: function approximation + bootstrapping + off-policy). Removing the target network causes more variance but is less catastrophic.
  • Bonus (6D): Discretization with 10 bins per dimension requires \(10^6 \times 4 = 4\) million Q-values. After 2000 episodes, less than 2% of bins are visited — the discretized agent fails. DQN, with only a few thousand parameters, generalizes across the full 6D space and succeeds. This is where DQN's advantage becomes clear.

Exercise 2: Continuous Warehouse Environment

A continuous-state warehouse floor for function approximation experiments ([@rl4:continuous-warehouse]). The robot has state \((x, y, \theta, v) \in [0,4]^2 \times [0, 2\pi) \times [0, 1]\) with 4 discrete actions (N/S/E/W). The hazard is at the center of the floor, directly in the path from start to goal.

import numpy as np
class ContinuousWarehouse:
    """Continuous-state warehouse with center hazard.

    State: (x, y, theta, v)
      - (x, y): position on the floor, [0, 4]^2
      - theta: heading angle, [0, 2*pi)
      - v: velocity, [0, 1]

    Actions: 0=North, 1=South, 2=East, 3=West
    """

    ACTION_DELTAS = np.array([[0, 1], [0, -1], [1, 0], [-1, 0]],
                             dtype=float)  # N, S, E, W
    N_ACTIONS = 4
    ACTION_NAMES = ['North', 'South', 'East', 'West']

    def __init__(self, goal_center=(3.5, 3.5), hazard_center=(2.0, 2.0),
                 goal_radius=0.5, hazard_radius=0.5,
                 step_size=0.5, noise_std=0.1):
        self.goal = np.array(goal_center)
        self.hazard = np.array(hazard_center)
        self.goal_radius = goal_radius
        self.hazard_radius = hazard_radius
        self.step_size = step_size
        self.noise_std = noise_std

    def reset(self):
        """Reset to a random start near the bottom-left."""
        x = np.random.uniform(0.2, 0.8)
        y = np.random.uniform(0.2, 0.8)
        theta = np.random.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi)
        v = 0.0
        self.state = np.array([x, y, theta, v])
        return self.state.copy()

    def step(self, action):
        """Execute action, return (next_state, reward, done)."""
        x, y, theta, v = self.state

        # Movement: step in the cardinal direction + noise
        delta = self.ACTION_DELTAS[action] * self.step_size
        noise = np.random.randn(2) * self.noise_std

        x += delta[0] + noise[0]
        y += delta[1] + noise[1]

        # Update heading toward movement direction
        if np.linalg.norm(delta) > 0.01:
            theta = np.arctan2(delta[1], delta[0])
        v = np.linalg.norm(delta)

        # Wrap theta to [0, 2*pi), clip position and velocity
        theta = theta % (2 * np.pi)
        x = np.clip(x, 0.0, 4.0)
        y = np.clip(y, 0.0, 4.0)
        v = np.clip(v, 0.0, 1.0)

        self.state = np.array([x, y, theta, v])
        pos = np.array([x, y])

        if np.linalg.norm(pos - self.goal) < self.goal_radius:
            return self.state.copy(), 1.0, True
        elif np.linalg.norm(pos - self.hazard) < self.hazard_radius:
            return self.state.copy(), -1.0, True
        else:
            return self.state.copy(), -0.01, False

    def normalize_state(self, state):
        """Normalize state to [0, 1] for neural network input."""
        s = state.copy()
        s[0] /= 4.0
        s[1] /= 4.0
        s[2] /= (2 * np.pi)
        # v is already in [0, 1]
        return s

Exercise 2: Tile-Coded Linear Q-Learning

Tile coding ([@def:tile-coding]) with 8 offset tilings over the \((x, y)\) position, combined with the semi-gradient TD update ([@eq:linear-q-update]).

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from continuous_warehouse import ContinuousWarehouse
class TileCodedAgent:
    """Linear Q-learning with tile coding over (x, y)."""

    def __init__(self, n_tilings=8, tiles_per_dim=4, n_actions=4,
                 alpha=0.05, gamma=0.99):
        self.n_tilings = n_tilings
        self.tiles_per_dim = tiles_per_dim
        self.n_actions = n_actions
        self.alpha = alpha / n_tilings
        self.gamma = gamma

        # Extra tile per dim for offset tilings (boundary handling)
        self.ext = tiles_per_dim + 1
        self.tiles_per_tiling = self.ext ** 2
        self.n_features = n_tilings * self.tiles_per_tiling
        self.W = np.zeros((n_actions, self.n_features))

        self.tile_width = 4.0 / tiles_per_dim
        self.offsets = np.array([
            [k * self.tile_width / n_tilings,
             k * self.tile_width / n_tilings]
            for k in range(n_tilings)
        ])

    def get_features(self, state):
        """Binary feature vector from tile coding of (x, y)."""
        phi = np.zeros(self.n_features)
        x, y = state[0], state[1]
        for k in range(self.n_tilings):
            sx = x + self.offsets[k, 0]
            sy = y + self.offsets[k, 1]
            bx = int(sx / self.tile_width)
            by = int(sy / self.tile_width)
            bx = max(0, min(bx, self.ext - 1))
            by = max(0, min(by, self.ext - 1))
            idx = k * self.tiles_per_tiling + bx * self.ext + by
            phi[idx] = 1.0
        return phi

    def q_values(self, state):
        phi = self.get_features(state)
        return self.W @ phi

    def select_action(self, state, epsilon):
        if np.random.random() < epsilon:
            return np.random.randint(self.n_actions)
        return int(np.argmax(self.q_values(state)))

    def update(self, state, action, reward, next_state, done):
        phi = self.get_features(state)
        q_sa = self.W[action] @ phi
        if done:
            target = reward
        else:
            target = reward + self.gamma * np.max(
                self.q_values(next_state))
        self.W[action] += self.alpha * (target - q_sa) * phi

Train the Agent

def train(n_episodes=1000, epsilon_start=1.0, epsilon_decay=0.995,
          epsilon_min=0.01, seed=42):
    np.random.seed(seed)
    env = ContinuousWarehouse()
    agent = TileCodedAgent()
    epsilon = epsilon_start
    rewards = []

    for _ in range(n_episodes):
        state = env.reset()
        done = False
        total_reward = 0
        steps = 0

        while not done and steps < 200:
            action = agent.select_action(state, epsilon)
            next_state, reward, done = env.step(action)
            agent.update(state, action, reward, next_state, done)
            state = next_state
            total_reward += reward
            steps += 1

        epsilon = max(epsilon_min, epsilon * epsilon_decay)
        rewards.append(total_reward)

    return agent, rewards

agent, rewards = train()

Learning Curve

def rolling_avg(data, window=100):
    return np.convolve(data, np.ones(window)/window, mode='valid')

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.plot(rolling_avg(rewards), alpha=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel('Episode')
ax.set_ylabel('Reward (rolling avg)')
ax.set_title('Tile-Coded Linear Q-Learning')
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('tile_coded_curve.svg', bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

Exercise 2: Deep Q-Network (DQN) Agent

DQN ([@def:dqn]) with experience replay ([@def:experience-replay]) and target network ([@def:target-network]) in PyTorch.

Architecture: state (4) → 32 → 32 → 4 actions ([@rl4:dqn]). (Reduced from 64-unit / 5000-episode spec for fast notebook build; students should use the full spec on their own machines.)

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
from collections import deque
import random
from continuous_warehouse import ContinuousWarehouse

Q-Network

class QNetwork(nn.Module):
    """Two-hidden-layer Q-network."""

    def __init__(self, state_dim=4, n_actions=4, hidden=32):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(state_dim, hidden),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden, hidden),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden, n_actions),
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x)

Experience Replay Buffer

class ReplayBuffer:
    def __init__(self, capacity=10_000):
        self.buffer = deque(maxlen=capacity)

    def push(self, state, action, reward, next_state, done):
        self.buffer.append((state, action, reward, next_state, done))

    def sample(self, batch_size):
        batch = random.sample(self.buffer, batch_size)
        states, actions, rewards, next_states, dones = zip(*batch)
        return (np.array(states), np.array(actions),
                np.array(rewards, dtype=np.float32),
                np.array(next_states),
                np.array(dones, dtype=np.float32))

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.buffer)

DQN Agent

class DQNAgent:
    """DQN with experience replay and target network."""

    def __init__(self, state_dim=4, n_actions=4, hidden=32,
                 lr=1e-3, gamma=0.99, buffer_size=5000,
                 batch_size=32, target_update=100):
        self.n_actions = n_actions
        self.gamma = gamma
        self.batch_size = batch_size
        self.target_update = target_update
        self.step_count = 0

        self.q_net = QNetwork(state_dim, n_actions, hidden)
        self.target_net = QNetwork(state_dim, n_actions, hidden)
        self.target_net.load_state_dict(self.q_net.state_dict())
        self.target_net.eval()

        self.optimizer = optim.Adam(self.q_net.parameters(), lr=lr)
        self.buffer = ReplayBuffer(buffer_size)

        # For ablation: toggle replay and target network
        self.use_replay = True
        self.use_target_net = True

    def select_action(self, state, epsilon):
        if np.random.random() < epsilon:
            return np.random.randint(self.n_actions)
        with torch.no_grad():
            state_t = torch.FloatTensor(state).unsqueeze(0)
            q_vals = self.q_net(state_t)
            return int(q_vals.argmax(dim=1).item())

    @staticmethod
    def _normalize(state):
        """Normalize state to [0,1] ranges."""
        s = state.copy().astype(np.float32)
        s[0] /= 4.0
        s[1] /= 4.0
        s[2] /= (2 * np.pi)
        return s

    def update(self, state, action, reward, next_state, done):
        s_norm = self._normalize(state)
        ns_norm = self._normalize(next_state)

        self.buffer.push(s_norm, action, reward, ns_norm, done)
        self.step_count += 1

        min_samples = self.batch_size if self.use_replay else 1
        if len(self.buffer) < min_samples:
            return

        if self.use_replay:
            states, actions, rewards, next_states, dones = \
                self.buffer.sample(self.batch_size)
        else:
            # No replay: train on most recent transition only
            states = np.array([s_norm])
            actions = np.array([action])
            rewards = np.array([reward], dtype=np.float32)
            next_states = np.array([ns_norm])
            dones = np.array([float(done)])

        states_t = torch.FloatTensor(states)
        actions_t = torch.LongTensor(actions)
        rewards_t = torch.FloatTensor(rewards)
        next_states_t = torch.FloatTensor(next_states)
        dones_t = torch.FloatTensor(dones)

        # Current Q-values for chosen actions
        q_values = self.q_net(states_t).gather(
            1, actions_t.unsqueeze(1)).squeeze(1)

        # Target Q-values
        with torch.no_grad():
            if self.use_target_net:
                next_q = self.target_net(next_states_t).max(dim=1)[0]
            else:
                next_q = self.q_net(next_states_t).max(dim=1)[0]
            targets = rewards_t + self.gamma * next_q * (1 - dones_t)

        loss = nn.MSELoss()(q_values, targets)
        self.optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        self.optimizer.step()

        # Update target network
        if self.use_target_net and \
                self.step_count % self.target_update == 0:
            self.target_net.load_state_dict(self.q_net.state_dict())

Training Loop

def train_dqn(use_replay=True, use_target_net=True,
              n_episodes=300, epsilon_start=1.0,
              epsilon_decay=0.985, epsilon_min=0.01, seed=42):
    """Train DQN agent. Supports ablation by toggling components."""
    np.random.seed(seed)
    torch.manual_seed(seed)

    env = ContinuousWarehouse()
    agent = DQNAgent()
    agent.use_replay = use_replay
    agent.use_target_net = use_target_net

    epsilon = epsilon_start
    rewards = []

    # Fill buffer with random experience first
    if use_replay:
        state = env.reset()
        for _ in range(500):
            action = np.random.randint(env.N_ACTIONS)
            next_state, reward, done = env.step(action)
            s_norm = DQNAgent._normalize(state)
            ns_norm = DQNAgent._normalize(next_state)
            agent.buffer.push(s_norm, action, reward, ns_norm, done)
            if done:
                state = env.reset()
            else:
                state = next_state

    for ep in range(n_episodes):
        state = env.reset()
        done = False
        total_reward = 0
        steps = 0

        while not done and steps < 200:
            action = agent.select_action(
                DQNAgent._normalize(state), epsilon)
            next_state, reward, done = env.step(action)
            agent.update(state, action, reward, next_state, done)
            state = next_state
            total_reward += reward
            steps += 1

        epsilon = max(epsilon_min, epsilon * epsilon_decay)
        rewards.append(total_reward)

    return agent, rewards

Full DQN Training

print("Training full DQN (replay + target network)...")
agent_full, rewards_full = train_dqn(
    use_replay=True, use_target_net=True)
Training full DQN (replay + target network)...

Ablation Study

We train three DQN variants to isolate the contribution of experience replay and the target network.

print("Training DQN without replay...")
_, rewards_no_replay = train_dqn(
    use_replay=False, use_target_net=True)

print("Training DQN without target network...")

    use_replay=True, use_target_net=False)

ax.plot(rolling_avg(rewards_full), label='Full DQN', alpha=0.8)
ax.plot(rolling_avg(rewards_no_replay), label='No Replay', alpha=0.8)

exe:policy-gradient-control.content:
Key implementation details:

The Gaussian policy requires computing \(\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\) analytically. For a Gaussian with mean \(\mu\) and std \(\sigma\):

  • \(\partial \log \pi / \partial \mu = (a - \mu) / \sigma^2\) — this is the "score function"
  • \(\partial \log \pi / \partial \log \sigma = (a - \mu)^2 / \sigma^2 - 1\)

The chain rule then gives the gradient with respect to the policy weights \(W\).

Common pitfalls:

  • Not normalizing returns in REINFORCE: without normalization, the gradient magnitudes vary wildly between episodes, causing unstable learning.
  • Using too large a learning rate for the actor: the policy can collapse to a deterministic (zero-std) policy before exploring enough. Keep the actor learning rate small (e.g., \(3 \times 10^{-4}\)) and the critic learning rate larger (e.g., \(10^{-2}\)).
  • Forgetting to clip actions to valid ranges before passing to the environment.

Expected results:

  • REINFORCE converges slowly with high variance in the learning curve. It may take 1500+ episodes to show consistent improvement.
  • Actor-critic converges 2–3\(\times\) faster with noticeably smoother learning curves, demonstrating the variance reduction from the critic baseline.
  • Both policies eventually learn to navigate toward the goal while avoiding the hazard, but the actor-critic policy is more consistent.
  • The linear policy may not achieve perfect performance (a neural network policy would do better), but it clearly demonstrates the algorithm mechanics.

Exercise 3 Solution: REINFORCE and Actor-Critic

Full solution for the policy gradient exercise ([@exe:policy-gradient-control]). We implement REINFORCE ([@def:reinforce]) and an actor-critic method ([@def:actor-critic]) on the continuous warehouse with continuous actions (thrust and steering).

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Continuous-Action Warehouse Environment

The robot controls thrust \(f \in [0, 1]\) and steering angle \(\delta \in [-\pi/4, \pi/4]\) directly ([@rl5:continuous-actions]).

class ContinuousActionWarehouse:
    """Warehouse with continuous state and continuous actions.

    State: (x, y, theta, v) in [0,4]^2 x [0,2pi) x [0,1]
    Action: (thrust, steering) in [0,1] x [-pi/4, pi/4]
    """

    def __init__(self, goal=(3.5, 3.5), hazard=(3.5, 2.5),
                 radius=0.4, noise_std=0.03):
        self.goal = np.array(goal)
        self.hazard = np.array(hazard)
        self.radius = radius
        self.noise_std = noise_std

    def reset(self):
        x = np.random.uniform(0.3, 0.7)
        y = np.random.uniform(0.3, 0.7)
        theta = np.random.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi)
        v = 0.0
        self.state = np.array([x, y, theta, v])
        return self.state.copy()

    def step(self, action):
        """Action = (thrust, steering) both clipped to valid ranges."""
        thrust = np.clip(action[0], 0.0, 1.0)
        steer = np.clip(action[1], -np.pi/4, np.pi/4)

        x, y, theta, v = self.state
        theta += steer + np.random.randn() * 0.02
        theta = theta % (2 * np.pi)
        v = np.clip(v * 0.8 + thrust * 0.4, 0.0, 1.0)

        noise = np.random.randn(2) * self.noise_std
        x += v * np.cos(theta) * 0.5 + noise[0]
        y += v * np.sin(theta) * 0.5 + noise[1]
        x = np.clip(x, 0.0, 4.0)
        y = np.clip(y, 0.0, 4.0)

        self.state = np.array([x, y, theta, v])
        pos = np.array([x, y])

        if np.linalg.norm(pos - self.goal) < self.radius:
            return self.state.copy(), 1.0, True
        elif np.linalg.norm(pos - self.hazard) < self.radius:
            return self.state.copy(), -1.0, True
        else:
            # Small reward for getting closer to goal
            dist = np.linalg.norm(pos - self.goal)
            return self.state.copy(), -0.01, False

    def normalize(self, state):
        s = state.copy()
        s[0] /= 4.0
        s[1] /= 4.0
        s[2] /= (2 * np.pi)
        return s

Gaussian Policy (NumPy)

The policy outputs mean \(\mu_\theta(s)\) and log-std \(\log\sigma_\theta(s)\) for a 2D Gaussian distribution ([@eq:gaussian-policy]). We implement a simple linear policy for clarity.

class GaussianPolicy:
    """Linear Gaussian policy: pi(a|s) = N(W_mu @ s + b_mu, exp(log_std)^2).

    Two outputs: (thrust_mean, steer_mean).
    """

    def __init__(self, state_dim=4, action_dim=2, lr=1e-3):
        self.state_dim = state_dim
        self.action_dim = action_dim
        self.lr = lr

        # Policy parameters
        scale = np.sqrt(2.0 / state_dim)
        self.W_mu = np.random.randn(action_dim, state_dim) * scale
        self.b_mu = np.zeros(action_dim)
        self.log_std = np.zeros(action_dim)  # learnable log-std

    def forward(self, state):
        """Compute action mean and std."""
        mu = self.W_mu @ state + self.b_mu
        std = np.exp(self.log_std)
        return mu, std

    def sample(self, state):
        """Sample action from the policy."""
        mu, std = self.forward(state)
        action = mu + std * np.random.randn(self.action_dim)
        return action, mu, std

    def log_prob(self, action, mu, std):
        """Compute log pi(a|s) for Gaussian."""
        var = std ** 2
        log_p = -0.5 * np.sum(
            ((action - mu) ** 2) / var + np.log(2 * np.pi * var))
        return log_p

    def update(self, grad_W_mu, grad_b_mu, grad_log_std):
        """Gradient ascent step."""
        self.W_mu += self.lr * grad_W_mu
        self.b_mu += self.lr * grad_b_mu
        self.log_std += self.lr * grad_log_std

REINFORCE

Monte Carlo policy gradient ([@def:reinforce]): collect a full episode, compute returns \(G_t\), and update using \(\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t|s_t) \cdot G_t\) ([@eq:policy-gradient-theorem]).

def reinforce(n_episodes=2000, gamma=0.99, lr=3e-4, seed=42):
    """Train REINFORCE on the continuous-action warehouse."""
    np.random.seed(seed)
    env = ContinuousActionWarehouse()
    policy = GaussianPolicy(lr=lr)
    rewards_history = []

    for ep in range(n_episodes):
        state = env.reset()
        states, actions, mus, stds, rewards = [], [], [], [], []
        done = False
        steps = 0

        while not done and steps < 200:
            s_norm = env.normalize(state)
            action, mu, std = policy.sample(s_norm)
            next_state, reward, done = env.step(action)

            states.append(s_norm)
            actions.append(action)
            mus.append(mu)
            stds.append(std)
            rewards.append(reward)

            state = next_state
            steps += 1

        # Compute returns
        H = len(rewards)
        returns = np.zeros(H)
        G = 0
        for t in reversed(range(H)):
            G = rewards[t] + gamma * G
            returns[t] = G

        # Normalize returns for stability
        if H > 1:
            returns = (returns - returns.mean()) / (returns.std() + 1e-8)

        # Compute policy gradients
        grad_W = np.zeros_like(policy.W_mu)
        grad_b = np.zeros_like(policy.b_mu)
        grad_log_std = np.zeros_like(policy.log_std)

        for t in range(H):
            s, a, mu, std = states[t], actions[t], mus[t], stds[t]
            var = std ** 2

            # d log pi / d mu = (a - mu) / var
            d_mu = (a - mu) / var  # (action_dim,)

            # d log pi / d W_mu = d_mu outer s
            grad_W += np.outer(d_mu, s) * returns[t]
            grad_b += d_mu * returns[t]

            # d log pi / d log_std = ((a-mu)^2/var - 1)
            grad_log_std += ((a - mu)**2 / var - 1) * returns[t]

        # Average over episode
        grad_W /= H
        grad_b /= H
        grad_log_std /= H

        policy.update(grad_W, grad_b, grad_log_std)
        rewards_history.append(sum(rewards))

    return policy, rewards_history

Actor-Critic

Reduce variance by using a learned baseline ([@def:actor-critic]). The critic estimates \(V(s)\) and the advantage \(\hat{A}_t = r + \gamma V(s') - V(s)\) ([@eq:advantage-td]) replaces \(G_t\).

class LinearCritic:
    """Linear value function approximation: V(s) = w^T s + b."""

    def __init__(self, state_dim=4, lr=1e-2):
        self.w = np.zeros(state_dim)
        self.b = 0.0
        self.lr = lr

    def predict(self, state):
        return self.w @ state + self.b

    def update(self, state, target):
        pred = self.predict(state)
        error = target - pred
        self.w += self.lr * error * state
        self.b += self.lr * error

def actor_critic(n_episodes=2000, gamma=0.99, lr_actor=3e-4,
                 lr_critic=1e-2, seed=42):
    """Train actor-critic on the continuous-action warehouse."""
    np.random.seed(seed)
    env = ContinuousActionWarehouse()
    policy = GaussianPolicy(lr=lr_actor)
    critic = LinearCritic(lr=lr_critic)
    rewards_history = []

    for ep in range(n_episodes):
        state = env.reset()
        done = False
        total_reward = 0
        steps = 0

        while not done and steps < 200:
            s_norm = env.normalize(state)
            action, mu, std = policy.sample(s_norm)
            next_state, reward, done = env.step(action)
            ns_norm = env.normalize(next_state)

            # TD error = advantage estimate
            if done:
                td_target = reward
            else:
                td_target = reward + gamma * critic.predict(ns_norm)
            advantage = td_target - critic.predict(s_norm)

            # Update critic
            critic.update(s_norm, td_target)

            # Update actor using advantage
            var = std ** 2
            d_mu = (action - mu) / var

            grad_W = np.outer(d_mu, s_norm) * advantage
            grad_b = d_mu * advantage
            grad_log_std = ((action - mu)**2 / var - 1) * advantage

            policy.update(grad_W, grad_b, grad_log_std)

            state = next_state
            total_reward += reward
            steps += 1

        rewards_history.append(total_reward)

    return policy, critic, rewards_history

Train Both Agents

print("Training REINFORCE...")
policy_reinforce, rewards_reinforce = reinforce(n_episodes=2000)

print("Training Actor-Critic...")
policy_ac, critic_ac, rewards_ac = actor_critic(n_episodes=2000)
Training REINFORCE...

Training Actor-Critic...

Learning Curves

Actor-critic converges faster and more smoothly than REINFORCE because the critic reduces the variance of the gradient estimates ([@cmt:actor-critic-unification]).

def rolling_avg(data, window=100):
    return np.convolve(data, np.ones(window)/window, mode='valid')

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.plot(rolling_avg(rewards_reinforce), label='REINFORCE', alpha=0.8)
ax.plot(rolling_avg(rewards_ac), label='Actor-Critic', alpha=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel('Episode')
ax.set_ylabel('Reward (rolling avg)')
ax.set_title('REINFORCE vs. Actor-Critic')
ax.legend()
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('policy_gradient_curves.svg', bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

Visualize Learned Policy

Sample the Gaussian policy deterministically (using the mean) at a grid of positions to show the thrust and steering fields.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))
titles = ['REINFORCE', 'Actor-Critic']
policies = [policy_reinforce, policy_ac]

grid_pts = np.linspace(0.5, 3.5, 8)

for ax, policy, title in zip(axes, policies, titles):
    for gx in grid_pts:
        for gy in grid_pts:
            state = np.array([gx, gy, 0.0, 0.5])
            s_norm = np.array([gx/4, gy/4, 0.0, 0.5])
            mu, _ = policy.forward(s_norm)
            # Interpret: mu[0]=thrust (magnitude), mu[1]=steering
            theta_act = mu[1]  # steering angle
            thrust = np.clip(mu[0], 0, 1)
            dx = thrust * np.cos(theta_act) * 0.2
            dy = thrust * np.sin(theta_act) * 0.2
            ax.annotate('', xy=(gx+dx, gy+dy), xytext=(gx, gy),
                        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->',
                                        lw=0.8 + thrust,
                                        color='#333333'))

    goal_c = plt.Circle((3.5, 3.5), 0.4, color='green', alpha=0.3)
    hazard_c = plt.Circle((3.5, 2.5), 0.4, color='red', alpha=0.3)
    ax.add_patch(goal_c)
    ax.add_patch(hazard_c)
    ax.text(3.5, 3.5, '+1', ha='center', va='center',
            fontweight='bold', color='green')
    ax.text(3.5, 2.5, '-1', ha='center', va='center',
            fontweight='bold', color='red')
    ax.set_xlim(0, 4)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 4)
    ax.set_aspect('equal')
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xlabel('x')
    ax.set_ylabel('y')
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.2)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('policy_gradient_fields.svg', bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

Final Performance

print(f"REINFORCE - last 200 episodes avg: "
      f"{np.mean(rewards_reinforce[-200:]):.3f}")
print(f"Actor-Critic - last 200 episodes avg: "
      f"{np.mean(rewards_ac[-200:]):.3f}")

Actor-Critic - last 200 episodes avg: -0.761

exe:final-rl.content:
(a) States: joint angles \((\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_6)\) plus end-effector position and possibly item location. Actions: 6-dimensional continuous vector of joint angle adjustments. The action space is continuous. The task is episodic (ends on pick, drop, or timeout).

(b) The state space is continuous (\(\mathbb{R}^6\) for joint angles alone), so there are uncountably many state-action pairs. A table cannot store values for continuous states — it would require infinite memory.

(c) DQN outputs one Q-value per action, which requires enumerating all possible actions. With continuous actions (\(\mathbb{R}^6\)), there are infinitely many — you cannot output a Q-value for each. The \(\arg\max\) over continuous \(a\) requires solving an inner optimization problem at every step, which has no closed form for a neural network.

(d) The action was better than expected: the critic predicted a return of 0.5 from state \(s\), but the actual outcome (reward 1.0 + nothing from terminal) was 1.0. The actor increases the probability of this action (and similar actions) at state \(s\), since it led to a better-than-expected outcome.
